Morgan Taking a step back, ever since the positive headlines around the Iran conflict in late March, both near- and medium-term Fed expectations began to reverse their moves as more easing was priced in (Figure 10). As we have done previously, we use our empirical fair value model (which incorporates the 3Mx3M/1Yx1Y OIS curve as a driver) to decompose recent curve moves into changes resulting from fundamental drivers to quantify the potential impact that this shift in Fed expectations may have had on swap yield curves. As Figure 11 shows, the decline in Fed expectations drove the majority of the steepen- ing of the yield curve, which our empirical model was able to capture directionally. Howev- er, curves further away from the front end, such as 2s/30s, steepened in excess of what our model would have implied, indicating that other factors (such as concerns around defense spending and Warsh’s upcoming confirmation hearing) could be steepening that part of the curve.

With load growth clearly starting to materialize, particularly in PJM, with growth over 3% YTD, conversations are focused on how to meet the moment, different avenues to get there, and alignment across federal, state, and local entities. One key bridge is behind-the-meter generation, where conversations suggest they are a near term solution, with long term potential to be a source of backup. Another is reform in PJM, with the reliability backstop procurement as a first step, and potential for broader reform to the capacity market framework. Finally, there remains focus on newbuild nuclear, and the requirements to derisk cost overrun potential, where federal support is needed. records.text: 2 Global Economic Weekly | 17 April 2026 Global Letter Claudio Irigoyen BofAS Antonio Gabriel BofAS The curious case of the Iran war The Iran war has sparked interesting questions on the observed price action of risk assets and its feedback into the real economy. Why is the US stock market trading back at pre-war levels? Why has gold sold off during the breakout of the war? Does the K- shaped dynamics of consumption make the US more resilient to supply shocks? We think stock markets learned the trade war playbook last year and the escalate to de- escalate strategy, which gets extrapolated as eventually a quick resolution to the war. In turn, lower gold prices can be rationalized as a combination of precautionary savings, insurance, and de-risking from speculative positions. This price action, coupled with the K-shaped economy, make the US economy more resilient (or vulnerable) to the oil shock. The curious case of the US stock market The stock market is trading back above pre-war levels, which is surprising given the still high degree of uncertainty regarding the potential outcome of the war. However, the stock market is trading as if the end of the war is near and its impact on the world economy second order. Moreover, the US stock market has been very resilient to the dynamics of the war since day one, with a peak to trough selloff of less than 10%. records.text: at the US and the EU could be optimising for different channels of AI value creation. The US frames AI as a geopolitical race. Its strategy is a private-sector-led model designed to lock in technological leadership (see America’s AI action plan, July 2025). This could let the US pull ahead quickly as AI production activity shows up faster in GDP. Faster adoption may amplify concentration on upstream developers and infrastructure owners, akin to the ICT revolution. By contrast, the EU could exploit AI to strengthen and harmonise the single market further, with gains arising through channels that are slower to appear in data. For instance, AI is a coordination and transaction-cost-compression technology. It reduces language barriers, synthesises legal systems, automates compliance and administration, and allows small firms to operate with the efficiency of larger organisations. When AI behaves ‘like’ electricity – diffusing broadly and enabling organisational redesign – returns accrue downstream. The gains emerge through adoption rather than invention. In this configuration, Europe stands to benefit materially. Since it starts with higher structural frictions, the marginal productivity gains for reducing them may be larger, though more gradual in translating into structural productivity improvements. records.text: Inflation up slightly, then down: Since we expect demand to rise faster than supply in the short run, inflation is likely to be slightly higher in the next few years (until 2028 or so) than in our baseline. It will take longer for inflation to benefit from higher productivity growth. While the nominee for the next Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, has argued that AI will lower inflation significantly, remarks from current chair, Jerome Powell, are consistent with our results. Resilient labour market: Our results also show a resilient labour market. Our pure model output suggest that the unemployment rate remains broadly unchanged relative to our baseline as the positive demand shock compensates for the job-replacing effect stemming from stronger productivity. In a nutshell, our modelling shows that the economy is not a zero-sum game. As there is more aggregate demand, demand for labour follows. However, we think our model output might underestimate the labour market strength. If technology increases output per worker (i.e. if AI turns out to be job augmenting), companies might respond by hiring more as they perceive a reduction in the marginal cost to increasing their output. records.text: More broadly, we think Warsh could suggest a comprehensive review of the Fed’s balance sheet and implementation policies and emphasize that the process of implementing any changes could take years. By way of background, Warsh has been consistently critical of the Fed’s active use of its balance sheet over the past ~15 years. Although he supported the Fed’s initial foray into QE in response to the GFC, he cautioned that later programs were not appropriate, possibly raising inflation and financial stability risks, as well as moving the Fed away from its core duties and into credit allocation policies that could distort markets. As he noted recently, “I worried mightily in the summer and fall of 2010 – a time of strong growth and financial stability – that the decision to buy more treasury bonds — would involve the Fed in the messy political business of fiscal policy. QE2 was announced. I disagreed with the decision, and resigned from the Fed soon after.”1 With respect to portfolio composition, the Fed is reducing its MBS holdings by reinvesting into T -bills and could speed that process with MBS sales. The Committee has not yet settled on a target steady-state Treasury portfolio, and we see reasonable prospe cts that under Warsh it could choose one that is significantly shorter-dated than the universe outstanding. Such stability is a good contrast compared with the price action in 2025, when 10s20s (and 10s30s) were much more sensitive to the central bank being ‘behind the curve’ and steepened fast to over 75bp (12bp steeper than now), although poor supply/demand balance was also another significant reason for the steepening. BoJ’s Communication Strategy: Avoiding Surprises If the BoJ’s recent communication was intended to prepare the market for a rate hike pause this month, it appears to reflect a strong commitment to “minimizing surprises in policy announcements”—a lesson learned from July 2024. At the July 2024 meeting, the BoJ raised rates from 0.10% to 0.25%, but with only about 35% probability priced in a week before the meeting, the decision surprised the market. Governor Ueda’s press conference included a hawkish remark: “With real interest rates still deeply negative, I don’t think a strong brake will be applied to the economy,” which contrib- uted to the so-called “Ueda shock” in early August, marked by a sharp drop in equities and a stronger yen. While the main trigger was a much weaker-than-expected US jobs report on August 2, criticism of the surprise rate hike grew, prompting the BoJ to place greater empha- sis on market communication. In terms of HICP impact, Spain stands out with a relatively large package combining V AT and excise cuts, the suspension of certain energy taxes, fuel rebates, and targeted industry support. These measures are complemented by steps to protect vulnerable households and increase flexibility in energy contracts. The package announced by the Italian and German govern- ments will also impact near-term inflation significantly, by directly reducing fuel prices. Meanwhile, the French response will likely have a modest impact on HICP prices. France has announced targeted support for companies facing difficulties in the transport, fishing and agricultural sectors. The govern- ment is also working on measures aimed at controlling fuel distributors’ margins. The French response contrasts with the 2022 episode. France at the time provided strong and direct support to consumers and producers by lowering gas and electricity prices, at a large fiscal cost. records.text: US Economic Perspectives17 April 2026 ab 26 US Economic Perspectives UBS Research Comparison to the forecast models As with most Phillips curve style models, our models were unable to forecast the inflation as it surged upward in 2021-2022 and, as expected, the majority of models were not a good guide as inflation has fallen. (Note that in the early part of 2022, the core PCE price inflation time-varying trend models and the component model remained above 4% throughout the forecast horizon, which at that point went through the end of 2024, compared to the 2.8% that has been published for 2024 inflation.) In particular, the models do not include an effect for changes in the mix of demand and the supply constraints that hampered efforts to satisfy this changing mix. We believe the combined effects of the changing demand mix and supply issues were far more important in driving the initial inflation surge in 2021 than were the standard Phillips curve driver of aggregate resource slack, though fiscal spending and monetary policy have likely accounted for a fair amount of the reason that inflation did not fall faster from that peak. Our forecast models have revised up notably this month as we have rolled forward to taking 2026Q1 as data. records.text: And first there was light: The electrification revolution took place between 1890 and 1929 in some European countries (e.g. the UK and Germany) and the US. We use the UK as reference, as it has more economic data than the US for this period. We measure that the early stage of electrification boosted UK TFP growth by around 30bp y/y and the late stage by around 80bp. When measuring TFP acceleration in this period for the US, we noticed bigger results. However, lack of data for the late 19th century might cause an upward bias, as might a different regulatory environment. Great volatility: The 40-year period of UK electrification starts in the late Victorian period and ends at the doorstep of the Great Depression, with WWI in between, so there is a lot of noise in the data. In this period, GDP expanded on average 1.6% y/y in the UK, with few years of output contraction up until the end of WWI. In the first 10 years of this period, investment rose by 25%, keeping significant momentum up until the war. While impressive, current US investment is outpacing this period, with a 10% increase in GFCF since 2023, and almost a 40% increase in AI-associated investment. This stark difference could be in part explained by the UK’s 1882 Electric Lighting Act, which constrained early investment (Kennedy and Delargy, 2025). We doubt the FOMC, given the uncertainty, wants to upgrade the assessment of the labor market and then be proven wrong before the June meeting. "Available indicators suggest that economic activity has been expanding at a solid pace. Job gains have remained low, and the unemployment rate has been little changed in recent months. Inflation remains somewhat elevated." "The Committee seeks to achieve maximum employment and inflation at the rate of 2 percent over the longer run. Uncertainty about the economic outlook remains elevated. The implications of developments in the Middle East for the U.S. economy are uncertain. The Committee is attentive to the risks to both sides of its dual mandate." Two good examples of this methodology are Acemoglu, 2024, and Tamkin and McCrory, 2025. Though the two studies employ comparable methodology, they reach different results due to different assumptions on time/saving and AI scope of application. Acemoglu estimates a meagre impact of AI on GDP (barely detectible in the short run), while Tamkin and McCrory show more sizeable results (nearly doubling the current long-term growth rate of labour productivity). While these papers focus exclusively on the productivity impact on AI, we are interested in the broader macro implications and take into account how the discovery of the technology gives rise to a significant sentiment boost (see page 14). Moreover, these studies do not account for further improvements in AI itself. Admittedly, Tamkin and McCrory are candid about this limitation in their approach and argue that their results – which are already higher than others – are subject to this upside risk. Both limitations make us more confident in our historical approach. Its main drawback is on its empirical calibration, which we think is compensated by our usage of a macroeconomic general equilibrium model, NiGEM. How we built our framework: We seek to bridge this gap with a two-step assessment of the potential productivity shock from AI between 2025 and 2034. ▪ We find historical parallels in major technological revolutions of other general- purpose technologies: electrification (1891–1929) and information and communication technology (1980–2004). We see these past experiences as the best comparators for the AI revolution, given their importance and their need for significant capex ahead of deployment. The assumptions we use are detailed in the Key drivers section below. Central to our modelling is our assumption that economic agents foresee the possible benefits of deploying AI, allowing us to replicate the sentiment boost that fuelled a stock market rally and strong capex in both 2025 and the late 1990s. For our systemic review of past productivity booms – including productivity metrics and other macroeconomic variables – see Historical approach. ▪ We apply the productivity gains measured in the past two eras to a macro- economic model (NiGEM) to simulate the impact on current economic conditions. We check whether our results broadly match history and explain the narrative as much as the numbers. We show a range of results on the basis of the two past tech revolutions. records.text: US Economics Weekly17 April 2026 ab 3 US Economics Weekly UBS Research Economic Comment: April FOMC meeting Oddly, not a lot has changed since the March meeting. Energy prices are still higher than they were before. Labor market trends don't look that different. However, that things haven't fallen apart is a data point in itself. The S&P 500 was roughly 6700 the days ahead of the March meeting and sits above 7100 as of this writing. The unemployment rate fell back to 4.3% in March, not much above the longer-run rate and initial and continuing claims remain low. Altogether, that would be unlikely to make the April meeting somehow more dovish than the March meeting, although there is another week to go. Not all the incoming data has been great, looking at the estimates of real consumer spending for January and February, for example, and the backup in mortgage rates will likely weigh on housing activity to some degree. Nominal wage growth cooled further in March, and the unemployment rate was helped by the shift of individuals to out of the labor force. If the LFPR had held steady in March, the unemployment rate would be 4.51%, and the two months of employment data together would average just 24K jobs per month. But at the very least, none of the concern that appeared in the March FOMC meeting minutes has been realized, at least not yet. That said we doubt there is much change in communication. PPI review: firm passthrough to PCE While the headline PPI measures came in softer than expected, details that affect core PCE were firmer than we had penciled in. records.text: M Idea 2 Interest Rate Strategy Japan | Japanese Investor Trends in FY2026 MORGAN STANLEY MUFG SECURITIES CO., L TD. Hiromu Uezato hiromu.uezato@morganstanleymufg.com +81 3 6836-8431 Koichi Sugisaki koichi.sugisaki@morganstanleymufg.com +81 3 6836-8428 Japanese Lifers: Even Higher Super-Long Yields Will Not Bring Them Back as Structural Buyers This week, we published a report with our Financials Equity Analysts and Credit/ Securitized Products Strategists on the evolution of Japanese lifers' investment behavior (see Japan Macro Strategy, Financials, and US Credit/Securitized Products Strategy: What Major Changes Involving Japan's Lifers and Households Mean For Fixed Income Markets (15 Apr 2026)). The core message of the report is that Japanese lifers are no longer the same structural, price-insensitive buyers of super-long JGBs they once were. We also do not agree with the view that, because yields on super-long JGBs have risen, Japanese lifers will turn back into buyers. Our view is supported by four key pillars: preparation for new regulatory framework, demographics, insurance sales trends, and changes in household preferences. For many years, lifers carried an Asset-Liability duration mismatch, with asset duration shorter than liability duration. Today, that gap has largely closed (see Exhibit 1 ) through: continued purchases of super-long JGBs, the use of swaps and swaptions, and asset-side repositioning ahead of Japan's new Economic Value-Based Solvency Ratio (ESR) frame

While these considerations are not directly reflected in the model, they influence our conditioning assumptions. Overall, although the total impact on GDP from the AI shock is smaller than in the US, improvements in productivity could help to alleviate price pressures over time. Demand shock first, followed by supply: We estimate that the level of UK GDP will be 3.5% higher than the counterfactual after 10 years. Initially, the improvement in growth is the result of a demand shock tied to UK wealth effects – our modelling suggests a stronger impact through this channel than in the eurozone. In the medium term, the improvement in productivity growth becomes more evident, paving the way for a positive supply shock (Figure 79). That said, uncertainty remains around the size of the shock and the impact on productivity, so we model a range of scenarios. The least impactful scenario, consistent with first stage ICT, would imply a 1.2% increase in both the level of TFP and GDP. records.text: KRW: From Headwinds to tailwinds. The KRW has been one of the laggards in n Asian FX this year, underpinned by persistent portfolio outflows from domestic and institutional investors. That underperformance persisted through the Iran War, which reflects South Korea’s sensitivity to energy imports as well as its correlation to global risk appetite. However, over the past 10 days, since the ceasefire announcement, the Won has rebounded and has outperformed Asian FX peers (along with MYR, which is positively leveraged to energy). Apart from the move lower in oil and rebound in risk sentiment, two other tailwinds are also pertinent. First, the government’s Management Committee for National Pension Service (NPS) announced that it would raise the strategic FX hedging ratio on its overseas investments from 10% to 15% and this level would be “baseline” as opposed to an upper cap. Previously, the NPS had a 10% cap for strategic FX hedging and 5% cap for tactical FX hedging (while the exact breakdown is not disclosed). Operationally, a permanent sub-committee (including MOEF and BOK) would be involved in discussing forex hedging and macro implications of NPS investments. The intention is that FX hedging would become more flexible around the new higher baseline with room to move it above and below that level. records.text: Many of the ‘jobpocalypse’ claims about AI have been made without support of empirical evidence or a clear theoretical framework. History has shown that despite fears, technology shocks have led to the creation of new jobs and tasks. If during the industrial revolution textile workers lost jobs due to automation of spinning and weaving machines, new roles appeared to operate and maintain said machines. This has been true for other innovation waves, the latest being the ICT and internet revolution, which, despite making some retail jobs obsolete, created demand for web developers, digital specialists and a plethora of roles in the new digital economy. So, despite some worker reallocation being likely with AI, history suggests that the net employment impact should be small. records.text: Analyzing the Potential Impact of Robotaxis on Uber & Lyft We view the rise of autonomous vehicles as having the opportunity to drive incremental industry growth, rather than be a zero-sum game. Within the rideshare industry, several friction points exist which could be solved by robotaxis today and on a longer-term time horizon (with lower prices - Exhibit 45). While autonomous vehicles provide an alternative to human rideshare today, we do not view the AV market as being fully disruptive of the industry (on the supply side), given a few key factors: Operating zones. Despite Waymo expanding its commercial operating zone by more n than 10x over the last four years, the company still operates on a small scale. Relative to the square mileage of the top 25 metro markets (based on the Census Bureau’s definition of metro markets & regions ranked by population), Waymo’s operating zone today represents <5% of this opportunity (Exhibit 46). Operational design & domain limitations. While AV technology and fleet n capabilities continue to improve, scaling operations often takes time due to ongoing city-mapping and ODD constraints. For example, Waymo announced Austin testing in August 2023 and did not fully roll out to the public (through their partnership with Uber) until early 2025. It is likely that in markets with more severe climates/regions where weather conditions & other driving patterns fluctuate, the commercial launch (and scaling) could take a longer amount of time. Looking ahead, a rebound in inventory investment is expected following the large negative contribution seen this time around. Furthermore, housing investment, which fell sharply due to institutional factors in Q3, is likely to recover. Companies are actively investing to address labor shortages and rebuild supply chains in response to tariffs, and we continue to expect consumption to recover gradually on support from large wage increases and easing inflation. That said, the surge in crude oil prices stemming from the Middle East conflict is likely to exert some downside pressure on the economy, particularly on consumption. As the magnitude and duration of higher crude oil prices could cause the adverse impact on the economy to evolve over time, careful monitoring is warranted. On the price front, we expect CPI inflation excluding perishables (core) to ease as a trend, albeit with fluctuations, in the near term due mainly to declines (y/y base effects) in goods, especially food. However, inflation is increasingly sticky, suggesting any deceleration will be more moderate than we previously expected. Against this backdrop, we have removed our lone Fed rate cut from this year and now see the Fed on an indefinite hold near neutral. Growth: Oil drag versus fiscal and FCI boost We have modestly lowered our growth forecast this year, with Q4/Q4 real GDP growth now projected at 2. 3% (down from 2.4% previously). This downgrade reflects the drag from higher oil prices ( roughly -0.2pp) as well as weaker consumer spending to start the year counterbalanced by continued tailwinds for growth (see Impact of oil price shocks a "frack"-tion of what they once were, Into the danger zone? Nonlinearities between oil prices and growth and How big of an oil shock can the Big Beautiful Bill handle?). These tailwinds include: supportive financial conditions, fiscal policy (larger tax refunds), robust productivity, and a continued strong pace of AI investments. Our growth forecast assumes oil prices broadly follow DB’s commodity team’s expectations that Brent will remain elevated in the near -term before moderating towards $75-80 per barrel by year end. The most notable risk to this forecast is a further escalation in Iran which leads to a more severe and protracted oil price shock. The St. Louis Fed already points to generative AI positively affecting US GDP (see Rubinto and Patro, 2026) while evidence of these effects elsewhere is scarce. Europe less well-positioned: Our modelling shows positive impacts on the eurozone and the UK as well, although to a significantly smaller extent than in the US, with GDP higher by 1.9% and 3.5%, respectively, than our baseline in 2034. These model results reflect the different economic structures across these geographies. The UK is a services-based economy where AI adoption can be widespread, but its tech sector is smaller than in the US and its labour market less flexible. The eurozone lags behind due both to the limited GDP share of tech services (and services in general) and a more rigid labour market, which makes technology shocks slower to feed through. Again, these results broadly match the historical experience of the ICT revolution, when the US pulled ahead of Europe. Our range on the Sep26 SEK-EUR 3M FRA spread was premised on a world in which the energy shock was actively widening the inflation differential between the Euro area and Sweden, and in which the ECB would consequently need to tighten more aggressively than the Riksbank. Swe- den's more favourable inflation starting point and better energy security meant the Riks- bank's response would be comparatively limited, and the spread would narrow as the market priced this asymmetry. Several developments have shifted this dynamic. First, the ceasefire has reduced the energy price impulse that was the primary driver of the asymmetric repricing across the two mar- kets. Second, the ECB itself has turned less hawkish, with our economists pushing back the expected hike path from April/July to June/September and flagging risks skewed to less tightening or potentially a full look-through. In other words, the asymmetric central bank response that was to drive the narrowing is now less pronounced on both sides: the Riksbank faces even less pressure to hike given the domestic data, while the ECB has itself stepped back from imminent tightening. And third, current valuations are not supportive either. With both legs of the trade moving in the same direction and the spread already towards the bot- tom end of our range, we turn neutral on the cross market spread at the front-end. But this phrase, "We are balancing these two goals in a situation where the risks to the labor market are to the downside—which would call for lower rates—and the risks to inflation are to the upside—which would call for higher rates, or not cutting, anyway," suggests the hawkish reaction is just not cutting, does that change? For this FOMC, the next move could be either a hike or a cut. In that sense a balanced risk assessment might be appropriate, and we give it close to even odds that happens this meeting. Inertia probably leaves the sentiment similar to what Chair Powell voiced in March, not cutting for a while is the hawkish option to try first. We do not think they are close to hiking. We think more evidence would need to accumulate that says hiking would be the right tool for the job before the bulk of the FOMC considers doing so. We're not there yet. Even as it is, they may not want higher rates to weigh on housing markets, and the economy and labor market still face downside risks. records.text: Stocks in Focus GOOGL (covered by Eric Sheridan) - We see Alphabet as positively exposed to multiple aspects of the AI theme scaling in the coming years across both consumer and enterprise computing. In addition, we see the mgmt team as remaining focused on striking a balance between growth investments and balance across operational efficiencies. In terms of Alphabet’s exposure to physical AI/autonomous vehicles, we view the company to be well positioned, as Waymo is currently the largest AV operator in the US, making over 500,000 paid trips per week as of March 2026. We are Buy rated on GOOGL. Our 12-month PT of $400 is based on an equal blend of (1) EV/GAAP EBIT applied to our NTM + 1 year estimates and (2) a modified DCF using EV/FCF-SBC multiple applied to our NTM + 4 years estimates discounted back 3 years. Key risks include: a) competition of product utility levels and advertising dollars; b) headwinds to monetizable (product) search from industry disruption; c) shifting media consumption habits; d) heavy investments depress operating margins for longer than our forecasts; e) no/low levels of incremental shareholder returns going forward; & f) regulatory scrutiny and industry practices altering the business model’s prospects. In addition, Alphabet is exposed to the volatility caused by the global macroeconomic environment and investor risk appetite for growth stocks. Among trusts that trade under 190bp (the top half of our sample), we see two trusts that are relatively well diversified with no tenants accounting for more than 30% of total revenue, one trust with a singular large tenant accounting for 40% of revenue and otherwise solid diversification, two trusts where a single tenant makes up more than 75% of total revenue, and two trusts with limited information publicly available about their tenants. It is becoming increasingly common for large “hyperscale” tenants to account for the lion’s share of revenue brought in by datacenter master trusts. Notably, “hyperscale” tenants within trusts are typically defined by their power needs and are not necessarily interchangeable with the “ AI hyperscaler” companies currently dominating headlines. Issuer track record is the best predictor of spreads presently We believe the market values issuer track record more than fundamentals and tenant composition. In other words, central banks sell gold to finance FX intervention to support domestic currencies (i.e. Türkiye) and governments sell gold to address their liquidity needs (i.e. Gulf States). As much as precautionary savings are used when someone lose its job, gold is supposed to sell off when the geopolitical event occurs. The curious case of K-shaped consumption Private consumption in the US has generally been quite resilient. A potential explanation is the wealth effects in a K-shaped economy. The strong rally in financial and real assets of the last few years disproportionately benefits high- and middle-income households that have higher exposure to these assets. In turn, households in the low-income brackets are under pressure, but they represent just 15% of consumer spending. We have shown in a recent report that the US economy has become less sensitive to the stagflationary effects of oil shocks (see The economy is more resilient to oil shocks ). A natural question that follows is whether K-shaped consumption dynamics make the economy more or less resilient to an oil shock. The answer is not just a function of the size but most importantly the persistence of the shock. However, a deeper dive reveals more vulnerabilities in foreign demand than indicated by the headlines. More specifically, Treasury demand has slowed since Liberation Day in two particular groups of countries: the BRIC nations and Europe. Demand from Asia also has slowed. The above blocs were sizable buyers of Treasuries over the last two decades. Figure 1 and Figure 2 show a clear inflection point in net Treasury holdings for Brazil, India and China since April 2025. (Russia’s holdings have been at zero since 2022.) Similarly, demand from France and Norway – two of Europe’s three biggest buyers of Treasuries – has dropped to nearly net zero in that span. It’s not clear if demand from these sources will return to Treasuries, especially with higher yields and issuance in Europe and Japan. Foreign demand for US Treasury debt has waned since Liberation Day in 2025, weakening in BRIC countries and even Europe. This is akin to the ICT revolution, which led to the dominance of a few US-based firms. As a scale-driven network technology, like other tech products, AI rewards integrated markets, deep capital pools, platform dominance and hyperscale ecosystems. When this dimension dominates, returns tend to concentrate upstream among developers and infrastructure owners. In this configuration, the US holds a structural advantage, creating more upside risks in the short term. Its advantages in upstream AI production, capital market depth, integrated scale, and infrastructure speed allow it to convert technological momentum into growth more quickly. Potentially manageable bubble: As studied in the case of the ICT revolution, there is a risk that the euphoria around AI translates into unsustainable equity market valuations that eventually lead to a stock market crash (see Tail risks 2026: BNP Paribas grey-swan analysis, dated 12 February). While the dot.com bubble is indeed a cautionary tale of this, our study of that period (see page 29) also highlights that the stock market crash did not prevent a continued acceleration in productivity. records.text: the shift in the marginal buyer of MBS Last week, we lowered our forecasts for agency MBS net issuance in 2026 to $225 billion, largely driven by the recent back-up in mortgage rates impacting the spring home-buying season. At the same time, the rate back-up should support MBS demand from domestic banks and overseas investors. Based on H.8 data, we estimate that domestic banks added around $42 billion of agency MBS during Q1 2026 (Exhibit 2). Similarly, overseas investors were net buyers of roughly $26 billion during January and February 2026 (Exhibit 3). Notably, most demand came from smaller holders, as three of the top four overseas holders (Japan, China, and Canada) saw their holdings decrease. In aggregate, we estimate that the money manager community experienced a decline in their agency MBS holdings during Q1 (Exhibit 4). Consistent with this observation, we note that several major money managers cut their agency MBS overweights in February. For the funds we track, we estimate that the aggregate overweight position declined from around 12 points to around 7 points. The decline was likely driven by the tighter spread levels earlier in the year. However, the timely decline may have helped the money manager community to weather March’s widening more effectively. records.text: RMBS HEIs continue to trade wide to CES Structure of HEI deals: Amongst the smaller segments of the RMBS market is the Home Equity Investment (HEI) deals, which have seen an uptick in issuance in recent years (Exhibit 5). HEI contracts are structured as junior lien loans where the homeowner (borrower) obtains an up-front, lump-sum cash payment. In return, HEI borrowers do not make any monthly debt payments but instead agree to provide the investor (lender) with a single future payment that is determined as a pre-fixed share of the home’s value at loan maturity/termination. This structure is relatively unique and has some resemblance with reverse mortgages. The proceeds from HEI resemble an equity-like payoff structure, as the loan’s intrinsic value is based on the realized home price appreciation/depreciation between issuance and repayment. HEI contracts are pooled together and securitized as HEI RMBS deals. Although borrowers do not make periodic payments, investors receive monthly interest payments from these HEI deals. Interest payments are funded by a cash account that is composed mainly of ongoing proceeds from HEI buyouts “Collections” and a “Reserve Fund.” The Reserve fund is financed from sale proceeds on the deal closing date and holds a minimum balance to cover interest payments and additional expenses for a pre-determined number of months. Stronger growth and a stable labour market do not require governments to expand their budgets. In fact, our results suggest an improvement in budget ratios across the main economies analysed. However, if labour markets are more disrupted than we assume, causing a bigger decrease in the labour share of income than expected in our model, there is a risk of a worsening of government balances, as profits tend to be taxed at a lower average rate than labour income (see Figure 30). In practice, we think this shock will require a significant role for fiscal and industrial policy, a point we made in Global economic impact of AI: The future is coming faster on 30 October 2023. Our bias is that actions will be redistributive in nature; but how they are engineered will depend on the market structure that AI firms settle into. Reinventing welfare: If a few firms end up holding significant market power on the provision of AI services and reap quasi-monopolistic profits, the chance of a more interventive fiscal policy is higher, in our view. This chance is further bolstered in the short term if AI causes big job losses, either at an aggregate or sectoral level. He has quoted AI’s possibility of sustaining annual GDP growth of 10–20% (see The adolescence of technology: Confronting and overcoming the risks of powerful AI, 2026). Economic models already struggle to make perfect predictions in a linear world. An exponential system where technology can improve itself is much harder to model – a challenge we try to overcome by using past examples of unprecedented shocks, such as the advent of electricity and ICT. A more extreme version would be the so-called technological singularity, which the Dallas Fed has described as AI surpassing human intelligence, leading to rapid and unpredictable changes (Wynne and Derr, 2025): “Under a benign version of this scenario, machines get smarter at a rapidly increasing rate, eventually gaining the ability to produce everything, leading to a world in which the fundamental economic problem, scarcity, is solved. […] Under a less benign version of this scenario, machine intelligence overtakes human intelligence at some finite point in the near future, the machines become malevolent, and this eventually leads to human extinction.” Fig. 9: BNP Paribas central case for AI impact and historic scenarios for US total factor productivity *Central scenario is computed as average of early and late-stage electricity. Rates, Inflation, and the Role of Bonds [00:04] Francis Yared: Sure. Let me start by making the point that the starting point, that is, where we were at the end of February, was probably overemphasizing the risk associated with the economy and monetary policy beyond what the subsequent data has justified. In a nutshell, if you look at the data we have so far, you're looking at an environment where inflation is going to be above target for the foreseeable future. On the labor market side, you have an environment where monetary policy is arguably not restrictive, fiscal policy is getting easier, and that's being reflected in the labor market, which is stabilizing. From that perspective, it's difficult to economically justify rate cuts from the Fed. So, moving back to pricing 2 to 4 cuts, which was the case prior to the conflict, is a little difficult, even if you leave the conflict aside. records.text: tly because oil transactions occur in USDs. One risk is to this equilibrium is that large FDI into the US promised by the GCC fall short following the war. The GCC has promised around USD 380bn of FDI per year through to 2035. The market may already view these targets as unrealistic and as such we don’t think FDI commitments not being realised in and of themselves will be sufficient to materially weaken the USD. Instead in the case of GCC we think de-dollarization would primarily manifest through non-USD oil trade (see pages XX-XX) and in the case of Norway a reduction in US asset holdings (see page XX). A change in the composition of energy trade in non-USD FX could result in a reduction of US asset exposure for oil exporters. In case of the GCC, it could also put into question existing outbound US FDI commitments. Oil exporters naturally tend to have large current account surpluses. As a result these countries have over the years accumulated large Net International Investment Positions (NIIP). Historically, a significant proportion of these large NIIPs reflect US asset holdings. One risk to this equilibrium is if the portion of oil traded in USDs begins to decline, resulting in fewer USD liabilities and with that less of a need to hold USD assets across reserves and sovereign wealth funds. We discuss this dynamic further on page XX. Additionally large FDI into the US promised by the GCC could be re-assessed The bloc has promised around USD380bn/year of FDI through to 2035.

records.text: US Economic Perspectives17 April 2026 ab 7 The risks over the next year or so: The risk is that AI investment continues to surge and the impacts on higher electricity prices and higher computer chip prices intensify. Additionally, higher costs for these items could push into higher prices for other items as electricity and memory chips are used widely as inputs for other goods and services. It is notable that in recent days Microsoft announced price increases for its Surface computer lines by around 25% compared to a year ago. The longer-run potential downward impact of AI inflation: Beyond the next year or so the impacts of AI are likely to be downward on inflation through a combination of labor market disruption and higher productivity. We note that in the late 1990s when productivity gains from computer adoption was showing up in the macroeconomic data, both inflation fell and wage growth rose for a few years. Overall risks are to inflation, and particularly goods prices, are to the upside of our forecast over the next year or so. However, over time as the impacts of each of these drivers of higher inflation begins to have second-round effect and broaden out beyond a handful of categories, it will be difficult to pin down whether the higher inflation is related to lagged effects of higher crude oil prices. higher tariffs, AI adoption, or something else. The study is part of our ongoing Big Data exercise over the years, now totaling 8.2 million trades ($4.8tn notional) from CLOs. While sales of AI-impacted assets unsurprisingly accelerated earlier this year, we are seeing managers pivot to de-risking in sectors directly affected by inflation and geopolitical risks. • AI-related sectors such as Technology saw a rise in US CLO sales activity of +4.5% in February, but then dropped by -2.5% in March. While demand from other investor groups is expected to surpass that of money managers—an unprecedented occurrence during calendar years when the Federal Reserve’s MBS holdings were in run-off mode—we do not consider this a signal that MBS spreads will necessarily tighten. GSEs have effectively become the new marginal buyers, and their demand could be quite spread sensitive as well. With banks primarily focused on CMO floaters, their demand is also largely spread sensitive. This is very different from the pre-SVB era when banks were largely yield-focused. Hence, it appears that the spread policing role played by money managers will be transferred to other investors. Origination volumes should experience a seasonal pickup over the coming weeks before peaking in June. This provides us with unbiased parallels that evidence the extent, shape and speed of productivity increases. We also study the broader economic context of the time, beyond the pure productivity gains. For example, we learn the importance of accounting for sentiment effects in our modelling, as they played an important role in the ICT revolution, especially in the 1990s dot.com era. The electricity revolution provides useful lessons too. Electrification started to spread in the US and parts of Europe in very volatile times, when economies were affected by World War I and even high inflation at some points. Despite these shocks, productivity growth accelerated. The parallel with today’s world is telling, even if current volatility falls short of the shock of WWI. Finally, the electricity revolution is an example of how to ‘manage’ the spread of a technology such that its benefits accrue mostly to consumers and not only a few companies. Economics US Economic Perspectives Date 16 April 2026 Outlook update: The (oil) drumbeat of war Introduction We entered 2026 with a constructive view on the economy. Our narrative was that headwinds from the historic trade policy and tariff shock from 2025 were likely to fade over the course of this year as tariff rates fell and that growth tailwinds were set to strengthen from monetary and fiscal policy, financial conditions, robust productivity and AI-related investment. While these pillars of our outlook have largely materialized as expected , the economy has been dealt another adverse shock from a spike in oil prices precipitated by the war in Iran. Our baseline is that as long as oil prices have peaked and are on a slow downward trajectory over the coming months, the economy is likely to weather another substantial shock relatively well. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 17 April 2026 13 Core inflation is likely to move up from 3.2% to 3.3% (20bps above the BoE’s forecast) with services inflation rising from 4.3% to 4.4% (30bps above the BoE’s forecast) and core goods flat at 1.3%. The decline in clothing inflation should offset the rise in core goods ex clothing inflation. Within services we expect airfares inflation to move higher and core services (ex-airlines, packaged holidays and education) to move somewhat lower from 4.3% to 4.2%. records.text: Michael Metcalfe 15 April 2026 1 Insights Classification: Complimentary Material Developed Markets Strategy Weekly : USD unwind unwound KEY THEMES THIS WEEK: Safety or just risk reduction. This time last year, the USD’s performance during volatile equity markets led many, ourselves included, to question the currency’s safe-haven status. So the fact that the USD was the best performing currency in a very turbulent March this year should have been more reassuring. But moves by investors to get back to benchmark may have flattered the USD’s performance. Our indicators show that asset managers came into March 2026 with a significant USD underweight position. Reducing risk therefore meant buying back this underweight rapidly. A process that now looks to be largely complete after the longest (32-day) consecutive run of USD purchases since November 2024 came to an end on 8th April. Tail wind not tail risk hedge. We regress TIPS index returns on benchmark-level carry and carry-adjusted real yield series to assess pricing relationships. To start, contemporaneous carry-adjusted real-rate repricing is the dominant driver of month- to-month variation in TIPS index returns. The estimated real yield sensitivities rise monotonically with maturity, at approximately -2.6 for the 5y bucket, -4.4 for the 10y bucket, and -8.0 for the 30y bucket; this makes perfect sense and is basically real yield duration at play. These magnitudes align with intuition, confirm that exposure to real-rate movements increases sharply along the curve, and explain the bulk of the volatility in TIPS index returns. In these projections, the most important points are the government's new fiscal targets: the government debt-to-GDP ratio and the primary balance (fiscal balance minus net interest payments). Three scenarios are presented in these projections, but the two realistic ones in our view are the "past trend case" and the "growth transition case" (the third, "high growth case," seems overly optimistic). In the "past trend case," the debt-to-GDP ratio will not continue to decline, whereas in the "growth transition case," a downward trend persists. As for the primary balance, both cases project a shift to surplus from FY2027 (with the growth transition case assuming an average nominal growth rate of 3.0% over the next decade, and the past trend case assuming 1.4%). The Takaichi administration is expected to adopt the "growth transition case." We believe it would present a primary balance near -1% over the next five years. This indicates that even with a fiscal deficit increase of 1–2.5 ppt of GDP compared to current assumptions, the debt-to-GDP ratio would decline, albeit at a slower pace. Beyond that, it becomes a tricky judgement between having sufficient evidence (on potential second round effects) in the survey data to act vs waiting for firm proof at which point it may be too late. The latter is obviously a greater concern given the possibility that inflation expectations have become more sensitive since 2022. In other words, the ECB and BoE both face two-way credibility risk. On the one hand, act too early and risk policy error via lower growth. On the other hand, act too late and risk policy error should energy inflation percolate into core. Policy setters will need to decide whether patience is a virtue. We suspect that the BoE will be more patient that the ECB. This partly reflects the starting point of policy rates, with the BoE likely still above neutral (meaning that holding rates is already a vote for restriction) while the ECB can arguably afford insurance hikes of 2x25bp and still be within the neutral range. It also reflects the emphasis BoE Governor Bailey has placed on limiting damage to jobs and growth – see European Rates Weekly:A new phase. The greater likelihood of ECB hikes vs the BoE is already reflected in market pricing, but we think the premium could be wider for the near meetings (beyond April) given the relatively high weight we would attach to a hike by the ECB while the BoE holds (repeating the respective 2011 playbooks). We also would expect a generally shrinking labor force with immigration changes to also imply a lower level of claims (both initial and continuing). Still, any large shift in labor market dynamics, especially towards any increase in layoffs, likely would be reflected in higher claims. But rather than the level of claims, we are more interested in the trend of claims over the coming months. If familiar patterns of weakening labor market data in the spring and summer were to repeat this year, we would expect claims to be one of the earliest signals of this trend. So far, other data like NFIB hiring plans (which weaken a few months before actual hiring does) have shown familiar patterns this year, falling to recent lows in February and March. A repeat of familiar patterns would imply initial claims rising more consistently within the next 3-4 weeks. T o us, this would signal that average job growth is likely to slow from a ~50k/month (private payroll) pace over the last 6 months to at or below 0k on average in Q2/Q3. We do not think this would be enough job growth to keep the unemployment rate from rising above 4.5% by late summer. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

GCC exports are mostly energy-based and priced in USD. GCC (ex-Kuwait) USD pegs allow stable conversion of export revenue into local currency for domestic spending. The USD pegs are defendable as surplus USDs are accumulated in reserves or sovereign wealth funds. When the surplus is invested abroad, there is an incentive towards US assets as the peg removes FX-risk. GCC do not disclose their reserve currency breakdown but most “guestimates” place it at almost all USD. As a guideline, Hong Kong is also pegged to USD and in its latest disclosure, reported a USD reserve allocation of 79.1%. China and BRICS’ share of GCC ex-Kuwait trade has grown considerably whilst the U.S. has declined to 5% (Fig.XX). If GCC export pricing diversifies away from USD, both the peg and reserve allocations would be misaligned with export revenues. We model a diversified reserve allocation to reflect these trade shares with 71% in USD. Assuming the starting point is 100% of reserves allocated to USD, a reduction to 71% could lead to selling of up to USD 250bn. While a change in GCC currency pegs is unlikely, to the extent that the vast majority of reserves are in USDs, changes in trade patterns could warrant a reassessment of reserve allocations. We have looked in detail at the pass-through of commodity prices into Euro area HICP prices. Here we focus on cross-country differences. The pass-through of Brent oil prices to consumer fuel prices is broadly similar across countries. Meanwhile, the pass-through of market energy prices to consumer gas and electricity prices varies greatly across countries, as wholesale and consumer market structures, regulations and policy inter- ventions differ across countries. Policy responses to the cur- rent shock have largely focused on fuel prices and have creat- ed idiosyncratic consumer price dynamics at the country level. As we wrote last week (see “Fed Notes: 5 things to watch at Warsh's hearing “), although we have not heard from Warsh recently, his comments prior to his nomination indicated support for rate reductions based primarily on a forecast that anticipates strong disinflationary forces from deregulation and AI. While we expect he will ma intain this narrative about the economy, recent developments have weakened the case for lower rates – labor-market data have stabilized, PCE inflation has surprised to the upside, and the war in Iran poses further upside risks to inflation. Although Warsh has argued for lower rates, we do not view him as structurally dovish. Instead, his views have tended to skew hawkish relative to others . The nuance for Warsh will be how he balances a desire to lower rates over time with an economic backdrop that does not call for rate cuts at present. Treasury Secretary Bessent’s assertion earlier this week “I understand if the Fed needs to wait on rate cu ts” may provide Warsh some cover in this regard. Warsh can talk about temporary inflation risks requiri ng vigilance for a short period before resuming policy easing. Other topics that Senators could query Warsh on will be the Fed’s balance sheet policy, communications policies, and undoubtedly – Fed independence. Page 3 The fate of Fed comms: Forward guidance, the dot plot, FOMC pressers, and more Will Warsh repeat his criticisms of Fed communications strategies and tools, and will he present concrete proposals for how communications should change? Warsh has been an outspoken critic of using forward guidance in "normal times." We expect he will repeat this criticism and ultimately lead a move away from its granular application, arguing its potential costs (impaired credibility, reduced flexibility) outweigh its benefits outside of a ZLB environment. While Warsh may be skeptical of the SEP dot plot, its complete elimination is unlikely to gain broad Committee support. Instead, we anticipate reforms designed to reduce its role as a near -term forecasting tool. Possibilities include: shifting to rolling w indows, focusing on a forecast central tendency or range instead of individual dots, or embedding projections within a broader discussion of risks and scenarios. We believe Warsh will retain the every -meeting press conference schedule as a critical platform to frame the FOMC's narrative. However, the content will change. Expect less focus on data dependence and near -term policy signals, and more emphasis on a longe r-term, narrative-based view of the economy —in the near - term likely centered on a productivity boom. Such demand may represent Treasuries bought for relative value trades (like swap spread longs, or the futures basis trade) rather than a fixed income investment, and is more vulnerable to volatility in the market. Unsurprisingly then, the evolution of the Treasury future basis trade lines up well with the increased uptake of Treasuries in overseas financial centres. Such a demand base has made the Treasury market vulnerable in stress events. During covid, Liberation day, and Iran conflict – Treasury yields ended higher, as “dash for cash”, or stresses in basis and swap spread trades, drove higher yields.

Norway represents another important oil exporter. Norway’s surplus oil revenues are transferred to the sovereign wealth fund, Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM) which in turn invests these abroad on an un-FX hedged basis. We estimate that NBIM is currently around 7% overweight US equities versus its benchmark. This is equivalent to over USD 100bn, which is around 16% of annual portfolio investment flows into US equities. NBIM are not strictly required to maintain allocations around the benchmark, however its risk constraints are set relative to the benchmark. So, an increase in the risk perception of US equities could prompt a change in the allocation closer to the benchmark. Norway structurally overweight US equities

Treasury Secretary Bessent acknowledges Fed could be on hold for now On Tuesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested the Fed could decide to hold rates amid uncertainty from the Iran conflict (link here). "If they want to wait for some clarity, I understand that, " he told reporters. Reporting suggests he was " highly confident" price pressures outside food energy prices would continue to subside, and that ultimately, "the impetus here is they will need to cut rates." With little expectation for the Fed to move rates now, Bessent is more focused on confirming the new Fed Chair nominee: "We should wait for the new chairman, Warsh, and let him lead the next cycle." Federal Reserve to lower reserve management purchase pace The Federal Reserve Bank of New York announced it would reduce bill purchases to a pace of $25 billion per month, in addition to ~$16bn in reinvestments (link here). records.text: Decomposing recent S&P 500 earnings revision strength A resilient earnings outlook has provided the fundamental underpinning for the equity market rally. The S&P 500 has rallied by 12% from its low on March 30, surging to a new record high alongside an increase in prediction market odds of an imminent end to the conflict in Iran. Since the start of the war, consensus estimates for S&P 500 EPS in 2026 and 2027 have each risen by 3%. As a result, while the S&P 500 ended the week 2% above its pre-war January high, the current P/E multiple of 21x is 5% lower than it was in January. While equity prices typically move more quickly than consensus estimates, the recent increase in earnings expectations is a marked contrast from the cautious sideways trajectory of analyst forecasts during the tariff-driven volatility this time last year. The recent revisions to the aggregate S&P 500 earnings outlook have been driven almost entirely by the Energy and Technology sectors, with 8 of 11 sectors experiencing no increase in EPS estimates. The upward revision to Energy sector earnings estimates alongside downward revisions for the consumer sectors and some Industrials reflects the typical redistributional impact of oil on S&P 500 EPS that we discussed last month. Tech earnings estimates have been supported primarily by the powerful idiosyncratic tailwind from AI investment spending. However, this does not take into account that if productivity increases, so does demand (via higher incomes and increased investment), and therefore new jobs are likely to spring up (see page 15). Companies will adopt AI and change their modus operandi significantly and immediately Markets have frictions The fast adoption of AI has sparked concerns that many jobs will be replaced immediately. We see two arguments against that claim. ▪ Human preference: Management practices, resources, customs and regulations make firms choose to employ people for functions that could be automated away, even without AI. ▪ Human liability: Despite their automation potential, some functions require accountability. This is particularly the case for jobs involving trust (finance, real estate), legal liability (legal advice) or a high social content (education). Though these arguments mean that productivity gains from AI will be slower to materialise, they give more time for the labour market to absorb some job cuts while new jobs are created. Warsh argued that shrinking the Fed’s balance sheet over time could reduce inflation by decreasing the money supply and tightening broad financial conditions, thus opening the door to policy rate cuts. While there was some excitement around this topic when Warsh was first nominated, our sense is that the consensus has coalesced around a drawn -out process that first requires changes in bank regulation to reduce demand for reserves. This case has been pres ented by a number of Fed officials, including Vice Chair of Supervision Bowman, Governor Miran, and Dallas Fed President Logan, among others. Focus will be on whether Warsh confirms this more gradual pathway to balance -sheet reduction. One key related poin t of interest will be whether Warsh endorses the Fed’s current ample reserves regime or advocates serious consideration of a return to scarce reserves. More broadly, we think Warsh could suggest a comprehensive review of the Fed’s balance sheet and implementation policies and emphasize that the process of implementing any changes could take years. By way of background, Warsh has been consistently critical of the Fed’s active use of its balance sheet over the past ~15 years. In this scenario, inflation concerns tend to outweigh growth concerns, and inflation risk premiums are likely to be reflected in the belly zone of the curve. Meanwhile, concerns about fiscal expansion—such as energy price countermeasures and strengthening supply chains—remain. The JGB curve is expected to see underperformance in the belly, or a bear steepening trend. “Effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz” scenario: Amid renewed concerns about severe economic deterioration, equities are again likely to underperform bonds, making pension rebalancing flows inclined toward bond selling and equity buying. Issuance in the super long sector is expected to be absorbed mostly by overseas investors, who will likely demand a high term premium due to concerns about expansionary fiscal policies. This scenario is the one where the super long sector is most prone to underperform. “De-escalation” scenario: This is the scenario in which equities are expected to outperform bonds the most. For pension funds, the main rebalancing flow is anticipated to be bond purchases and equity sales. While this creates an environment in which the BoJ can more easily raise interest rates, excessive fiscal concerns also subside, making it likely that the JGB curve will tend to twist flatten.

The last stage of the price propagation process involves wages. This is especially true in the highly staggered wage-setting framework prevailing in most of Europe. We construct an inflation heatmap to track timely data to monitor these propagation effects. We select indicators based on the experience of the 2022-23 inflation shock. We include other non-oil commodity prices (food and raw materials commodities, with the HWWI indices, and wholesale power prices) and firms selling price intentions (from monthly business surveys) across several sectors of the economy. We also include delivery times (from the manufacturing PMIs) and shipping costs (WCI- Composite Container Freight rate) as gauges of supply disruptions beyond energy. Both these indicators behaved as very early signals of the inflation shock four years ago (starting to accelerate already in mid-2020). records.text: Stand on EA Macro Euro Area Macro | Powered Down: Lower EA Growth Ahead Euro Inflation Watch | First Step Up, More Ahead Norway | Going Back Up UK Inflation Watch | Forecast Revisions This week, Claire Thürwächter and Jens Eisenschmidt discuss the potential impact of Germany's fiscal measures on inflation and growth. Next week, all eyes will be on April PMIs and UK inflation. This week in Europe: The potential impact of Germany’s fiscal measures This week was relatively light in terms of data and the focus was firmly on the policy side. There was a lot of central bank communication alongside the IMF and World Bank Spring meetings. What we heard aligns very well with our thinking. For the ECB – reflected for example in remarks by President Lagarde here and Executive Board Member Schnabel here – we note that a hike in April is unlikely (we expect a hike in June and September, conditional on energy prices remaining elevated for some time). And staying in the policy sphere, the German government announced some policy measures to address the issue of high energy prices. We had flagged some weeks ago that we thought a large fiscal splurge was unlikely (see here and here). And the German measures were fully in line with that assessment. While they follow the template of the 2022/23 policy response, they are at a much smaller scale and (at least for now) are designed to have no impact on German debt. Let’s take a closer look at the German package and its likely macroeconomic impact.

records.text: European Economics 16 April 2026 Citi Research 2 An Inflation Heatmap for Second-Round Effects The inflation outlook, and the ECB next moves, crucially depend on (a) how long oil prices stay at current elevated levels and (b) the extent to which elevated oil/gas prices start lifting other prices/wages. In general, second‑round effects arise as the initial energy cost‑push impulse propagates through pricing behavior, price expectations and wage‑setting. We would categorise second-round effects into four broad categories: 1. First, the behaviour of other commodity prices other than oil, such as power and other non-energy commodities, such as food and raw materials. The production function of most other commodities displays a large share of energy inputs and hence their prices tend to be highly correlated with oil/gas. ECB President Lagarde noted in March that they will be “particularly attentive to all commodity markets” . 2. Other, less direct, propagation effects of higher oil prices depend on firms’ pricing behaviour, in particular on firms’ ability to pass on the increase in input costs onto their final prices. Typically, this pass-through is higher in upstream sectors (eg intermediate goods) and diminishes further along the pricing chain, as the initial cost push is more diluted among other costs (eg distribution costs, marketing, wages…). 3. records.text: US Economics Weekly17 April 2026 ab 11 Fedspeak: FOMC waiting, watching, and weighing risks Commentary from Fed officials this week signaled continued uncertainty over the impact of the oil price shock. Governor Barr spoke briefly on impact of the Iran conflict:"Given rapidly changing circumstances, it is much too early to know the path for prices as events in the Middle East unfold." FRB of Chicago President Goolsbee shared the added price pressure could push out the timing of a rate cut: "The longer this goes, where we never got to see the decrease in inflation, and if inflation stays up, realistically, I think that starts pushing it out of 2026," Goolsbee said in an interview with AP (link here). When later asked if cuts are off the table for 2026, he responded: "As you know, before there was the war, I was on the more optimistic side that there could be more than one, multiple rate cuts in '26. I just wanted some evidence that inflation was heading back down to two percent. That the tariff inflation was actually going to prove transitory. I have a little concern to pile this on top of inflation before the other one[tariffs] went away. That’s a dangerous, slippery spot to be in. The longer this inflation disruption goes, the more likely it is, in my view, that the appropriate rate cutting would be put off" (link here). Most tangible results are expected with respect to the energy crisis response and the competitiveness push. With respect to the former, the EC is set to partly embark on a replay of the 2022 crisis playbook, but its response will not include relaxing EU fiscal rules. On Wednesday, the European Commission will reveal its “EU energy toolbox” (also called Accelerate EU), just ahead of the meeting. A leaked draft of the document (see here) suggests that no game changers are to be expected. records.text: M Update Morgan Stanley Research 3 G10 | Summary of Our G10 Currency Views USD Our view: Neutral Risk skew: Neutral Watch: Retail Sales, PMIs We remain neutral on the USD overall given the elevated level of uncertainty and volatility in the Middle East. A resumption of hostilities would likely boost the USD as the only G10 safe haven currency that is also a net energy exporter. Also, tax refunds appear to be smaller and less stimulative to US growth than we and others had anticipated. And higher gas prices likely more than offset refunds' boost to demand, weighing on US growth. Given many investors' expectation that tax refunds will substantially boost growth, USD may soften as growth disappoints their expectations. EUR Our view: Neutral Risk skew: Neutral Watch: ZEW Survey, S&P PMIs, German IFO Survey EUR/USD has made a round trip since late February, returning to near the 1.18 level at which it traded prior to the conflict in the Gulf. EU-US yield differentials have moved substantially in the EUR's favor since June 2025, when EUR/ USD first touched 1.18. And yields have continued to move in a USD negative direction since early March. The continued shift in yields in the EUR's favor suggests more upside to the EUR, and the fact that 25d EUR/USD risk reversals remain well below pre-March levels suggest that significant hedging via EUR/USD puts remains outstanding. Economics Europe Blog Date 15 April 2026 From costs to prices: insights from survey data The escalation of the conflict in the Middle East has prompted a renewed build- up of inflationary pressures. From a central bank perspective, the key question is whether higher input costs will be absorbed by margins or passed through into final output prices . The latter would have implications for the path of core inflation. In this blog we examine the latest signal s from survey -based price indicators to assess the extent of current cost pass-through in manufacturing. The economic costs from the energy shock are already visible. Headline inflation in the euro area rose by 0.6pp in March to 2.5% YoY – the highest since Jan-25 – largely driven by higher fuel prices . Survey-based indicators point to a similar picture, with the composite PMI input prices index increasing sharply across the board (Figure 1). The rise in output prices, however, was smaller and mixed across countries, with France even recording a slight decline (Figure 2). This suggest s that firms in both services and manufacturing are currently absorbing part of the in

Labor market: stabilizing around full employment • The labor market has been buffeted by shocks to supply (immigration restrictions) and demand (tariff uncertainty, AI, DOGE). In our view, the supply shock is likely to be the bigger driver of soft job growth this year, especially as labor demand starts to recover on the back of fading tariff uncertainty, a positive fiscal policy impulse and consumer resilience. Hence, we have payrolls averaging 40k in 2026. Immigration tightening likely lowers breakeven job growth to about 20k, keeping payrolls close to full employment. Our revisions to the GDP trajectory should imply slower job growth. But with GDP still close to trend, we wouldn't expect the labor market to roll over. Hence, we see the u-rate at 4.5% in 2Q26 and then dropping to 4.4% by 4Q26. Fed: two cuts in 2026 but on hold under Powell • The Fed held rates steady at 3.5-3.75% at its Mar meeting, as expected. In the characterization of current conditions, the Fed emphasized that the economic implications of the Iran war are uncertain. Powell’s comments discussed at length the ongoing inflation overshoot and upside risks to inflation, but barely discussed downside risks to the labor market. We still expect the Fed to cut rates by 50bp this year, but we push back our expectation for cuts from June/July to September/October, and acknowledge high risks that these cuts may not materialize. records.text: 2 Insights SPOTLIGHT VIEWS: CONFLICTING HEADLINES; USD UNWIND UNWOUND Conflicting headlines. The outcome of the war in the Middle East remains uncertain. Prediction markets still place the chance of a permanent ceasefire by May at only 50/50. But financial markets or investors appear to be erring on the side of optimism. Our Behavioural Risk Scorecard has swung rapidly back to risk seeking (see top chart page 3) and the impact on the DXY of headlines related to international conflict is beginning to fade (Figure 3). The lesson from 2022 is that conflict coverage can be intense, but their impact on the markets is more episodic. USD unwind, unwinds. Given the USD was the best performing currency during the peak impact of conflict headlines in March, this removes a potential support for the currency. Investor behaviour, meanwhile, points to another diminished tail wind. Since mid-February our metrics showed evidence of asset managers attempting to reduce their significant USD underweight. The 32- day run of significant and consecutive days of USD buying ended on 8th April (Figure 4). Selling began with domestic investors, which is important given those investors are already overweight the USD (see page 3), but non-US investors joined in on the 9th and 10th. The result has been the largest daily USD sales by asset managers seen since last August (13th), as the interest rate markets were ramping up their rate cut expectations. As illustrated in Figure 13 on the previous page, our modelling of the impact of AI works differently to other approaches in the literature in two key respects: we model the economy in a general equilibrium sense, assuming that agents foresee the gains from AI and react by investing in the technology immediately (this is one of the key lessons from the 1990s and was visible in 2025 as well); and we allow for the technology to evolve over time, in line with the experience of the electrification and the ICT revolutions. To estimate the impact of AI on policy rates, we layer our modelling on neutral rates (see US: How will immigration and AI impact the neutral rate?, 20 November 2025) on top of our NiGEM outputs.

records.text: M Idea 2 Interest Rate Strategy United Kingdom | Stay in SONIA Forward Steepeners FY 2026/27 Gilt Remit – April Revision Preview. Next week the DMO will publish the April revision to the FY 2026-27 remit. Overall, we do not expect a major market-moving event, given only limited scope for the gilt remit to be revised lower, by around £1–2bn in our estimates. The main driver should be the gap between the March 2026 Spring Statement assumptions for FY 2025-26 and the subsequent outturn. On our estimates, the 2025-26 CGNCR ex outturn is likely to come in around £2bn below the Spring Statement forecast, while NS&I (including Green Savings Bonds) may undershoot the current plan marginally. By contrast, the T-bill contribution appears broadly in line with the current £11bn target, and we do not expect a meaningful revision there. Other financing remains difficult to pin down and injects some residual uncertainty (see Exhibit 1 ). Taken together, these components point to a modest downward revision to the FY 2025- 26 financing requirement, which should feed through into a slightly more negative financing adjustment carried forward into FY 2026-27. In our central case, this translates into a £1–2bn reduction in the FY 2026-27 gilt remit relative to the Spring Statement plan (see here). Given the small size of the expected adjustment, the DMO may opt to absorb the change via a modest reduction in the unallocated bucket (see Exhibit 2 ). records.text: Strong recent earnings revisions have provided the fundamental backing for n the equity market’s surge to new highs. The S&P 500 has rallied by 12% from its March 30 low alongside an improving geopolitical outlook. While the S&P 500 now trades 2% above its January high prior to the start of the war, consensus estimates for earnings in 2026 and 2027 are 4% above January levels. The increase in consensus S&P 500 earnings estimates has been driven by n narrow pockets of strength. The Energy and Information Technology sectors have accounted for nearly the entire positive revision, with the median S&P 500 company experiencing no revision to 2026 EPS estimates during the past few months. Micron (MU) and Exxon Mobil (XOM) have together accounted for more than 60% of the consensus revision to S&P 500 2026 EPS estimates since the start of the war. Recent rotations within the equity market have generally tracked with n earnings revisions. Mirroring the narrow breadth of EPS revisions, our preferred measure of market breadth has dropped to the lowest level in recent decades outside of the Dot Com bubble and mid-2023. Among sectors, those with the strongest revisions have generally outperformed, and the rally in our EPS revisions factor shows a similar dynamic among stocks within sectors. A continuation of the recent improvement in the geopolitical outlook should n help broaden both the earnings outlook and equity market breadth. records.text: EM – LOC AL EY ES F OR A GLOBAL VI EW The last stage of the property downturn: The sector remained the biggest drag in Q1. Property investment fell 11.2% y/y, new starts dropped 20.3%, and sales volume fell 10.4%. That said, positive signs suggest the sector has likely passed most of the downturn . ▪ The double-digit decline occurred despite a tough base effect; Q1 last year saw a material recovery after the sizable stimulus package in September 2024. ▪ Secondary-market prices improved. In March, prices in tier-1 city rose 0.4% m/m, the first rise in 12 months. Declines in tier-2 and tier-3 cities narrowed sharply versus last year. High-frequency data from the first two weeks of April show the recovery continuing . ▪ Unlike last Q1’s recovery, this price improvement occurred without visible policy stimulus . This suggests that after four years of sharp contraction, the market is gradually finding a bottom. A bottoming property sector means its drag on growth will fade gradually, but it is too early to forecast a cyclical recovery, given still -tepid consumer confidence and high inventories in both primary and secondary markets (for more, read China’s property downturn: Not following Japan’s path, dated 15 October 2025). . Overcapacity a major overhang: Manufacturing investment rose to 4.1% y/y in Q1, up from 0.6% last year, but capacity utilisation fell to 73.6%, the lowest Q1 level since 2017.
