And, in our latest deep-dive, we focused on the prospects of Euro adoption: we look at past Euro area accessions and use our GSDEER model to link structural shifts in inflation and productivity to currency developments. Euro adoption would first require participation in ERM II for at least two years without ‘severe tensions’ and without unilateral devaluation. Most countries that adopted the Euro already had tightly managed currencies on the path to Euro accession, with few exceptions. In Slovakia, SKK appreciated by 20% vs. EUR through its convergence process due to large productivity gains and inflows because of both EU and euro area accession (Exhibit 3). HUF also appreciated over that period due to similar underlying drivers. However, higher inflation (and a higher inflation target) since then explains the trend higher in EUR/HUF that followed. In this context, sustained inflation convergence towards 2% would point to a more stable EUR/HUF level. And, if better economic prospects post-election lead to higher productivity growth, this would point to a lower EUR/HUF fair value. For this reason, we think that the SKK convergence story would become a more relevant parallel if there were a meaningful improvement in Hungarian productivity growth. Our economists continue to think that the most likely scenario is the BoE on hold for 2026, suggesting further declines in Z6 pricing (~25bp of hikes). However, with inflation risks likely to linger, any sense of resilience in the real economic data may see pressure transfer from the front-end to the belly of the curve. For this reason, we think 2s5s will continue to steepen in the relief phase for front-end rates, until flat pricing for 2026 allows for a re-focusing on the weakness in the UK labour market and potential 2027 cuts. Like in Europe, SFIZ6Z7 is too steep given the hikes priced into 2026, but we have a stronger view that this is likely to resolve via lower Z6 yields than in the case of the EUR curve. Further out the curve, while we expect relief from the rate expectations component, we are a little more cautious on the Gilt risk premium given the potential for concerns around inflation and fiscal policy to attenuate the effect of the front-end on Gilt forwards. Intuitively, front-end TIPS offer a solid correlation with realized inflation, with less real duration exposure than the 1-30y benchmark. As such, when inflation is realizing above breakeven rates and the real term premium is rising, front-end TIPS should do relatively well. records.text: Spotlight on Tesla Tesla is focused on real-world AI development, including for vehicles and robots. The company has articulated a view that while getting to more generalized AI capability is a difficult problem, it will allow Tesla to scale quickly when ready, especially given its vertical integration and the low cost of its vehicles. Tesla began operating a portion of its robotaxi business in Austin without an in-vehicle safety monitor starting in December 2025 (albeit the percentage of driverless vehicles in the fleet was relatively limited). It initially launched its robotaxi service in Austin in June 2025, but with a safety observer. Tesla also launched a ride-hailing service in the San Francisco Bay Area in July 2025, but Tesla does not currently have the regulatory approvals to operate a driverless service there. We believe investors are increasingly looking for data on the performance and progress of Tesla’s robotaxi service, including the ratio of rides in Austin without a monitor, and expanding to more locations. Recall Tesla stated on its 4Q earnings call that it plans to expand robotaxi operations to 7 other metros (including Dallas, Houston, Phoenix, and Miami) in 1H26 (and we believe this would include using safety observers and/or drivers to start). That in itself is a data point however, and does not imply the April meeting is more dovish than the March meeting, but the contrary. We derive our 12-month target price of US$30.0 based on an EV/EBITDA multiple of 20.1x (using our estimate of the company’s 2031E EBITDA), which is based on the correlation of EBITDA growth and EV/EBITDA of the global peers of Pony AI. We then discount back to 2026E using a COE of 11.5% (equity risk premium of 6.5%, risk free rate of 3.0%, and a beta of 1.3; similar to what we apply for our coverage). Consensus estimates show revenue growth for the median S&P 500 stock decelerating from 7% year/year in Q4 2025 to 5% in 2026. Our consumer equity analysts have recently trimmed their estimates for consumer spending, particularly at the low end of the income distribution, to reflect higher oil prices. They note that pressure on low-income consumers is amplified by the previous cuts to Medicaid and SNAP benefits. In contrast, consensus estimates show the Technology sector driving 8% growth in aggregate S&P 500 dollar-weighted revenues this year. Consensus forecasts also show a gradual deceleration in hyperscaler capex growth in coming quarters, which should lead in turn to decelerating Technology revenues. However, these capex estimates have been repeatedly revised higher, including an increase of roughly $130 billion to 2026 capex forecasts last quarter. records.text: Higher, not lower, import prices: We lean against the view that, should AI lead to a synchronised boost to productivity across DM, as we model in our simulation, production costs will fall across the globe, meaning firms and consumers will benefit from cheaper imports, regardless of where these come from. First, AI is likely to give a disproportionate productivity boost to services, which are less tradeable than goods. The boost could also be diminished by countries tightening trade policy, for example by restricting data sharing to capture a higher share of the AI value chain or by imposing tariffs, although the US has largely spared semiconductors and other electronic components until now. While trade policy is exogenous (i.e. non-reactive) in our simulation, protectionism poses a non-negligeable downside risk for GDP and an upside risk to inflation. Data shows that AI-related US capex is uncorrelated with domestic production, but reliant on imports instead. There is severe upward pressure on the prices of some imports despite their remaining tariff-free. For example, amid tight supply, prices of certain DRAM and NAND memory chips from South Korea have increased by around 20x and 8x, respectively, since January 2025. These are critical inputs for major US tech companies and extremely difficult to substitute. records.text: US Economic Weekly | 17 April 2026 9 Core views Growth: to remain trendlike • The Iran conflict poses stagflationary risks as the oil shock is likely to weigh on consumer spending and business investment. But we still see several tailwinds supporting growth this year, including lagged benefits from Fed rate cuts, more supportive trade policy, ongoing AI-related investment, and favorable shutdown- related base effects. Taking these factors into consideration, we marked down our 2026 GDP forecasts. We now look for growth to come in at 2.2% on a 4Q/4Q basis and 2.3% on the annual average. Inflation: to remain stuck above the Fed’s target through 2027 • We now forecast headline PCE inflation to peak in 2Q 2026 at 3.8% and to remain 70bp above our prior forecast for the rest of this year due to higher oil prices. We expect headline inflation falls quickly next year, as oil retraces. But we project price levels at the end of next year to be 30bp above our prior forecast, capturing higher food inflation and some lasting impact on global supply chains. The surge in energy prices is likely to pass through to core inflation as well, with a lag. We now expect 4Q/4Q 2026 core PCE to come in at 3.1%, vs. 2.8% previously. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 16 Apr 2026 13:52:07 ET │ 17 pages Canada Economics Weekly Echoes of 2025 CITI'S TAKE The spring of 2026 is feeling very similar to the spring of 2025. The BoC is keeping rates on hold with a new supply shock creating upside risks to inflation (tariffs then, oil now). CFIB price plans have risen above the target range as input costs rise, and could signal some near-term stickiness to core inflation, including in next week’s March CPI report when headline inflation should rise a substantial 1%MoM. But demand indications remain soft, and the unemployment rate is averaging around 6.7%. The next few months of data are unlikely to shift the BoC’s stance, with modestly rising employment, a mechanical pick-up in home sales from a weak Q1, and somewhat stronger core inflation. But also like last year, we expect softer activity than the BoC forecasted at the start of the year to have officials cutting rates by 50bp in H2. records.text: AI as a GPT: We consider AI to be a GPT, i.e. a type of technology characterised by “i) pervasiveness, ii) continuous improvement over time and iii) innovation spawning” (see Calvino et al., 2025). GPTs are inventions such as electricity, the personal computer, the steam engine or printing, which have been widely adopted and led to a “cascade of innovations in new goods or services, production processes, and business structures” (Governor Michael Barr of the Federal Reserve System, speech, February 2026). We see two advantages to our analysis referring to the historical impact on TFP growth of comparable GPTs. ▪ Historical comparisons enable us to cross-check that the forward-looking impact of our technology shock on the broader macroeconomic environment is consistent with history. For instance, did risk sentiment improve due to the deployment of the technology? Did the output gap widen? How did the central bank respond? ▪ Historical comparisons can account for the further evolution of technologies. Studies show that measures of the cost/time savings from current iteration of AI technology do not to capture the potential evolution of the technology. While AI differs technologically from earlier GPTs, we consider the economic mechanisms governing diffusion – complementarities, organisational adjustment, skill upgrading and capital deepening – to be structurally similar. records.text: 17 April 2026 Rate Check: Where Macro Meets Markets Page 4 Deutsche Bank AG dollar, George? George Saravelos: Good question, Shreyas. Actually, before I answer that, I was surprised to read from Yellen overnight that she actually still thinks the Fed will be cutting later this year, because arguably she shouldn't be as politically influenced as Warsh. So there's definitely still a debate there. From our perspective, we've got to shore up the dollar again. It's not putting on a position we had before the conflict, because as far as Euro-dollar goes and the DXY, the developed market dollar, we were neutral. We had the short dollar view in Emerging Markets (EM), but we took that off after the conflict. In terms of the narrow DXY, we didn't have that one. So the question is really what has changed from February to today? [00:09] George Saravelos: The first thing is monetary policy. As Francis mentioned, we've taken out rate cuts from the Fed. But what's interesting is we've actually added in a fair bit of hikes in the rest of the world. A key input into our cyclical views for currencies is the shape of the curve and the relative ranking of US yields. records.text: 16 April 2026 2 www.GlobalMarkets.bnpparibas.com BDCs and PC CLOs address the lack of a liquid and transparent market for Private Credit loans differently. BDCs prefer forbearance measures such as restructurings and Payment-in-Kind (PIK). These measures do not necessarily align with a default definition based on missed payments, which is standard in CLOs. BDC Fair Value is an accounting value and it is disclosed once a quarter. It is less dynamic than CLO reported Market Value, which is updated once a month (see Appendix). In Q3 and Q4 2025 reporting, BDCs made headlines for posting sharp portfolio markdowns on certain impaired credit. Markdowns happen through posting depreciation charges. In BDCs , the accounting loss is typically incurred at a later stage in the restructuring process and it’s closer to a write-off. Lastly, CLOs have concentration limits, typically up to 20% in the top sector. Hence most concentrated CLOs would avoid the extreme Software concentration that some BDCs have, in our view. records.text: 17 April 2026 UK Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 The upside risks to the gilt remit There will be plenty of risks surrounding this year's gilt remit total, which will only get reflected in the autumn update following the OBR's fall projections. As such, despite expectations of a larger carry-over financing adjustment from the last fiscal year to the current, we remain vigilant around upside risks to borrowing which could likely offset some of the gains likely to be set out in the week ahead. We highlight two main risks below: Updated macro conditions : Since the OBR's spring projections, the world has dramatically changed. Energy prices are up. Debt servicing costs will be up. Growth expectations have been revised lower. Unemployment projections have been revised (marginally) higher. And inflation will also inevitably run higher – at least for the near-term – given the energy spike (and associated indirect effects). While the translation into cash borrowing isn't straightforward, our projections still point to some upside to CGNCR. On our updated projections, we expect this to add somewhere close to GBP 5.5-8.5bn to 2026/27 borrowing. Energy support: At present, the Government has announced only a GBP 53m support package for those on heating oil. records.text: A nuanced approach to a very large sector The Financials sector—namely US Banks—took center stage this week, following a wave of Q1 earnings and subsequent debt issuance deals. The new CDX Financials Index also began trading on April 13th, further focusing attention on the sector. We continue to have an overall constructive view on Banks, owing to what we view as a ‘core holding’ role in a variety of market scenarios. For example, in a slower but non-recessionary growth backdrop, we expect the sector’s strong capital and liquidity characteristics to benefit performance. By contrast, if growth proves more resilient, we see scope for the sector to benefit from exposure to more cyclical parts of the business (capital markets, lending) as well as reduced concerns around potential credit losses (as has been topical as of late). But importantly, relative value is not uniform across this large sector. Financials— broadly defined—represent 32% of the market value of the Bloomberg USD IG Corporate Index. And the Banks subsector represents 21%. As we detail below, we have two key relative value preferences and would use the supply-driven widening as an opportunity to selectively add exposure to Banks. First, we favor the US Money Centers subsector over both Yankees and Regionals. Second, our broad preference is to remain up in the capital structure given rich valuations across bank types. records.text: ab 16 April 2026 Global Research European Economic Comment Eurozone: Fiscal response to energy shock – moderate, so far Fiscal policy responses to the energy shock As energy prices remain elevated and inflation rates continue to increase, many European governments are implementing fiscal support measures to counter the energy shock. In our recent downward revision of the Eurozone GDP forecast, we assumed governments would provide only limited fiscal support, amounting to less than 0.5% of GDP . How much stimulus has been announced so far, what is the likely macro impact, and how does it compare to 2022/23? Fiscal response so far around 0.1% of GDP ... So far, around half of all Eurozone countries have announced fiscal support measures, with costs estimated to amount to EUR18bn or 0.1% of Eurozone GDP (Figure 1F i s c a l m e a s u r e s t o c o u n t e r t h e e n e r g y s h o c k a n n o u n c e d i n 2 0 2 6 s o f a r i n t h e E u r o z o n e ). The largest packages have been implemented in Croatia (0.5% of GDP), Spain, Slovenia and Latvia (0.3% of GDP each). Among the large countries, we estimate Germany's package amounts to 0.14% of GDP (similar to Italy at 0.13% of GDP), while France has presented the smallest package (<0.1% of GDP). Most of the measures focus on temporary energy tax cuts for households and firms rather than broad-based price caps. Our commodity team’s forecast is tracking in between the ECB’s baseline and adverse scenarios, and energy product prices (including jet fuel, diesel, etc) have increased much more than their typical relationship with commodity prices would have suggested. Also, our commodity team continues to see upside risks to the energy outlook given the absence of a peace agreement and the slow pickup in shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. As a result, we see significant pass-through into inflation in coming months. We forecast headline inflation to peak at 3.2% and core inflation at 2.5%, somewhat above the ECB’s baseline. Also, we see some delay in the normalisation of wage growth as a result of the energy shock. Finally, the ECB’s communication has remained largely hawkish on the path ahead. President Lagarde, for example, argued this week that we are now in between the ECB staff’s baseline and adverse scenario, noting that the baseline is conditioned on two rate hikes. She also emphasised that it could be difficult to “look through” the shock given risks to inflation expectations. Other speakers have argued that market expectations for two hikes are reasonable (Kazaks) and that the ECB will take forceful action if the energy shock is persistent (Makhlouf). records.text: The different drivers of strategic vs. sponsored M&A In our view, the different pace of M&A activity between the strategic and sponsored cohorts speaks to the underlying drivers and motivations for the deal making. Strategic buyers are typically more focused on long-term business objectives (scale, diversification, new capabilities, entering new markets) and pursue acquisitions as long-term additions to their businesses. While not immune from macroeconomic volatility (which can influence funding access and costs), they tend to move forward with strategic imperatives in a wide range of environments. By contrast, financial sponsors tend to be more sensitive to the macroeconomic landscape, as financing costs weigh more heavily into the overall calculus and rationale for a deal. Additionally, for such transactions, an eventual ‘exit’ (IPO, sale) to monetize the investment are top of mind. These sponsor-related deals are typically not pursued in order to be integrated into businesses on a long-term or permanent basis, as is often the case with strategic deals. As shown in Exhibit 9, median existing holding periods have increased for US PE-backed companies based on data collected from PitchBook LCD. This is largely driven by muted US PE exit volumes over the course of 2022-2024. While exit activity increased in 2025, it was more heavily weighted toward PE firms’ larger ($1 billion+) assets. Over our forecast horizon (2026–27), the growth impact is around 0.1pp. Our assumption on the spillover of US productivity shocks to European countries is based on historical cross-country correlation of TFP growth shocks (see page 12). History suggests the bloc could see almost half the productivity shock of the US. So far, this is consistent with actuality, with the eurozone’s productivity growth lagging behind the US. Our results show a smaller investment boost in the eurozone, which caps the growth of the economy’s productive capacity. Intuitively, these results are consistent with recent decades’ productivity trends, which show a clear divergence in US and European TFP starting from the mid- 1990s and exacerbated in the post-GFC era (see Figure 69). Although there could be several causes, we think it might partly result from the US being the ‘winner’ in the ICT revolution while Europe lagged behind. The model responses of inflation and the policy rate are limited, and given the magnitudes and the horizons involved, we consider them to be negligible. The same holds for the unemployment rate. The market looks to be giving up the April hike because the central bank usually provides clearer communication one or two weeks before the meeting if it is to hike, but it has not done so. However, we recognise that the situation is more fluid than in the past. The two-week ceasefire ends before the BoJ meeting (Figure 2). If the BoJ is seen to be less behind the curve, the terminal rate element in the 10y rate could retrace and allow the bear steepening in 5s10s to retrace, in our view. Just like 10s20s stopped steepening as a structural trend (Figure 5), 5s10s could also stop steepening. As a caution, we note a totally different factor which could explain the 10y underperformance: banks’ risk-taking capacity for duration, due to a change in the so-called ‘core deposit model’. The model was used to measure “effective duration” of demand deposit in their ALM (asset liability management). As a good amount of demand deposit tends to stay in the bank as ‘core’, banks can assume a longer duration (often 5-10y), justifying investing in long maturity JGBs. However, banks have started to review the model as interest rates rose and the deposit may not be as fixed as before. Banks therefore require sufficient yield to invest in the 10y sector (in JGB and swaps). However, it is not a simple matter to analyse what level is sufficient, and asset duration can be managed by barbell exposure (such as O/N and 10y) rather than simply shifting from 10y to 5y. records.text: he effective rate has fallen to 9%, instead of increasing to the 15% in the CBO baseline. We believe tariff revenues from other replacement measures are likely to fall short of the CBO's $3trn estimate over the next 10 years. In addition, the president requested increased defense spending in FY27 to $1.5trn from $1.05trn in FY26, though it remains to be seen if Congress will pass these increases and if there will be offsets from spending cuts. We do not believe the market is pricing fiscal slippage from higher defense spending, which would affect 30y spreads. For context, a 1% increase in deficits as a % of GDP or the equivalent of a $400bn/year increase could tighten 30y swap spreads 10-15bp. We continue to favor belly/intermediate swap spreads and believe they have more upside than front-end spreads. That stance reflects increased leverage capacity from SLR reform, supportive GSE hedging flows from MBS purchases, regulatory tailwinds from Basel 3 and FASB proposals that encourage hedging activity, bank portfolios reinvesting maturing securities into higher- yielding assets, and a supportive supply backdrop in the sector. Our preferred expression is a beta-weighted 2s7s spread curve steepener (see here). The spread curve should steepen from the front end to the intermediate sector if outright spreads continue to widen. The beta- weighting mitigates against the risk of fiscal-driven tightening that would weigh on longer-tenor spreads and flatten the spread curve ( Figure 8).

records.text: JPY: A less dubious funder, for now. Coming into this year, we argued that two-way n macro and fiscal risks (as well as elevated intervention risk) would likely result in higher Yen volatility as we expected markets to continue trading both themes, pushing JPY in both directions as the backdrop evolved and challenging the case to use it as a funder. While those risks remain and probably return to the forefront over time, we think the energy shock has justifiably suppressed Yen volatility (Exhibit 6). Uncertainty around the global growth and inflation outlook has risen, leaving domestic fiscal risks less in focus for now. Moreover, the US’ relative insulation from the shock and the better-than-expected state of the US labor market could mean higher for longer yields as it takes some time to assess the economic impact. Together, these developments have left JPY more rangebound throughout the past six weeks and probably keep it a more limited mover over the near-term. We still think the asymmetry remains to the downside in USD/JPY, given the market’s vulnerability to an increase in recession odds (especially as markets have priced in greater optimism on the resumption of flows) and still-elevated intervention risk (reinforced by Katayama’s latest comments on continued discussions with the US). This release is important as it will determine if Italy exits its Excess Deficit Procedure a year early – and will thus need to do less fiscal consolidation. As we wrote last week, Italy's national statistical agency (ISTAT) has released figures that point to a deficit of 3.07%, just missing the crucial 3% threshold. records.text: 94 companies representing 15% of S&P 500 market cap will report earnings. Analyst estimates currently point to 12% year/year EPS growth for the S&P 500 this quarter, the strongest expectation at the start of an earnings season since 2021, followed by a sharp acceleration to roughly 20% growth in the remainder of 2026. Going forward, our top-down S&P 500 EPS forecasts imply a gradual decline in consensus earnings estimates, as is usually the pattern. However, risks to our forecasts are two-sided but skewed to the upside. We forecast 12% S&P 500 earnings growth this year ($309), below the 18% bottom-up consensus forecast but roughly in line with the top-down strategist consensus. Our 2027 forecast for 10% EPS growth is also substantially below the bottom-up consensus of 17%. During the past few decades, the bottom-up consensus forecast has typically been revised down by 4%-5% per year. If repeated, this would bring bottom-up forecasts close to our top-down estimates by the time earnings are realized in both 2026 and 2027. However, the recent upward trajectory of 2026 estimates has diverged from that pattern, and the idiosyncratic impact of AI that has driven those positive revisions creates the risk that the divergence persists. In contrast, the largest downside risks to the earnings outlook stem from the recent increases in commodity prices. With Waymo (which has traditionally used maps) now scaling, we think there is increasing evidence that using maps is a workable approach, at least for commercial applications that operate in a geofence, although others, including Tesla, have suggested that a generalized approach without maps will allow for faster scaling longer-term. How much does AV development cost for capex? One of the objectives of this report is to gauge capex demand and ROI tied to AVs. BoJ’s Communication Strategy: Avoiding Surprises If the BoJ’s recent communication was intended to prepare the market for a rate hike pause this month, it appears to reflect a strong commitment to “minimizing surprises in policy announcements”—a lesson learned from July 2024. At the July 2024 meeting, the BoJ raised rates from 0.10% to 0.25%, but with only about 35% probability priced in a week before the meeting, the decision surprised the market. Governor Ueda’s press conference included a hawkish remark: “With real interest rates still deeply negative, I don’t think a strong brake will be applied to the economy,” which contributed to the so-called “Ueda shock” in early August, marked by a sharp drop in equities and a stronger yen. The government estimates that the tax cut is a total relief of €1.6bn (0.04%-GDP) for consumers and industry (it is funded through pulling forward tobacco tax rises). The consumption split of fuels between personal and goods traffic suggests that the majority of that (around 70-75% see here) is for households. For the consumer price impact, we estimate that a total tax reduction of 17ct/l could lower fuel prices by 7-8%, taking as reference the latest weekly prices and assuming a high pass- through (in line with estimates from 2022, see here). Based on the HICP fuel weight this would reduce German headline HICP inflation by ca. 25bp, which is a reduction of 7bp at the euro area level. Next, let’s have a closer look at the second measure, allowing employers to make tax-free one-off payments. More explicitly, this is not a payment made by the government but rather the government waives the tax and social security contribution payments for up to €1,000 of additional pay. The aim is to provide employees with a net income rise that buffers to some extent the inflation shock while at the same time reducing the labor cost for employers. records.text: US Economic Perspectives17 April 2026 ab 4 While our baseline is that the rise in crude oil prices will only have a muted impact on core price inflation, we think the risks on balance are to the upside of our baseline. The rise in the near-term Brent crude oil price might be understating the current market stress. Spot Brent crude oil prices (currently around $116 per barrel) are notably above the front-month futures price (around $99 per barrel). This is an abnormally large gap between these series. Since the front-month futures are for June settlement it is likely that they embed a significant probability of the situation improving in coming weeks and the front month futures might not reflect the current tightness in physical crude oil markets. Further, the conflict and the rise in crude oil prices could be more extended that currently embedded in crude oil futures. The lack of ships through the Straits of Hormuz could lead to supply issues not only for gasoline, but also related items like jet fuel, bunker fuel for ships, and fertilizer prices, which could distribute the crude oil price shock to consumer prices more broadly than we have seen up to this point. If the shutdown is prolonged, the large rise in oil prices coming after a period of elevated inflation could lead to non-linear effects on output prices and a notable impact on inflation expectations. The pending home sales index, a measure of new contract signings that typically precedes existing home sales, saw significant drops in December (- 7.4%) and January (-1.0%). Pending home sales only recovered modestly in February (+1.8%). Furthermore, cold weather in January may have pushed contract signings into February, explaining some of the revised strength in February and relative weakness in March. Affordability had made steady improvements since June of last year, though it remains historically weak. The National Association of Realtors' housing affordability index fell 3.8 points to 113.7 in March, the first decline since June 2025, but the level remains noticeably down from the ~160 average in the five years prior to the pandemic. The Mortgage Bankers Association's 30-year contract mortgage rose 10 bps to 6.19% at the beginning of March before inching up to 6.57% in the week ending March 27. Meanwhile MBA's index of mortgage applications for a home purchase edged up in the first half of March before retracing down in the latter half. records.text: arly basis. The results are clear: without AI, the trajectory of growth in major economies would look significantly worse over the next 10 years. In a few instances, the AI shock is large enough to more than offset headwinds facing major economies. US AI boost overshadows rest: By 2034, in the US, our estimate of the AI boost is comfortably larger than any other negative shock we estimate. While slower population growth than in the previous decades is set to stifle growth, the technological revolution is likely to mute that impact. In the near term (2026–27), however, negative shocks seem to (more than) offset the positive ones. Eurozone helped by AI and fiscal boost: From 2025 to the end of 2034, our analysis suggests that the eurozone economy will benefit from the AI boost and the deployment of the German fiscal package, paired with higher defence spending across the bloc. These positive shocks will more than offset the drag coming from higher trade tariffs, possibly higher-for-longer energy prices and slower population growth, as the demographic decline in the eurozone starts to bite. The potency of the tariff and energy shock in 2026 and 2027, paired with the slow improvements on the AI front, are likely to leave GDP below baseline in these initial years of the simulation. Volatility filter: We remove all variables with more than 1.25 times the volatility of the EPS change. Correlation filter: If two independent variables have a correlation greater than 80%, we keep only the one with the highest p-value when regressed against the EPS change. Model training: Find the best lag and best return for each variable: ▪ The 6m change in EPS is regressed against each independent variable, using different lags (up to 52w) and different returns (4w, 12w, 26w and 52w). ▪ The lag and return horizon are chosen to maximise the r2 between the variable and the EPS, which must exceed the coincident r2 by at least 10%. Narrowing the variables: We retain the 10 variables with the best p-value when regressed against the change in EPS. Rolling stepwise regression: A 5y rolling stepwise regression is used to identify the best three variables to use at each step. These are used in the final model. Validation: Out-of-sample fit: The model is tested against out-of-sample data. The results in the top chart show the out-of-sample fit, where each forecast point represents the 6m fwd forecast of the model. Edited

records.text: Consumer AVs - partially and fully autonomous vehicles poised to grow The vast majority of the global car parc and miles traveled come from personally owned vehicles rather than shared mobility/rideshare, making consumer applications of autonomous capabilities a particularly large potential market for the long-term. Numerous auto OEMs are focused on bringing either L3 (which is situationally eyes-off autonomy, such as on a highway in nice weather) or L4 technology (which is fully eyes-off and hands-off driving within a geofenced area like a part of a city) to consumer vehicles. Currently L4 AV technology is only available in commercial vehicles (e.g. rideshare applications). However, as operational design domains (ODDs) expand into wider areas and the need for remote assistance declines, we think L4 technology can be utilized by consumers (potentially with a subscription for remote assistance). While some AV vehicles have expensive hardware (e.g. Waymo), we do not believe vehicle costs will be a long-term barrier to adoption. The cost of AVs in China even with sensors (including lidar) and compute are already in the sub $40K USD range (less than the average price of a new vehicle in the US at ~$45-50K), and Tesla believes its current consumer vehicles (with prices in the US starting in the mid $30K range) have L4 capable hardware. A rate hike in June is something the market has already priced in, but it would confirm the half-yearly pace of rate hikes (the previous hike was in December 2025). Whether 1.5% by June 2027 is seen as the terminal rate, or rate hikes continue until end-2027 as priced in by the market, will depend upon the overall environment at the time, including inflation. While market pricing of this is diminishing, over the past two years the Fed has cut its policy rate as employment has worsened in the summer. A similar pattern repeated under the new chairperson this year also could force the BoJ to look to hike before the Fed. We would expect rate hike pricing to lessen at times along with this. The market is conscious that the ECB could hike at its June meeting and ensuring that it does not act later than that may be a factor in the BoJ’s decision-making. records.text: of the war since day one, with a peak to trough selloff of less than 10%. Does this price action make sense or is the stock market under-pricing the risk of further escalation and, more importantly, a prolonged war? The market pricing is completely rational, but it is based on extrapolating the US Administration’s reaction function during the trade war, i.e. the escalate to de-escalate strategy, into the Iran war. In both cases, the price action can be explained by the concept of game theory as in the game of penalty kicks. To understand this, imagine two players: the US Administration and a representative trader (i.e. the stock market). The US Administration can either escalate or de-escalate. The representative trader can buy or sell risk (i.e. a market rally or selloff). The critical assumption here is that if the market sells off, the US has an incentive to de-escalate. As can be seen, this game does not have a Nash equilibrium in pure strategies. If market participants reduce risk and trigger a selloff, it is optimal for the US to de-escalate, triggering a rally on the back of the de-escalation. But then in anticipation, the market does not sell off as market participants stay put. But then in anticipation, the US escalates since the market, by not selling off, is subsidizing the cost of escalation. However, this game has an equilibrium in mixed strategies. In this case, both players (the US and the market) are indifferent between playing any of the two possible actions.

records.text: In this note, we update estimates for U.S. Majors (XOM, CVX, COP) ahead of 1Q26 earnings to reflect mark-to-market commodity prices and refining margins. While large timing effects and recent Middle East disruptions may create noisy quarterly results, we generally expect U.S. Majors to maintain prior plans for production growth, capital spend, and shareholder returns, even amid currently higher commodity prices. We continue to highlight ConocoPhillips (COP), on both the US Conviction List and our Top 10 Ideas. With an estimated ~21% total return potential, we expect shares to benefit from a free cash flow inflection as capital spend rolls off and major projects come online (NFE, NFS, Port Arthur, Willow). The combination of these projects, coupled with ~$1 bn in cost reductions and margin enhancements, should deliver a ~20-25% free cash flow per share CAGR through 2030 at a long-term Brent price of $75/b. As conflict in the Middle East persists, we find the company’s assets in Alaska, Canada, and the Lower 48 provide a lower geopolitical risk profile relative to global peers. Even though major currencies such as the EUR and GBP have recovered to their pre-Middle East conflict levels, USDJPY has stayed around three yen above the pre-war level of 156, marking a limited JPY gain. Snap back in vol risk premia favors hedging short vol exposure. With the Fed n likely to be in “wait and see” mode for now, we have sympathy for the drop in top-left implied vol that has now fully reversed the post-conflict spike. As we noted, relatively static policy with a moderate growth backdrop is typically supportive vol-selling even taking the vol premium compression into account. Episodes of higher volatility over the last year—such as the tariff announcements and the threats to Fed independence—have shown that vol markets tend to move swiftly towards relief, establishing a range after the first sign of de-escalation, even in instances where the ultimate outcome or impacts have remained uncertain. While not an impediment to short vol expressions working on average, the decline in vol does leave a thinner cushion to renewed vol spikes, something we think favors overlaying short-vol strategies with hedges such as long vega exposure. Beware of comparative (dis)advantage: Since the start of Donald Trump’s second mandate, the US has stepped up its own production of semiconductors and other electronic components (14% above the 2010–24 trend). However, China and other Asian producers have so far comfortably retained their comparative advantage – and this is not something that tends to shift from one country to another year in, year out (for more, see South Korea and Taiwan: Fair winds set to boost chip sector, dated 31 October 2025). As the US is set to remain a price-taker for the foreseeable future, our simulation embeds higher (non-commodity) import prices, not just in the US but elsewhere across DM too. This is not to say that the US and Europe will import inflationary pressure from each of their trading partners. For example, our simulation eventually finds lower input costs in China, even if wages were to move somewhat higher, consistent with ample power availability in the country. This is one reason why China’s export prices end our simulation well below the baseline. Still, the net impact is likely to be inflationary, albeit not extraordinarily so, our modelling finds. 22 Fig. 37: Prices of DRAM and NAND memory chips* have skyrocketed amid tight supply KEY DRIVERS 15/04/2026 International trade: Do not bank on cheaper imports Niccolo Carrara, Emerging Markets Economist | BNP Paribas London Branch Sources: US Census Bureau, US BEA, Federal Reserve, Macrobond, BNP Pariba

records.text: . Methodologically, we regress changes in Z6 STIRT yields across liquid DM curves (ex-JP) against the upside and downside components of oil returns using 10- minute frequency data. We show in Figure 3 that the beta to the downside moves of oil have materially increased since March 20th. We repeat the same procedure for G9 USDccy pairs in Figure 4. We interpret the widening gap between downside and upside beta as evidence of a shift in reaction function. Whereas rates previously responded symmetrically to oil price action, they are now significantly less sensitive to oil rallies than oil sell-offs. We think a similar story can be said in FX though the dollar has historically reacted more negatively to the downside of oil which gives us further confirmation in our short USD positions (vs SEK, AUD & JPY). This surprise has become a seasonal norm, driven partly by front-loaded policy support that secures a strong start to the year. The global energy shock due to the Middle East conflict did not have much of an impact on China’s economic activities in March and Q1. Like the pattern in recent years, we expect a mild slowdown in Q2 because of an unfavorable base effect for retail sales and weaker policy support after a strong Q1. Policy on hold in Q2: Chinese policymaking is reactive, not pre-emptive. The quarterly Politburo meeting later this month will likely deem Q1’s performance satisfactory and see the economy on track to meet the 4.5%–5% growth target this year. Although the energy-crisis impact may become slightly stronger in Q2, policymakers are likely to stay calm and adopt a wait-and-see stance rather than jump the gun. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 16 Apr 2026 10:18:07 ET │ 10 pages US Economics Another few weeks of lower claims before May increases CITI'S TAKE Initial claims fell to 207k the week of April 11, pulling back about as expected after a holiday week. Continuing claims rebounded to 1818k the week of April 4 but have been on a downward trend since late 2025. While this could reflect increased hiring, we would caution that continuing claims will be a less reliable indicator of total unemployment the longer that a gradual weakening in the labor market is primarily driven by low hiring. While initial claims continue to suggest layoffs remain low, we are on the lookout for familiar patterns of rising claims into the summer months. This would imply another 3-4 weeks of stable initial claims before larger increase in May/early-June. If these familiar patterns repeat, this would suggest to us that still-low hiring is enough to push the unemployment rate above 4.5% by late summer. The Dollar continued to weaken over the last n week, which is consistent with the recovery in global risk sentiment. The price action on Friday in particular demonstrated that FX markets for now continue to respond according to a combination of risk betas and commodity exposures as markets assess the tails around the conflict and its implications. While we expect the FX responsiveness to spot commodity price moves to fade (eventually), we think the growth implications—which are directly linked to terms of trade—will take longer to be fully understood and reflected. Based on the forecast revisions we have made so far, we expect this to lead to a selectively stronger Dollar relative to what we forecasted prior to the conflict. records.text: e between current employment levels and those needed for current value added levels under pre-Covid productivity trend Source: BofA Global Research BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH Less value added than output losses, but employment still looks high There is a certain dichotomy between output and value-added data in the manufacturing sector in particular. Compared to 2019 average levels, manufacturing value added was down “only” c 5% in Germany, while manufacturing output contracted by more than double that. That is a relative silver lining, as production reallocation elsewhere may have succeeded in limiting more severe outcomes for the macroeconomy (Exhibit 8) But regular readers know our concern over the risk of labour hoarding in the Euro area. We got the timing wrong after Covid. But the persistent decline in German manufacturing (both output and value added) has eventually triggered job shedding, with sector employment now down c 7% vs 2019 levels. A comparison of actual productivity and pre-Covid trend implied productivity was suggesting labour hoarding for a while. The gap has reduced. But unfortunately, it was labour shedding rather than sector growth that delivered the adjustment. That has us worried on two fronts: 1) the resilience in the German labour market is gone. Additional manufacturing weakness may pass through immediately to the labour market now, amplifying domestic demand weakness via the consumer. 2) For the rest of the Euro area, labour hoarding seems to be ongoing.

Second, it is likely that this partly reflects the fact that commodity markets have priced this as a temporary shock throughout. We pointed this out in the early days of the conflict and it remains true today, which helps explain the lingering effects in some physical markets like dated crude—and, to a lesser extent, front-end rates—compared to longer-duration assets like FX. Third, especially when comparing to the 2022 energy shock, it is worth noting that this crisis is most acute for the countries with more managed currencies—up to and including the Dollar pegs in the GCC. It should not be a surprise that currencies in Asia tend to be more stable than other regions (Exhibit 2), and a raft of currency management decisions in some of the countries that are likely to see the biggest shift in their current account balances can also help account for the more muted broad Dollar response thus far. Relatedly, we believe this also accounts for the drop in US custody holdings, rather than a sign of accelerated de-Dollarization efforts (more in the CNY bullet and last week’s Trader). Page 12 From terminal to 10y Matthew Raskin | Strategist | +1-212-250-1741 Earlier in the week we looked at terminal pricing. We argued that the recent rise in terminal SOFR overstates the shift in expectations for the Fed’s (real) policy stance given that the higher rate mostly reflects increases in near -dated term premia and inflation expectations. Today we look out the curve to consider implications for the 10 -year Treasury yield. As the chart shows, since the Fed concluded its hiking cycle in July 2023, the terminal rate (measured as the trough in SOFR futures) and 10y UST have tracked closely, though with a discrete shift in the spread between them last April. We interpreted that shift as driven by an increase in term premia though noted that the pricing-in of additional cuts -through-neutral should also widen the terminal - 10y spread (see the earlier note’s appendix on this). Over the past year, terminal and 10y have continued to correlate highly, but very recently the gap between them has narrowed alongside the rise in terminal. This likely reflects a bear-flattening of term premia as investors hedge risks associated with the energy supply shock, as well as some pricing-out of cuts-through-neutral (and pricing-in of hikes) given the outlook for growth and inflation. records.text: M Idea 4 EGBs & SSAs EGB spreads spent most of the week in a tight range before tightening on positive Middle East news. We recommend an overall neutral stance on EGBs focusing on some RV opportunities. We remain of the view that EGB tighteners do not offer particularly good value given 1) historically tight levels, 2) higher vol, making carry to risk ratios worse, 3) a potential delay in the rating upgrade cycle in the periphery and 4) lingering risks ahead: should Middle East tensions fade, upcoming political elections could dampen appetite for carry. To be clear we are not arguing for widening either. The recent newsflow has clearly been supportive of spreads: 1) Despite failing to reach an agreement, Iran and the US have maintained a ceasefire, now extended to Israel–Lebanon, which markets have interpreted as signalling limited appetite for escalation on both sides, 2) the election in Hungary last week is seen as positive for euro area policymaking in general, at the margin supporting tighter EGB spreads. On supply, over recent days, euro area sovereigns have taken advantage of the risk on window to access the market via syndications. In particular, this week we have seen new bond syndications from France (with a new green 10y benchmark despite the country already being scheduled to come to the market with regular auctions) and Italy. records.text: CHF and SEK: Rates Strategy Neither too fast nor too late Through the fog, central banks are signalling a middle road between reacting abruptly and moving too slowly. The SNB continues to emphasize currency risks, as opposed to energy price concerns. In Sweden, recent data were dovish, but markets shouldn't extrapolate. We recommend paying SEK 5y5y vs EUR. Scarred by the 2021-22 global inflation episode, markets assumed that central banks would now rather err on the side of pre-emption, given the non-negligible reputational cost of being late twice. However, as we approach another round of meetings, most central banks appear to be signalling a middle road between reacting too abruptly and repeating past delays, thereby pushing back against the idea of a clear, mechanical link between higher energy prices and policy rates. Perhaps they are also hopeful that the recent US-Iran ceasefire could translate into a more sustainable outcome, allowing energy prices to fall further. In fact, EU natural gas prices have already reversed the bulk of their post Iran conflict rally across the curve, while bottlenecks in oil products remain ( Figure 1). Despite surface similarities, the current inflation backdrop – and accompanying monetary conditions – are undeniably different than they were ahead of the Ukraine-war energy shock, potentially affording policymakers greater scope for patience. Since our estimate is based on data on union negotiated wages and unions are likely trying to actively limit substitution, the economy-wide share for additional pay could be lower. Second, for the qualitative angle we looked at Bundesbank’s data for negotiated wages with and without one-off payments and assess differences in the catch-up pattern with inflation. From this we note three things: First, in pre-covid times, one-off payments hardly mattered for total pay growth; second, once the scheme was in place they accounted for a sizable share of negotiated wages (around 20-30% of wage growth came from one-offs); third, compared to the actual inflation surge total negotiated wage increases were initially much lower than usual (in 2015-19 one percent of headline inflation was associated with nominal wage growth of more than two percent compared to a factor of less than one during 2022-23). And from the fact that wage growth even with a large share of one-off pay was lagging, we conclude some (and potentially a lot) of the one-off pay was likely substituting for regular pay increases, at least initially. These include stretched equity valuations in the US tech sector, which has high energy demand, and growing risks in opaque private credit markets, particularly where they intersect with the IT sector. • Diverging Views on Second-Round Effects: There was a significant internal discussion on the potential for second-round inflation effects. Conversely, since the start of the Iran conflict, sectors vulnerable to energy/commodity price inflation (such as from oil/nat gas/fertilizer etc) have been sold more, with swings to Chemicals, Transportation, and Consumer Products, as well as in Gaming/Leisure and Retail, with the last two presumably on concerns around consumer sentiment. Chemicals, for example, decreased in February by -0.6% in the US and -0.4% in Europe but then increased in March by +2.3% in the US and +0.2% in Europe. On 5 March, EM vol surpassed DM for the first time since ‘Liberation Day’. However, as March passed, volatility failed to gain traction. At its peak, EM FX vol reached a level consistent with its long -term (20yr) average. However, since then, vol has declined (Figure 2). In part, FX intervention on behalf of central banks helped, as does the existence of sizable strategic oil reserves in the world’s largest e conomies. However, by all measures this has been an unusual geopolitical event. Call it complacency, or a desire to believe that the US and Iran are on the brink of a deal, global markets, for want of a better word, are calm. Some currencies, like HUF, BRL and ZAR have snapped back strongly. There is already evidence in the pattern of FX flows that institutional investors began April with a less negative mindset with a resumption of flows into the ZAR and INR, two highly volatility currencies that, of any in EM, are sensitive to high oil prices. Good news from the cycle. Throughout last year, the one standout in terms of economic data was the resilience of EM Asia to President Trump’s tariffs. Exports soared. Conversations at industry events have highlighted a push-pull between a recognition that cost protections are needed post Vogtle, but also that utilities/developers need to have some incentive to keep costs within budget. Even so, we expect prices to remain higher than up to February, and a range of nations are likely to build up reserves over the next few years. If it is to take some time for adjustments to inflation outlooks, any decline in interest rates is likely to be muted. In the money market the pricing of an April rate hike has receded further. A rate hike would in itself be possible if there is freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz after this weekend. This means the meeting at end- April is likely to take place before uncertainties have been completely eliminated. Also, we think the government will want the BoJ to take only gradual action. CNY: The short and the long of it. After pausing for energy in March with small FX n outflows, CNY has resumed its grind stronger in recent weeks, and both the CNY fix and offshore spot are now at stronger levels versus the Dollar than at the start of the War. In the short-term, the war has imparted a negative impulse to China’s trade balance with both higher energy prices and downward growth revisions to China’s trading partners, particularly in lower-income EM economies that account for almost 40% of overall exports as per our China team. In the long-term, however, China may prove an unlikely beneficiary from recent events. On the trade front, it would not be surprising if the Iran War accelerates global investment in energy security and renewable sources, which would provide a positive impulse to China’s exports given its dominant position across clean energy supply chains. Over the short-term, we are also sceptical that recent developments will straightforwardly translate into more ‘petro-yuan’, not least because energy exports from the middle-east are currently crimped and prioritisation of immediate capacity rebuilding may dominate, so there are likely to be smaller surpluses to recycle. ECB—Less Urgency to Act Recent developments point to reduced urgency for ECB rate hikes. First, energy prices have fallen from their peak following last week’s ceasefire, as April shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has slowly picked up and risk premia have declined (Exhibit 1). TTF gas prices, for example, have declined from above 60 EUR/MWh in mid-March to almost 40 EUR/MWh now. As a result, our energy index— which averages Brent and TTF prices—has declined 24% since its March peak (but remains up 52% since the start of the year). Second, recent price-related indicators have not moved up decisively (Exhibit 2). Several price surveys have increased materially, including firms’ input prices and short-term inflation expectations. But March flash inflation moved up less than expected (with headline at 2.5% vs 2.7% initially expected), while surveys on output prices (especially in services) and longer-term inflation expectations have moved little so far. Also, the incoming activity data have been softer, including recent surveys (particularly the expectations components) and the pre-conflict hard data (pushing down our Q1 GDP tracking estimate from 0.3% to 0.2%). records.text: November through February. Poland 2.0? This election echoes the Polish election in 2023, where the populist government brought a more EU friendly leader into power, unlocking EU funds and triggering a sharp rerating of assets. Markets rallied sharply into and out of the Polish election, with backend yields compressing and the zloty strengthening 4%. The rally continued until mid-December (Figure 11), approximately two months. We have seen similar price action in Hungarian assets out of this election and we do expect the rally to continue, barring any escalation in the Iran conflict. There are some key difference between Poland in 2023 and Hungary today (Hungary faces 27 "super milestones" vs Poland's 3, see Hungary Economics - Post-election challenges for more details). However, the Tisza supermajority in parliament gives Prime Minister Magyar more power than President Tusk had at the time and Brussels also seems willing to support the unfreezing of funds with credible commitment. There is an August deadline for EUR 9.5bln in funds from the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) that seems out of reach, but our economists expect some of the funds to be released (Hungary Economics - Post-election challenges). records.text: ABS Operator track record takes center stage in datacenter ABS Last week we discussed the variances within datacenter ABS master trusts and introduced a framework for underwriting some of the nuances of the sector. Today, we take a closer look, equalizing fundamental metrics between trusts and exploring possible drivers of secondary market spreads. We argue that, while the market is most clearly prioritizing operator track record, fundamentals and tenant mix should still be heavily considered by investors when choosing trusts. Normalizing inconsistencies in DSCR reporting Datacenter master trusts typically report a debt service coverage ratio, but the methodology varies by trust, with two main issues driving most of the differences. First, whether or not interest expense from lower rated classes of debt outstanding should be considered, and second, whether or not debt service coverage ratios should be limited to interest expense only, or include a mortgage style amortization of principal as well. While there is no definitive standard as to how DSCR should be calculated, we compare two approaches to the measure of a trust’s debt servicing capacity: the least conservative version of the calculation (no lower class interest expense and no amortization are considered) and the most conservative (all classes of interest expense as well as amortization are considered), as these represent the reasonable outer bounds of a trust’s debt servicing capacity. records.text: The turtle and the hare: While our model results suggest the US benefits the most from an AI boom, they might underestimate the long-run benefits for the eurozone. Although the bloc has probably missed out on the AI investment boom, we think it can extract significant ‘user surplus’ from this technology. AI does not necessarily just yield a first-mover advantage; there could also be a second-mover advantage from smart and fast adoption of AI, without having to commit large investments to its development (see Garicano, 2025). By compressing transaction costs and reducing frictions, AI might help further integration and unify markets. Under this view, the EU could get a large benefit from the adoption of AI, and while the US might lead early, Europe could benefit later. This could mean that rather than a permanent structural divergence, there is a risk of asymmetric timing effects with positive absolute gains for both. This requires a regulatory framework that enables experimenting and switching between AI solutions seamlessly. As discussed on page 30, such a regulatory framework enabled the US investment boom during the late-stage ICT revolution, while a restrictive environment slowed down early electrification in the UK. Different strategies: The argument is rooted in the idea that the US and the EU could be optimising for different channels of AI value creation. The US frames AI as a geopolitical race. records.text: Frontier FX and the Energy Shock. Most Frontier currencies have seen limited n volatility since the start of the Iran war, particularly relative to the evolution of their terms of trade (Exhibit 8). This largely reflects the heavily managed nature of most of these currencies. But there are exceptions to this, with the outperformance of currencies of oil exporters such as KZT and NGN versus the EGP which has depreciated by more than 10%. Our GSDEER model points to an extension of this relative performance driven by terms of trade, with stronger fair values across oil exporters and weaker fair values for managed currencies of importers. In particular, in a higher-for-longer energy price world, we see risks as skewed towards appreciation in the Nigerian Naira and the Ghanaian Cedi. We have revised our USD/NGN forecasts stronger to reflect this. We also expect a break from the currency stability or appreciation trends of energy importers Kenya and Pakistan in a scenario of a continued terms-of-trade shock, given heavy Middle-East energy import dependence and the potential for foreign reserve deterioration from thin buffers the longer the shock lasts. We see TRY and EGP as potential longs in the event of a sustained geopolitical de-escalation, especially as EGP seems to have lagged the retracement of post-war losses within EM FX. records.text: Why we built our framework: The bleeding-edge technology in Douglas Adams’s The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy throws up absurd outcomes, such as the appearance of a whale and a bowl of petunias above an unsuspecting planet. While we do not expect AI to deliver that level of unknown unknown, its enormous implications do justify the recent proliferation of analyses on its economic impact. We join the fray because we see a ‘double gap’ in the literature. ▪ In our view, most of the research thus far lacks a rigorous general equilibrium framework that considers not only the mechanical impact of stronger productivity but also positive sentiment effects and associated demand boosts. We think computations of the impact of AI are skewed if they do not consider the massive wealth effects already created by the stock market rally and the trillions of capex dollars pledged to data centres. Productivity shocks are not just about supply; demand is a factor too. ▪ Most research employs a quasi-accounting approach, which calculates current time/cost savings based on current AI technology. Though such estimates can be revised as technology evolves, we believe that methodology should embed a recognition of AI as a general-purpose technology that will develop further and whose scope of application will expand. While companies can make different choices on how to implement this, most companies use it as a phone a friend type role for unusual situations or extra advice, not to regularly remote control them. AVs only implement the advice coming from remote assistance if they can do so safely. For example, as noted by Waymo, if an emergency vehicle is occupying a lane with its lights on and appears parked at the entrance of a lane, and the robotaxi is uncertain if the lane is closed, it could query a remote assistance agent to verify if the lane is open. Looking to FY2026, any (tactical) buying will probably require banks to sense that JGBs are cheap relative to their expectations for the BoJ’s terminal rate level. records.text: US Economics Weekly17 April 2026 ab 8 Balance sheet update The Federal Reserve ended balance sheet runoff on December 1, and began "reserve management purchases" (RMP) on December 12 with bill purchases running ~$40 billion per month on top of reinvestment purchases. This week, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York announced it would reduce the RMP to a pace of $25 billion in the coming period April 14 - May 13, in addition to an estimated ~$16 billion in reinvestments (see here). This step down in the pace of purchases was signalled last month when the FRBNY published expectations of this adjustment in a blog (see here): “After the TGA peaks in April, there won’t be a need to continue RMPs at the present elevated pace, consistent with the Desk’s December statement. Accordingly, the monthly RMP pace is likely to be significantly reduced beginning with the purchase period spanning mid-April to mid-May; to account for uncertainty and other factors, the reduction may be somewhat gradual.” We updated our balance sheet projections to take on board the specifics, assuming a ~ $25 billion per month pace of reserve management purchases to year-end. We'd assume that pace needs to pick back up at some point, and pencilled in that the monthly pace of purchases will be lifted to ~$40 billion per month in 2027 and ~$50 billion per month in 2028 in order to ensure ample reserves as the economy and the Fed's other liabilities rise. If GCC countries were to reevaluate their US ties, this could lead to redirection of petrodollars away from the US. A larger share of energy being traded in currencies other than the USD could mean reduced US asset exposure for oil exporters. For the GCC countries, this might also cause doubt around existing commitments for US investments. Oil exporters typically recycle their current account surpluses in USD. This could change via three channels: 1) unrealized FDI commitments, 2) non- USD-denominated oil transactions and 3) reduced buying of US assets. This is negative for the USD, but we do not anticipate a meaningful move given that GCC makes up just 4% of the total foreign holdings of US assets. Oil exporters naturally tend to have current account surpluses. Historically, a large proportion of this is recycled to the US. Additionally, as oil is predominately traded in USDs they have had a natural preference for the USD. Below we explore the channels through which this could shift. The three entities to focus on are the GCC, Russia and Norway (Fig.1). With Russia increasingly not a buyer of USDs we instead focus on the GCC and Norway. That said, for investors looking for incremental spread and yield and comfortable moving down the capital stack, Money Center subordinated debt provides a more compelling opportunity vs. other subsectors. USD IG Banks: Supply-driven widening creates a better entry point Banks have underperformed Non-Financials year to date. We view the move as largely driven by heavy supply and rich starting valuations and not driven by a meaningful deterioration in fundamentals. USD IG Bank sector spreads entered the year trading 13bp tight to Non-Financials, but that relative value relationship has attenuated as the sector has cheapened by roughly 10bp (Exhibit 1). The main driver of the widening, in our view, has been investor anticipation and digestion of the heavy primary calendar for debt issuance. Banks have already issued $242 billion year to date, marking the strongest issuance pace of the past two decades. Importantly, this has not been a story of one specific part of the capital structure doing the heavy lifting. Supply patterns have been relatively balanced, which, in our view, pushes back against the narrative that prospective deregulation will materially reduce the cost of capital for large banks via lower ‘bail-in’ debt needs (which refers to debt that would be ‘loss absorbing’ in stress scenarios). Bail-in bonds have still accounted for roughly 60% of gross bank supply in 2026

We expect for the length of rides completed by AVs to converge with n the average miles per trip completed by a human driver as Waymo expands their operating zones within existing markets. Specifically, we expect for the average miles per trip of a Waymo to scale from 7 miles in 2025 to 10 miles by 2035. ASP per mile. Today, both the broader AV industry and Waymo have a higher ASP n per mile relative to human rideshare. While this has improved over the last several months, we still view the industry to have higher ASPs (on a per mile basis) than human rides, with AVs charging $2.90 per mile (GSe) in 2025, compared to human rideshare of $2.50. By 2030, we expect the ASP per mile of an autonomous vehicle to be lower than that of a human driver. Given these growth drivers, we expect for Waymo to grow gross bookings at a 51% CAGR over the next 10 years (2025-2035) and reach $8.5 bn in gross bookings by 2030 and $20 bn+ by 2035. We forecast that US gross bookings will remain >85% of total bookings in 2030, and by 2035, that international markets will become more meaningful in terms of their contribution to gross bookings. If this holds, a downward revision of similar magnitude in the FY26/27 financing requirement would be published and this might see a modest reduction in gilt supply. We would see this being most easily accommodated by a reduction in the unallocated issuance basket (currently £30.5bn). Implicitly, this would reduce the upsizing of future syndicated supply and tenders and maybe viewed as supportive for long-end spreads since the limited long-end supply program (£8bn in auctions, £15bn in syndications) would leave it as a natural beneficiary of additional intra-fiscal-year discretionary supply. This leaves the outlook for spreads as complex. The near-term bullish impetus that might come from limited supply and potential reduction in the overall gilt supply for FY26/27 has to be balanced against a more sombre medium-term picture of ongoing spending pressures and a potential for heightened political risk in the aftermath of the local elections on 7 May. All told, we would expect to see better selling of gilt spreads into strength from discretionary macro investors. The stabilising of this move would have to come from domestic asset swap investors but if volatility remains high and political risk unresolved, they might well be more circumspect in managing their flows. records.text: Commodity price volatility relative to rates and equity market volatility appears to be a key driver of the difference. In the current shock, shifts in volatility have been more coincident across assets than they were in 2022 (Exhibit 4). Rates and equity volatility also increased more sharply than commodity price volatility. Intuitively, in that scenario, FX investors can get caught wrong-footed if purely positioned around the terms of trade implications. That suggests that if rates and equities volatility fall more quickly than commodities volatility, TOT could become the more dominant driver again. But it also raises the risk that shifts in volatility remain more correlated across assets, meaning that positioning in FX purely based on the TOT implications would yield poorer results. However, trading TOT through expressions that minimize the beta to risk should more consistently produce positive returns, even if rates and equity vol pick up again alongside an increase in commodities vol. A basket of long BRL, AUD, NOK and short SEK, ZAR, KRW has so far followed a strikingly similar path of returns as in 2022 and should be an effective USD-neutral expression if the lingering upside risks to energy prices materialize (Exhibit 5). But if energy prices see further relief, that basket should see some reversal. records.text: US Economics 16 April 2026 Citi Research 2 Data – Initial jobless claims pulled back to 207k for the week of April 11, a bit more than consensus expectations, after rising to 218k the week of April 4. Initial claims fell the most (seasonally adjusted) in NJ (-1.8k) and OR (-2.2k) and rose in states like CA (+2.1k) and VA (+2.6k). Continuing claims rose to 1818k the week of April 4 from a downwardly revised 1787k the week of March 28. Citi’s view – Both initial and continuing jobless claims remain at low levels indicative of a still low-firing labor market. Continuing claims have declined substantially from higher levels in mid-2025. The pullback in initial claims could also reflect some normalization after a holiday week the week before. In theory, the decline in continuing claims could reflect a pick-up in hiring and a decline in the unemployment rate. But as the weakening trend in the labor market has been driven by low hiring over the last ~ 3 years, continuing claims will become a less reliable signal for total unemployment. Laid-off workers could expire the usual 26-week benefit for unemployment insurance (and drop off continuing claims) without being rehired in a low-hiring environment, while new flows into unemployment insurance would remain low with low layoffs. Continuing claims have not been as reliable an indicator for the unemployment rate since around 2024, earlier in the cycle of a gradually weakening labor market. The only way to conclude that this risk is not under-priced would be to assume that, absent the war, the US stock market would have had a strong rally. The curious case of gold The case of gold is also worth exploring. Gold is the preferred asset to hedge against inflation but also against geopolitical risk. Since the US decided to impose sanctions on Russia and effectively weaponize the dollar, the demand for gold skyrocketed as central banks and governments substituted away from US Treasuries into gold. The interesting issue is that, when the Iran war erupted, gold sold off instead of rallying, despite the war being a textbook geopolitical shock. This is also a totally rational price action. The selloff has two components. The first one is easy to see. As central banks and foreign governments started to buy gold, speculative positions mounted on top. As the risk-off shock of the war induced de-risking, gold was impacted as any other risky position. The second component is more subtle. Gold was bought by central banks and governments as insurance, a form of precautionary savings. As the probability of having a geopolitical event goes up, the demand for gold increases, pushing up its price. But when the geopolitical event occurs, those who bought gold as a form of precautionary saving now use those savings in gold to cushion the shock. records.text: Michael Metcalfe 16 April 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Alt data update: Forecasts look out of time In mid-April, financial markets appear to assume the Middle East conflict will soon be over, yet are only starting to digest the economic impact of the shock. The alternative data we track suggest inflation and growth forecasts are both at risk, albeit in different directions. In terms of economic contagion, this is first and foremost an inflation shock. Since early March, State Street PriceStats has reinforced Alberto Cavallo’s warning that large shocks travel fast: our US series recorded its largest ever month-over-month rise, jumping 1.4% (nsa). A few weeks later, the BLS official data (ex shelter) matched that move almost exactly (Figure 1). The good news is that core inflation remained tepid—consistent with our forecast and in sharp contrast to 2022. The March takeaway is that headline inflation was hit materially, but pressures into core have so far been contained, helping explain the relatively benign reaction from forecasters and markets. But will that last? PriceStats also gives an early read on April (first eleven days). The message is similar: the average price level is ~80bps above March. Let’s take a closer look at the German package and its likely macroeconomic impact. The package consists of two measures: (i) a two-month reduction in energy tax levied on fuels together with a lower VAT payment of around 17ct/l (effective 1-May at the earliest) and (ii) the possibility of a one-off payment by employers to their employees of up to €1,000 during 2026. The lump sum is exempted from income tax and social security contributions (effectively a gross-equals-net payment). To start off with our headline finding: We estimate that the growth upside could be around 5-20bp for 2026, mostly through private consumption (which could be 10- 30bp higher). The main impact should come from the one-off payment. For inflation, we expect a temporary dampening of around 25bp for German headline HICP (7bp for euro area) from the tax cut, all else equal. This will reverse once the tax rate is normalised. Before we dive deeper into our assessment, let’s briefly recap our thinking of the growth downside for Germany from higher energy prices. We recently lowered our forecast for GDP growth to 0.5%Y in 2026 and 0.9%Y in 2027 from previously 1.0%Y and 1.3%Y respectively (see here). records.text: US Economics Weekly17 April 2026 ab 4 Updating the FOMC reaction function weights Last year we extended our analysis of the FOMC reaction function using the Summary or Economic Projections' assumptions of appropriate policy, or 'dot plot' to estimate the weights being placed on inflation versus the labor market in the setting of monetary policy. The results were somewhat surprising and do not suggest a high bar to more rate cuts to come. We added the March SEP to the analysis, and that only further emphasized that the FOMC reaction function had shifted over the course of the last five years to put the labor market on more equal footing with inflation. Many clients argue that the FOMC has been too dovish. Or, they argue the FOMC shifted too far to prioritizing the labor market. We spent a lot of 2025 writing about Chair Powell's risk management framework. However, when we look at the data, the FOMC has merely gone from ignoring the labor market to putting it on more equal footing, as their legal mandate suggests. In their latest interpretation of their goals, the FOMC writes " if the Committee judges that the objectives are not complementary, it follows a balanced approach in promoting them."
