Page 4 With this background, we expect Warsh might go out of his way to emphasize the importance of Fed independence and distance himself from the administration’s strong calls for rate cuts. Other topics: Timeline for his nomination and Fed personnel Will Warsh comment on the DoJ investigation and Powell’s openness to staying on the Board as a governor? A critical unknown is when Warsh’s nomination will move through the Senate Banking Committee and to the full Senate for approval. Senator Tillis recently repeated his commitment to block all nominees while the Department of Justice’s investigation of Chair Powell is active. Thus, Warsh is likely to be asked about his views on that investigation. He will likely decline to comment on this topic, as he looks to balance the administration’s support for this investigation against the Fed’s stance. Relatedly, Warsh is likely to be asked about the potential for Powell to remain on the Board as a governor after his term as chair ends, a possibility Powell has left open so far. Officials in the Trump administration have been critical of this possibility. However, given Warsh’s need to be able to effectively lead the Committee once his nomination is approved – a Committee that could well include Powell – we expect he will not express a strong opinion on Powell’s plans. records.text: AV trucking market is currently small but now poised to ramp We now estimate that the AV trucking market in the US will reach $16 bn in 2030, slightly down from $18 bn prior (as volume in 2026 is more likely to be filled with upfitting than OEM lineside integration), and we introduce our 2035 forecast of $105 bn. When including global markets, we estimate that the AV trucking market in 2035 could be ~$560 bn. This is enabled by the US AV truck fleet growing from low levels today, to ~24K in 2030, and ~161K in 2035, and a global fleet growing from a few thousand today (primarily in China) to ~1.27 mn as well as increasing miles per truck as ODDs expand. AV trucking companies in North America, including Aurora, Kodiak, Waabi, and Plus plan to scale commercially in 2026/2027, with Aurora expecting to expand from 10 AV trucks at the end of 2025 to >200 by the end of 2026 (and we assume to over a thousand starting in 2028). We expect that part of the increased adoption and deployments through 2035 will be driven by the cost of AV trucking improving relative to a human driver. At present, we believe the additional upfront costs to make an AV truck in the US are ~$125K-$150K, and we expect this to decline to a premium of ~$35-40K in 2035, driven by improved hardware costs and economies of scale. Given the nature of the shock, which is concentrated in demand before improvements in supply are realised, we estimate inflation could rise around 0.2pp in the near term, before productivity gains give way to a disinflationary impulse in the medium term. This is broadly similar to the dynamics that we expect to see in the US, simply at a smaller magnitude. Benign implications for labour market: These results point to a relatively benign outcome for the UK labour market. While there are risks around this (see page 17), we assume limited impacts on headline unemployment figures due to the experience of past productivity shocks and an overall positive demand impact. This looks broadly consistent with the Bank of England’s February 2026 agents’ summary of business conditions, which suggests a bias among firms to tackle any increase in demand with investment growth (spending more on automation and AI) rather than employment growth (increasing headcount). So far, UK employers have not resorted to active job shedding – at least not due to AI. Moreover, the UK Employment Rights Act (which starts to take effect this year), should provide more protections for workers, including those facing collective redundancy proposals, and help mitigate some of the potential negative impact. records.text: he output of our simulations is outlined over the next few pages and detailed in the Results section. What our main findings are: Economic actors are forward looking, and demand tends to ramp up early in a boom. We expect robust demand to support re- employment even if the AI shock disrupts entire occupations or industries. The actual productivity boom might take time to play out, as firms figure out how to apply the new technology efficiently at scale. We think the net effect of the AI boom could be inflationary, especially early on. Individuals might face difficulty with the labour market transition, even with robust macroeconomic outcomes, highlighting the importance of social support. Where we might be wrong: In the Key drivers section, we identify our NiGEM calibration assumptions and the implications if they are different. Given we use past productivity shocks as a reference, our estimates might grossly under- estimate GDP outcomes. Risks are not just about calibration, though. ▪ ‘Irrational exuberance’ among firms and investors could cause a bust akin to those that ended the 1920s and 1990s booms, especially if involving leverage. ▪ Policy uncertainty and macroeconomic volatility might dampen the impacts of AI. ▪ In calculating central banks’ policy, errors could arise in either direction from rising neutral rates and significant effects on labour markets. ▪ Unlike in the past, the AI revolution may be too fast for the labour market to absorb, increasing unemployment.

records.text: The pace of autonomous technology commercialization has accelerated since our June 2025 report, “Framing profit pools in rideshare, trucking, and insurance as AVs move from concept to commercialization”. This is being driven by both a growing number of deployments in the US and China, and also international expansions into new geographies including EMEA. These deployments are enabled by both captive technology development (e.g. at Waymo, Tesla, Pony AI, etc) and a growing set of merchant Physical AI tools including from companies such as Nvidia (e.g. Alpamayo). In fact, Nvidia discussed numerous Physical AI and AV partnerships at GTC 2026 including with Mercedes, Uber, GM, BYD, Geely, and Hyundai. We expect there to ultimately be multiple providers of autonomous technology. With the now more global ramps of several companies, we update our AV profit pools analysis to include key global regions for robotaxis and Class 8 trucks, and we also frame the market potential from “robots that drive” more broadly including delivery bots. In addition, we update our estimates for the mix of partially and fully autonomous consumer vehicles (e.g. L3-L5 classifications). We now estimate that the AV robotaxi market in the US will reach $19 bn in 2030, up from $7 bn prior, and we introduce our 2035 forecast of $48 bn. records.text: M Update 2 Policy implications: The biggest risk to our forecasts, outside another potential uptick in commodity prices, remains the policy mix. Per the just released IMF forecasts, UK is due for easily the largest fiscal tightening in all of G7. As noted, the BoE has already tightened financial conditions meaningfully. Despite the considerable resilience of the externally-oriented high value-added sectors, we struggle to see how this policy mix yields growth that can be, at best, modestly positive. We, hence, think the recent easing in financial conditions probably has more to run through this year, as we see the BoE on hold throughout 2026. Governor Bailey's remarks from DC reaffirm our post-March meeting views. That said, we continue to see the MPC as positing the policy dilemma as one between a long hold or "precautionary hikes" at the meetings in April and June, with the July meeting more likely to bring a meaningful shift in tone in the dovish direction - should the supply of oil and gas normalise, of course. A healthier starting point for the economy implies the Bank can be more focused on inflation risks in the very near term. We also note that while one should not extrapolate much from just one GDP print, a relatively solid starting point for the economy reaffirms our view that the fiscal fallout from the events in the Middle East - with commodity prices at their current levels - can be relatively easily managed. We expect to monitor a range of AI-related job displacement measures in coming quarters in order to tell whether reality is following our modelling results (see page 18). As a cautionary parallel, although the US’s ‘jobless recovery’ in 2001–03 was the result of more than just tech-related displacement, it shows that strong productivity and growing GDP growth do not automatically entail lower unemployment. Harder to quantify, we wonder about the drag on human capital if early-career workers find it harder to break into the job market or if offloading cognitive work to AI tools impairs human learning and judgment. Instead of flattening the playing field, such developments cascading from AI could increase stratification and inequality. Past is prologue: In the more pessimistic alternative, we suspect the unemployment rate could prove more volatile in the US than Europe. The US job market is historically more flexible – faster job cuts, but also faster matching – while the eurozone and other economies have tended to favour job-retention schemes. The assumption that displaced workers will quickly find new employment relies on three conditions: rapid up-skilling; sufficient demand for augmented-skill jobs; and modest frictions in labour mobility. Recent geopolitical events have highlighted the challenges faced by euro area public finances. In the near term, there is pressure to mitigate the impact of higher energy prices on households, and several governments have already implemented relief measures such as energy tax cuts. In the medium term, there is an increasingly obvious need to achieve strategic autonomy in defence, technology and energy, in addition to meeting climate targets. These trends could increase the demand for capital, thereby implyi ng upside risks for interest rates and term premia, especially real term premia. Looking at a simple metric 2, EUR real term premia have indeed risen since early 2025, broadly in line with nominal term premia (Figure). Valuations are now back at the levels observed around 2012 -2013, though still well below 2006 -2012 averages; before 2006 term premia were more tha n twice current levels, while fiscal deficits and debt levels were lower. Against this backdrop, the risk is that term premia widen further in the medium term, with real term premia perhaps proving more resilient (than nominal term premia) in case an Iran resolution or rapid AI progress were to weigh on perceptions of inflation risk. At the start of this year, moreover, we thought that relatively less of a price upswing in 1H26 vs 1H25/24/23 might also mean that the ONS will be better placed to more accurately seasonally adjust the GDP data. In recent years, note, UK growth tended to surge in 1Q, and flat-line through the remainder of the year - an issue we chalked down, in part, to ONS methodology. But after today, we worry a bit more about the residual methodological impact on the quarterly data from here. records.text: Price of power: In our model, energy prices are fully endogenous. The model suggests that energy prices remain above the pre-AI baseline for the entire duration of our simulation, but not enough to put the brakes on energy demand. We are comfortable leaving energy prices endogenous in the model for three main reasons. ▪ Our productivity shock is calibrated using historical analogues of other general- purpose technologies. These historical examples faced non-trivial implementation frictions themselves, as well as gradual adoption. As such, our productivity assumption embeds some frictions. ▪ Even if energy costs rise and constrain compute-intensive expansion at the frontier, diffusion across users can continue. Aggregate productivity can therefore increase through broader adoption, even if energy prices limit the pace of scaling at the top end. While such a binding constraint may have an impact on equity markets (which we also leave endogenous), it is not clear that it would significantly hamper long-run productivity trends. ▪ AI systems and supporting hardware may become more energy efficient over time. Improvements in algorithms or chip design could reduce the energy per unit of output. We would argue that this is somewhat embedded in our first consideration – and is also near impossible to forecast. There would likely be additional software revenue from L2 features (FSD, for example, is currently L2), but we expect this market to be increasingly competitive longer-term (with some OEMs in China now providing L2 technology as a standard feature). Addressing risks to personal ownership from AVs There is a view from some investors that the proliferation of AVs will materially lower the size of the personal vehicle market, given that personal vehicles are not used the majority of the time. While this is a possibility, our base case view is that this is too negative due to economic and use considerations. First, the cost of owning and operating a personal vehicle in the US was $0.77 to $1.00 per mile in 2025 according to AAA (at 10K and 15K miles traveled annually, respectively). This remains well below the cost of rideshare at >$2 nationally. records.text: For virtual driver models, similar to what Aurora plans to launch in partnership with Aumovio, we expect costs in the US (including hardware depreciation, cost of remote operation, etc.) to decline from >$1 in 2027 (when Aurora expects to launch with Aumovio) to ~$0.20 in 2035, as remote operators can supervise more vehicles and AV hardware costs decline. We expect revenue per mile in the US to decrease from $1.00 in 2027 to $0.60 in 2035, driven by increased competition and better costs (implying solid gross margin potential for a virtual driver). We estimate that the revenue potential for virtual driver technology will increase from $0.1 bn to ~$24 bn from 2027-2035 assuming all AV trucks in the US were to use a virtual driver model (although we believe that not all AVs will operate with the virtual driver model). Across the global fleet, the potential revenue under a similar assumption would be ~$116 bn in 2035, increasing from a relatively small level in 2027. Regulations In terms of regulations for AV trucks, similar to robotaxi and passenger AVs, AV trucks must also comply with the relevant FMVSS standards at the federal level, with AV-specific regulations set at the state level. Hesai (covered by Tina Hou) - Hesai is a leading lidar provider whose products cater to applications across advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS), autonomous mobility, and robotics with 33% revenue market share in 2024 globally. The company’s ADAS lidar shipments more than doubled in 2025 to 1.4 mn units and robotics shipments (inclusive of robotaxis) grew by more than 4x to ~239k units. We are Buy-rated. Our 12m target prices of US$34/HK$265 for ADR/H share are based on a 20x P/E multiple applied to Hesai’s 2030E non-GAAP EPS and discounted back to 2026E at a CoE of 11%. Risks include slower LiDAR adoption, intensified competition, customer pricing pressure, policy risk. The credibility risks are two-sided, however, between raising rates too early or too late. We suspect the BoE will take the advice more willingly than the ECB and stay received of Jun26 MPC SONIA. Calls for patience: The IMF advised this week that credible central banks should not rush to raise policy rates in response to conflict in the Middle East as it may “suffocate growth” (see Bloomberg, 15Apr26). BoE Governor Bailey said this “serious advice” would be taken into account and that judgements can’t be rushed (see Bloomberg, 15Apr26), adding to his push back on market pricing over recent weeks. The ECB’s Schnabel also said in Washington that the ECB “do not need to rush” (Bloomberg, 15Apr16) with President Lagarde saying earlier in the week that the ECB does not have a tightening bias (Bloomberg, 14Apr26). Data judgements and two-way credibility risk: Hikes at the April ECB/BoE meetings in two weeks seem highly unlikely, as is now priced. The question is whether this patience can extend to the June meetings in 8/9 weeks? First and foremost, much will depend on the conflict, whether the ceasefire (currently due to end next week) extends, whether a deal is found, and whether the Strait of Hormuz re-opens. records.text: 15 April 2026 Europe Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 2 The figures also illustrate how these dynamics could evolve over the coming months, based on a simple scenario in which commodity prices follow current forward curves , with all other factors held constant. Under these assumptions , the model suggests that input cost pressures could rise somewhat further in April, before gradually moderating, albeit remaining well above pre -war levels. Output prices would continue to trend higher for some months, stabilising also above pre- war levels by the end of the year. That said, both indicators would still be below the 2022 peaks. The implied increase in manufacturing output prices poses clear upside risks to goods inflation over the next 6 -12 months (Figure 13). If the risks were to materialise, core goods HICP could rise to an average of 0.9% YoY in 2026 vs our current forecast of 0.5%. Beyond energy-driven cost pressures, c oncerns around the emergence of broader supply chain disruptions are rising. The March PMIs already provided some evidence of mounting stress, with supplier s’ delivery times lengthening to the greatest extent since September 2022. Such pressures could amplify the inflationary shock (Figure 14). In a recent note, we find evidence for the UK that the passthrough from PMI output prices to inflation is stronger when supply chains are tighter. The ECB will need to remain vigilant on this. records.text: Outlook for the economy and prices (last updated 19 March) Real GDP growth in Q4 25 was revised up to 1.3% in the second estimate, reflecting strong capex, among other factors. Looking ahead, a rebound in inventory investment is expected following the large negative contribution seen this time around. Furthermore, housing investment, which fell sharply due to institutional factors in Q3, is likely to recover. Companies are actively investing to address labor shortages and rebuild supply chains in response to tariffs, and we continue to expect consumption to recover gradually on support from large wage increases and easing inflation. That said, the surge in crude oil prices stemming from the Middle East conflict is likely to exert some downside pressure on the economy, particularly on consumption. As the magnitude and duration of higher crude oil prices could cause the adverse impact on the economy to evolve over time, careful monitoring is warranted. On the price front, we expect CPI inflation excluding perishables (core) to ease as a trend, albeit with fluctuations, in the near term due mainly to declines (y/y base effects) in goods, especially food. However, inflation is increasingly sticky, suggesting any deceleration will be more moderate than we previously expected. Furthermore, services inflation has become increasingly robust as the dynamic synergy between wages and prices strengthens on the back of irreversible structural changes in the labor market. We take 2.12% (USD212k) profit on our long AUDCAD trade idea we opened on 19 March (see FX: CAD support to wane). The energy price shock from the Middle East- conflict has led the CAD to outperform the G10 complex, partly due to improved relative terms of trade. This had benefited Canada more than other energy exporters, which we thought was unjustified. Hence, we saw scope for the currency to come under pressure. This proved correct. Since the start of April, markets have been trading headlines suggesting potential de-escalation more actively. This has supported our position as markets re-engage with carry trades, of which AUD offers the highest vol-adjusted yield in G10, and given that AUD has one of the highest sensitivities to global risk sentiment. We would also point to CAD acting as a USD proxy as a reason for the price action. Given the scope of the rally and that our risk premium metrics have now moved to stretched levels, we are now wary of some consolidation. As such, now is an opportune time to lock in profits. We still see scope for the cross to extend higher in the medium term, as superannuation funds hedging away USD risk supports AUD structurally and because the CAD is particularly vulnerable to US trade policy

Nonetheless, risks to this call are biased to the dovish side in our view, with the ECB possibly delivering only one hike or looking through the shock entirely given it remains uncertain whether second-round effects will emerge once we consider the disinflation dynamic before the conflict. Although OIS markets have priced out expectations of a cut in April (~4bp priced), the OIS curve still reflects expectations of two further ECB hikes with around 55bp priced in cumu- latively by the end of 2026. While we continue to see ECB hiking twice this year, risks to this baseline are tilted to an underdelivery given that it can’t be ruled out that the ECB could look through the shock, especially as the recent ceasefire talks decrease the likelihood of adverse tail risks. Hence, current market pricing of 45bp cumulative ECB hikes looks some- what hawkish in our view. Amid still elevated uncertainty around the conflict and energy price developments, we refrain from outright positioning but rather recommend expressing bullish views via option structures only (e.g. 6Mx(1Yx1Y) receiver fly and 2s/10s condi- tional bull steepener). THEME OF THE WEEK: EM FX HOLDINGS DIVERGE The fallout from the Iran War in terms of EM FX Holdings was stark, by dint of the fact that February saw broad overweights. The unwind in positions that followed, however, has been different depending on the region. EMEA has taken the brunt of the position adjustment, partly because overweights in the region were the most extended to begin with. Geographical proximity hurt the TRY and inflation fears saw CEE countries hit, especially as these countries had reorientated away from a Russian crude. Asia experienced only a squaring of positions rather than the creation of deep underweights in EMEA. Latam was the least impacted. By late March, overweights were being rebuilt. Geographical distance has probably helped, so has good central bank credibility. EUR short-expiry, short n maturity volatility has retraced since the late March peak, but currently sits richer than USD — a market feature that historically has not sustained for long. With the outcomes for front-end rates narrowing, we think this vol decline is likely to continue, with the potential for volatility to migrate further out the curve given the potential for focus to shift to medium-term fiscal responses to address energy and defence challenges in Europe. We think the skew in front-end rates is also likely to moderate on the de-escalation path, with receiving, for example via selling ATMF+50bp payers and buying ATMF-50bp receivers on 1y1y EUR (collecting around 5bp at current pricing), could take advantage of hike pricing, elevated vol and payer skew. records.text: labor cost for employers. Such a scheme was also implemented in 2022. At the time, it covered up to €3,000 of pay between Oct-22 and Dec-24 and the number of employees that could potentially receive the pay was 40 million. To derive the growth impact, we need four ingredients: (i) the take-up rate, (ii) the average payment conditional on take-up, (iii) the degree of substitution for regular pay, and (iv) the split between consumption and saving. The substitution assumption is key. Even if existing pay obligations cannot formally be shifted into the scheme, employers could still use it against wage increases they would otherwise have granted. At one extreme, the scheme acts mainly as a labor-tax cut on compensation; at the other, it is a genuinely additional employer-financed income boost. The truth is likely somewhere in between (e.g., an ifo survey documents that 50% of firms used the one-off pay to take advantage of lower taxes). Let’s put some numbers to this. We assume a take-up rate of around 40%, somewhat below the 2022-24 experience (studies from IW, IMK and ifo report rates between 53% and 72%). We expect lower take-up this time because the energy price shock is smaller, the implementation window is shorter, the growth backdrop is weaker, and public-sector workers are likely absent (here), which account for more than 3 million eligible employees. For similar reasons, we assume an average payout of around 50%, or €500, versus roughly 70% last time (see here and here).

Our analysis of the economic impact of AI does not assume a particular number of data centres being built; however, with current technology, if current capex pledges are met in full, this could significantly boost power prices, diminishing the positive productivity effect from AI deployment. As well as higher demand, disrupted supply due to geopolitical shocks could push up energy prices (see US economic activity: Crude estimates, 20 March). Energy n prices have fallen from their peak following last week’s ceasefire, recent price-related indicators have not moved up decisively and recent ECB communication has shown little urgency for a near-term policy change. We therefore no longer expect a hike at the April meeting. We maintain our forecast for two hikes this year, which we push back to June and n September (vs April and June before). This is because we expect energy prices to remain persistently high through the year, significant pass-through into inflation is likely in coming months and the ECB’s communication has remained largely hawkish on the path ahead. That said, any hikes are unlikely to be sustained for long given more limited n pass-through into core inflation than in 2022 and a weaker demand environment. We therefore expect the Governing Council to cut the deposit rate back to 2% in 2027. Moreover, we believe that the risks around the two-hike baseline have shifted n significantly. We now believe that it is a close call whether the ECB hikes twice or holds rates unchanged, while the odds of a decisive tightening cycle have fallen significantly. Whilst we expect this to be approved in short order, SAFE loans will be disbursed and funded in 2026-30 so the impact will be over multiple years. As with all SAFE loan beneficiaries, Hungary is entitled to the 15% pre-financing payment, but this is only €2.4bn. The removal of Hungarian veto on the EU’s loan to Ukraine is more significant to EU’s funding needs. Whilst Hungary’s now likely access to EU funds might put some marginal upward pressure on EU’s funding needs, the removal of Hungary’s veto on the EU’s €90bn loan to Ukraine is more important. records.text: AI tech capabilities and capital - gauging costs and growth Datacenter capex from leading public hyperscalers is now approaching ~$700 bn USD, roughly 10X the level in 2020. In fact, consensus capex estimates were revised higher yet again with the most recent set of earnings reports, with the bottom-up aggregation of 2026 GS capex estimates for the leading hyperscalers now 14% higher relative to the start of 4Q25 earnings. GS analysts now expect 67% yoy growth in capex in 2026, and 16% in 2027 (Exhibit 8). This growth is primarily to drive AI model development and datacenter capacity, and we take a look at recent developments in this section of the note. One measure of progress with AI models is Epoch AI’s Capabilities Index (ECI), which is a generalized benchmark intended to capture the overall capability of AI models by aggregating performance across several established tests covering reasoning, coding, math, and language. Unlike individual benchmarks which can saturate as models approach near‑perfect scores, ECI adjusts for task difficulty and combines results to show relative differentiation across models and over time. Higher scores indicate broader capability, while models optimized for specific tests may perform well on individual benchmarks but rank lower on ECI due to limited generalization. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Financial Conditions: The market is doing the Fed's work so far Following the conflict in the Middle East and the uncertainty it brings for the next steps for monetary policy, we include the evolution of our FRB/US-based model of financial conditions, which aims to capture how changes in asset prices weigh on future economic activity. The index includes five daily variables: the 10-year Treasury yield, S&P 500 returns, the corporate BBB credit spread, the valuation of the U.S. dollar, and the price of oil. These are aggregated based on their estimated growth elasticities relative to the federal funds rate, using the Federal Reserve’s FRB/US model. As a result, the index can be interpreted as the equivalent change in the federal funds rate, expressed in basis points, required to generate a similar effect on economic activity. Since hostilities in the Middle East began on February 28, the tightening in financial conditions is equivalent to about a 30bp rise in the federal funds rate. Since the April 7 ceasefire announcement, however, financial conditions have eased by 42bps. This March tightening reversed all of the easing seen earlier this year, most of which occurred between the December and January FOMC meetings, and was primarily driven by a weaker U.S. dollar. His strong advocacy for rate cuts is likely to run into ques- tions about how he views the appropriate policy stance— especially as other more dovish Fed governors, including both Waller and Miran, this week indicated somewhat less support for easing given recent inflation data. Warsh also is likely to be quizzed on how he intends to maintain Fed independence. For his part, Warsh is likely to argue against “institutional bloat” and for a smaller balance sheet. Beyond politics, next week’s key data developments will be March retail sales and the April flash PMIs. Although gas prices spiked in March, our Chase card data has shown retail sales continuing to perform well, which could in part reflect the disbursement of tax refunds, which by mid-April were $36bn higher than the same time last year (Figure 2). On the PMIs, the key thing to watch will be if PMI services can recover, after steadily falling since last July and dipping below 50 in March.

records.text: 25 Three stages: To find the right periodisation of our chosen comparable GPTs, we split technology shocks in three stages: replacement, market penetration and innovation, based on work by Crafts, 2002, and Devine, 1982. ▪ Replacement: In the early stage, old technology is replaced by new in performing the same task. This is a good benchmark to see the immediate impact of a technology on the economy. ▪ Market penetration: In this phase, the new technology is widely adopted across the market. Productivity growth impacts tend to be limited at this stage. ▪ Innovation: In the late stage of the shock, the technology leads to significant innovations and changes in production processes, illustrating the full potential of the economic impact of an invention. Our modelling considers the first (early) and last (late) stages, as these show the most variation in TFP. We define these as 1891–1900 and 1920–29 for electrification and 1980–86 and 1994–2004 for ICT. Gauging impacts: To measure the acceleration of TFP from its non-technology shock baseline, we HP-filter the TFP series and take the difference of the early or late stage of the technology cycle relative to the pre-shock average. records.text: Trip Assumptions On the back of growing fleet supply (both within existing and new markets), we model Waymo reaching 960K annualized US paid weekly trips during 2026. Our growth assumptions are anchored around the company: a) expanding its operating zones in existing markets; b) launching operations in new regions; & c) increasing rider frequency among existing riders. In recent years, particularly in markets such as Phoenix and San Francisco, Waymo has successfully expanded its service area (Exhibit 46) - and we believe that Waymo’s operating zone will continue to expand in the coming years. In addition to expanded operating zones, a meaningful unlock toward driving trip volume, rider adoption, and gross bookings is anchored around airport trips. Airport trips compose a meaningful portion of rideshare gross bookings today - for example, during 2025, Uber generated 15% of total mobility GBs from trips that started at, or were completed at an airport. Over the next 5-10 years, with the broader AV industry expected to offer riders more affordable trips (lower ASPs on a per mile basis) in comparison to human drivers, the industry is likely to see both new riders come onto the various platforms, and existing riders increase the frequency of their rides. We take recent developments from German factory orders as a guide to those sectors, that may be particularly exposed to higher defence spending. Sectors are listed in Exhibit 7. Data availability bites. While we get output and weights at granular detail in Germany, and for most sectors in Italy, we get only output data at Euro area level, and not even that in France and Spain. As a consequence, we use a weighted average of Italian and German weights (the economies account for c 50% of Euro area manufacturing output) as proxy for Euro area weights. From what we can infer from German, Italian and Euro area data, German dynamics don’t look exceptional at the Euro area level. The underlying trend has not (yet) accelerated in response to the 2025 fiscal policy changes and plans to raise defence spending from sub-2% to 3.5% by the end of the decade (Exhibit 3). That leaves hope, but with a manufacturing share of less than 4%, the defence-exposed sectors are too small to move the manufacturing needle, and we doubt that can change. Whether or not city banks end up buying ultimately depend on which of the following three scenarios comes to pass. “Ongoing supply constraints” scenario: Suppose that the Strait of Hormuz situation is resolved quickly and that Brent crude peaks at USD110/bbl in 2Q 2026 before dropping to USD90/bbl by year-end. Our economists are forecasting that the BoJ would hike its policy rate in June 2026 and then once again in April 2027 under this scenario even if growth slows. We would expect a wider risk premium to be priced into the belly zone of the curve due to inflation concerns outweighing growth concerns. Such cheapening could potentially induce some tactical buying by the banking sector. “Effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz” scenario: In a risk scenario where Brent crude oil prices exceed USD150/bbl, our economists point out that the BoJ would halt its policy rate hikes at 0.75%, given the risks of negative economic growth and subsequent downward pressure on prices. We are encouraged by the resilience the economy has shown through the last 5 years of supply-side shocks - but momentum is likely to soften in 2Q. February | Back at it: Monthly GDP growth came in at 0.5%M in February - a healthy, broad-based pick-up. A couple of sub-sectors drove the beat relative to our forecast: aided by car sales and wholesale trade, the distribution sector boosted headline growth by ~25bp more than we had expected. Construction was also much stronger than we had pencilled in, and that high-frequency and survey data suggested; finally, the rebound in administrative services was stronger than we had pencilled in. Mining and utilities boosted industrial production, where manufacturing contracted, missing versus our forecast modestly. But zooming out, while volatile, growth data at the turn of the year was healthy and consistent with a decent rebound following what really was an exceptionally weak 2H25. While the distribution sector outperformed at the start of the year, the upswing really is down to the "non consumer-facing services". The output in these sub-sectors - ICT, professional, administrative services - effectively flatlined in 2H25 and January, surging by 0.6%M in February. We’d observed that the lack of n follow-through in longer-dated inflation forwards through the oil shock could be partially explained by the muted response of oil futures contracts further out the curve. While less in focus as a driver of day-to-day volatility, the risk that increased AI adoption will cause more widespread disinflation in the future may also be lingering—even after the rebound from the post-shock lows, longer-term inflation forwards are still only back around late February levels and some 5-to-10bp below January levels. We have previously highlighted the co-movement of inflation forwards with software and other stocks considered to face disruption risks from AI, which have lagged the S&P 500 through the bulk of the recovery amid a broader increase in media attention on the macroeconomic consequences of AI (Exhibit 2). While AI-related considerations can remain a constraint on upside in longer-term inflation pricing, we would be surprised if the headwinds to long-end traded inflation were to intensify in the near-term without evidence of AI disruption in the labor market data—in which case we would expect a clearer shift towards pricing deeper cuts and lower real rates. Even as energy prices moderate, we think there’s still some value in beta-weighting long real exposure for scenarios of less (or slower) inflation relief, or labor market concerns that warrant easier medium-term policy. records.text: EUR: The sidelines not the center. Up to this point, EUR/USD has been mostly n responding to global developments rather than sitting at the center of FX markets. This is somewhat unusual for the pair given that typically it is one of the only crosses where domestic data can regularly override global betas, and because it was much more in focus during the 2022 energy shock. The latter likely helps explain why EUR/USD moves specifically have been somewhat underwhelming relative to initial expectations following the start of the conflict. European energy prices have been comparably contained relative to other regions and—especially—the 2022 experience. In our models, EUR/USD moving back to flat is a function of two things (Exhibit 5). First, the energy move (particularly natural gas) has been fairly manageable so far. Second, and perhaps most notably, the impact from global risk sentiment has now entirely unwound. It is also worth noting how the currency has moved remarkably closely to this simple model during an especially volatile period, which underscores our point about this being mostly a global story. But after the steep recovery, we now think domestic developments can play a more central role, or at least make EUR/USD a compelling hedge for a longer disruption. As we move beyond the most uncertain phase of the conflict, we expect the domestic outlook to become an important driver once again. records.text: Katya Vashkinskaya +44(20)7774-4833 | katya.vashkinskaya@gs.com Goldman Sachs International Euro Area: Final Inflation Details Show Underlying Inflation Unwinding Most of the February Boost 17 April 2026 | 10:08AM BST BOTTOM LINE: The final release of Euro area inflation for March showed headline inflation at 2.55%yoy, revised up from the flash reading of 2.52%yoy, and core inflation at 2.29%yoy, up 3bp from the flash print. Services inflation remains the main driver of headline inflation but its contribution went down to 1.49pp in March, while the contribution from Energy moved up to 0.48pp, its highest reading in more than 3 years. Our summary indicator of sequential underlying inflation ticked down in March to 0.19%mom after increasing notably in February, partly unwinding the Olympics-induced tourism- and hospitality-related boost. The change in our sequential summary measure reflects a sequential deceleration across most of the metrics we track, with the biggest moves in the supercore (-0.26pp), HICPXX (-0.16pp) and domestic (-0.13pp) measures. We continue to see year-over-year core inflation at 2.4%yoy in 2026, peaking at 2.5%yoy in Q3 and then falling to 2.4%yoy by end-2026 and to 2.2% by end-2027. As for headline inflation, we see it averaging 2.9%yoy in 2026, peaking at 3.2%yoy in Q2, and at 2.0%yoy in 2027. The risks, however, remain to the upside. In this case, both players (the US and the market) are indifferent between playing any of the two possible actions. So, from the perspective of one player, the other player can choose each action with certain probability p. One way of rationalizing it is that the market is not sure at what price threshold (say for oil, S&P 500, or 10y rates) the US will de-escalate and vice versa. The equilibrium of this game is one where it is optimal for risky assets to selloff but only in proportion to the probability of escalation once strategic interactions are considered, which is exactly the observed price action. Being a dynamic game, players learn about each other’s reservation threshold over time. Under the stated assumptions, market pricing is rational as the US signaled the end of the war, which would explain the resilience of the stock market. However, the risk is that even when the US claims the war is over, Iran could refrain from reopening the Strait of Hormuz to maximize its deterrence effect. records.text: The decision to hold rates was framed as a prudent measure amid "exceptional uncertainty," providing an "option value of waiting" before a potential hawkish move. The Council’s experience with the 2022 energy shock, where inflation proved highly persistent, has created a bias against underestimation. It is therefore monitoring a list of indicators heavily skewed towards finding early warnings of persistent inflation, such as inflation expectations and firms' selling price intentions. While hawkish arguments dominated, several dovish factors were acknowledged but subordinated. The primary dovish consideration is that the energy shock will dampen economic activity, with the 2026 growth forecast revised down from 0.9% to 0.4%. It was noted that this weaker outlook could naturally limit second-round effects, as firms may struggle to pass on costs and a cooling labour market could restrain wages. In conclusion, the ECB faces a classic stagflationary dilemma. The meeting accounts show a clear hierarchy of concerns, with the risk of unanchored inflation taking precedence over the negative impact on growth. The rate hold is a temporary, data-gathering exercise, and the Council is communicating its readiness to act decisively. If modelled to maturity, PC CLOs have a similar Weighted Average Life (WAL) to BSL CLOs around 5 years. In practice, we expect them to be shorter since they typically lack the flexibility to reinvest after the end of the Reinvestment Period and they are callable. Over the last 2 years , effective maturities have been short with realised WAL closer to the length of the non -Call period (given the high refi/reset activity). However, in the case of a Private Credit market downside scenario, we think refinancing activity should slow down and realised WAL to be longer than the length of the non-Call period. Should PC CLO fail their junior OC test, a n early amortisation mechanism would shorten the AAA WAL. We expect PC CLOs to be structured more conservatively to reflect the current market sentiment around Private Credit and to mitigate excessive concentrations in the Software sector. We undertook a stress test to determine the break-even default rate that causes a principal shortfall on PC CLOs AAA, finding that with 0% Recoveries and 10% Prepayments, the structure could withstand on average 54% cumulative defaults. We expect softer demand to limit the pass through of higher energy prices to core inflation, especially as core inflation has been particularly soft in recent months and will provide some near-term buffer against higher core prices. Very strong gas prices will likely be excluded from trimmed-mean core inflation measures in March, but we expect monthly core inflation in March could still be stronger than recent months. 3-month core inflation is currently running around 1% on an annualized basis, but we would not be surprised to see this back at or a bit above 2% in March. This may correspond with annual measures rising to around a 2.5% average from a 2.3% average in February. This increase may be somewhat mechanical in nature - some stronger components that otherwise would have been excluded from core calculations may now be included as stronger energy prices are excluded. Some details like shelter prices may also be a bit stronger as new home prices rose in February and will boost March homeowners’ replacement costs. But ultimately, we still expect core inflation on an annual basis to remain within the BoC’s 1-3% target range this year, suggesting little need for rate hikes as the labor market remains weak and the output gap negative. Odds of rate cut have fallen in H2: The PBoC reaffirming its moderately loose stance on 31 March suggests that there’s some room for cuts to the policy rate or RRR. Yet, with China’s shift from deflation to mild inflation and a 4.5–5.0% growth target, the threshold for another cut is higher . A cut would require either growth slowing to 4.5% or lower in Q2 due to external or internal shock – e.g., a severe supply-chain disruption due to the Middle East conflict or a renewed property slump – or a meaningful rise in banks’ net-interest margin. The first scenario is not our base case; the second is unlikely as loan demand remains weak. Consequently, we still see an easing monetary policy bias, but the likelihood of a rate cut in H2 has dropped . records.text: ndeed data show labour demand has softened but not collapsed (Figure 5), while wage growth for newly posted jobs is running at only 2% (Figure 6). Both are a stark contrast to 2022, when the labour market was much tighter and headline inflation was more likely to perpetuate. Put differently, growth risks look much higher in 2026 than they did in 2022. Even so, there is limited discussion of recession or layoffs in the media so far (Figure 7), though that could change. The first estimate of the Chicago Fed CARTS series implies a 1.3% rise in nominal retail sales in March, but in real terms (partly deflated using PriceStats) a 0.7% decline. With 3-month trends in real PCE and real personal income already flirting with recession levels (Figure 9) ahead of March, alongside weak employment growth, that would be troubling if realised. Consensus Q1 growth remains above 2%, but the Atlanta Fed nowcast has dropped to 1.4% from close to 5% at the start of the quarter (Figure 10). As inflation risks look skewed to the upside, the next move in US growth expectations seems more likely to be down. records.text: 17 April 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Week in review Euro area IP in February (Wed) Euro area industrial production (IP) rose 0.4% m/m in February. However, the headline figure masks underlying weakness across the region. The positive result was driven almost entirely by a sharp rebound in Ireland's volatile production figures (+5.7% m/m). Excluding Ireland, euro area IP would have contracted 0.2% m/m, with production falling in Germany, France, and the Netherlands, and remaining broadly flat in Italy and Spain. This IP February gain is insufficient to alter the weak outlook for the industrial sector; the carry-over from previous months still points to a significant contraction in industrial production for Q1 as a whole, following a modest increase in Q4 2025. This weakness in the industrial sector, combined with other soft indicators like contracting retail sales and falling consumer confidence, reinforces our view that euro area growth momentum remained weak in the first quarter. Our nowcasting models suggest Q1 GDP growth will be close to zero, and we are forecasting 0.1% q/q growth. This indicates a potential downside surprise to the consensus and ECB baseline forecasts of 0.3% q/q, suggesting the euro area had a smaller growth buffer to absorb recent energy price shocks than previously thought. records.text: 27 After the war, the UK entered in a period of economic downturn: output contracted by 9.7% y/y in 1921 and the unemployment rate, which averaged 5% before the war, reached 11% in the same year. The 1920s slump was caused by a quick unwind of the war economy with associated cuts in spending and a contractionary monetary policy aimed at returning to the pre- war gold-standard system (NIESR, 2021) since inflation ran out of control during the war. CPI inflation, which had been relatively stable until the start of WWI, skyrocketed to around 20% y/y in 1917. The Bank of England’s actions at the time were not informed by an official inflation target. Statutory monetary policy objectives were only established in 1998. records.text: the one-off pay was likely substituting for regular pay increases, at least initially. So, to reflect the uncertainty around the degree of substitution we assess two cases, one in which the pay is 80% additional with only 20% substitution of regular pay rises and the opposite split of 20% additional and 80% substitution. And compared to 2022-24, we note that, given the lukewarm industry response to the scheme, substitution is likely to play a larger role now (see here and here). With this we can pin down the net income effect. We would expect that the total pay under the scheme is around €8bn (40% of 40 million eligible employees receiving on average €500). Under high substitution, only €1.6bn would represent additional income; under low substitution, the figure would be €6.4bn. If we assume that around 60% of that pay gets consumed (in line with Bundesbank estimates for consumption out of unexpected cash transfers), German private consumption could be between 10bp and 30bp higher in 2026 (5-20bp of GDP). From the fiscal point of view, the forgone fiscal revenue (ca 60% levied on our estimate for the substituted wage pay) could range between €4bn (in case of high substitution) and €0.6bn (under low substitution) (and the other side of the coin is a tax gain for corporates). To sum up, we see a slight growth upside from the announced measures out of Germany, which could lift our current GDP forecast for 2026 of 0.5%Y by up to 5- 20bp. records.text: posed employment has slowed: A deeper look into the US job market shows that industries with higher exposures to potential AI disruption have experienced soggy job growth relative to other industries. However, we see other factors at play as well. We use AI industry exposure estimates (see Felten et al., 2021) to sort over 100 detailed industries available in the nonfarm payroll report. Net job gains in those most-exposed industries slowed sharply in the aftermath of ChatGPT’s release in the autumn of 2022 (see Figure 28), effectively adding no jobs since then. But other factors also at play: While the AI dimension appears to explain a portion of the slowdown in employment, we’re sceptical that it is the main driver. Other relevant factors have been the Fed’s rate-hike cycle, normal post-pandemic workforce adjustments, tariff uncertainty and shocks, and stricter immigration policy (Figure 29). Indeed, even the industries least exposed to AI have seen job growth decelerate sharply in recent years (Figure 28). In the US, we see a low-hire, low-layoff job market as an uncomfortable yet ultimately sustainable equilibrium. Rolling growth scares, plus tariff and trade uncertainty, have been reasons for employers to keep a tight leash on new headcount. Yet we expect businesses to remain reluctant to let workers go en masse in an environment where aging demographics and tight immigration policy will be structural headwinds to labour force growth. Pension funds: Rebalancing Risks Skewed Toward Bonds to Equities Pension funds continue to be driven primarily by relative performance across asset classes. Following the oil price shock triggered by the deterioration in the Iran situation in March, equities underperformed bonds (see Exhibit 15 ), leading us to expect bond selling and equity buying rebalancing flows at the start of April. However, by mid April, equities had rebounded sharply at a pace comparable to the March sell off and have instead begun to outperform bonds. Looking at bond futures positioning in early April, trust banks were net buyers of equities in the first week of April, but in the second week they turned into sizeable net buyers of bond futures, while equity positions were broadly unchanged (see Exhibit 16 ). Going forward, rebalancing flows will naturally depend on developments in the Middle East, but given the rapid recovery in equity performance, there is a growing risk that the scale of bond to equity rebalancing will be more limited than initially expected. “Ongoing supply constraints” scenario: Assuming the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz is resolved early, equities are likely to outperform bonds, making rebalancing flows favor bond purchases and equity sales. On SEK spreads, these are less directional and, as we argued recently, we see little fundamental justification for the market to price a sustainably wider policy-rate differential in favour of the euro area versus Sweden. To reiterate: first, the differential has rarely been materially wider in the ECB's favour over the past decade – if anything, the opposite has more often been the case. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 1Q GDP tracking 2.2% Our 1Q GDP tracking remained at 2.2% last week. The Atlanta Fed estimate remained at 1.3%, with no updates to input data. The NY Fed figure inched down to 2.3% from 2.4%. In our forecast, a couple of factors temporarily boost 1Q GDP: Government expenditures rise 4%, as output moved back to trend after the 4Q shutdown. The government does not make up for lost output, but output does return to its (slowing) trend. One reason that the Atlanta Fed GDP tracking is slower than ours is that it does not appear to allow for rebound in real federal government consumption. A plunge in reported software prices adds to 1Q real investment in intellectual property. Software prices are volatile enough in recent quarters that we would not extrapolate the decline into later quarters. Together, those temporary factors contribute about ½ of a point to our 1Q GDP estimate. However, we estimate a similar drag on GDP from the upward bias to 1Q consumer prices. In recent years, real consumption has appeared to slow in 1Q because of residual seasonality—giving a false sense of the underlying pace. This year, its drag on 1Q GDP growth is mostly offset by the combination of rebound in federal output and plunge in software prices. Terms of trade (TOT) has n been a key driver of FX returns since the start of the war with Iran, consistent with the typical pattern in periods of elevated commodity price volatility. But broader risk sentiment has played a nearly comparable role, leading to the underperformance of some key energy exporting currencies relative to their shifts in terms of trade (e.g., NOK, CAD) and less intuitive day-to-day correlations that have made tactical trading more challenging relative to the energy shock of 2022. Commodity price volatility relative to rates and equity market volatility appears to be a key driver of the difference. In the current shock, shifts in volatility have been more coincident across assets than they were in 2022. Intuitively, in that scenario, FX investors can get caught wrong-footed if purely positioned around the TOT implications. If rates and equity vol pick up again alongside an increase in commodities vol, investors can more consistently benefit from trading TOT when positioning only in high-beta energy exporters and importers. records.text: discussed in the Morning Call, the EU has underperformed versus swaps and other EGBs, led by longer maturities since the announcement of the loan to Ukraine in December last year (see Figure 3 in the MC). We continue to believe that this underperformance is unlikely to reverse soon, especially for the longer end of EU’s curve for a couple of reasons. First, whilst supply impact of the Hungary elections on EU supply is likely to be limited, and the EU can mitigate part of the impact due to the Ukraine loan by relying more on Bills, eventually this funding is likely to be termed out eventually and the investors know to expect this. Second, despite the highest volume of YTD issuance (€60.4bn; Figure 15) the EU has reduced its longer dated issuance this year. Since 2021 the weighted average maturity (WAM) of its YTD supply (up to 16 April) has always been higher than its annual WAM. In other words, it has issued most of its longer dated supply earlier in the year. This year, it has issued the lowest share of its YTD funding in 20-30y (18%, and this is after this week’s €6bn 20y deal) and the WAM of its YTD supply is at 11.5y the lowest since 2018 (Figure 21). Whilst this has reduced the supply pressure on the long end of EU’s curve, we believe this relief will be only temporary as the EU still has €30bn to issue in H1 and since 2021 it has issued in 20y+every year in May. Cross asset reactions have become less sensitive to the upside moves in oil — Using high frequency data, we show that rates, equities and FX have materially become less responsive to oil rallies than to oil sell-offs. However, we argue that the distribution of this asymmetry calls for rates and FX to be the most attractive medium to chase risk. The picture is more nuanced in equity space, European indices exhibit similar asymmetric behaviour while US equities continue to move more symmetrically with oil returns. Petrodollar recycling? Focus on Asiadollars — We argue Asia CA surplus recycling, rather than petrodollar recycling, is a more important theme to watch going forwards. In our view, the bearish-case scenario for the USD would be Hormuz flows returning, allowing RoW equity flows and a dovish Fed to re-emerge, but with risk premia in oil staying high enough to cap Asia CA surplus growth. Have macro betas to oil shocks changed? — Oil intensity of global GDP and the beta of global energy expenditure to the “all-in” price of oil have both structurally fallen over time. This doesn’t mean that a fragile situation cannot get worse, but it suggests the bar for an oil shock to cause lasting damage to the global economy is growing higher by the year. Services prices to remain steady We don't expect services momentum to shift meaningfully in March. Within housing, we see private rents up 0.3% m-o-m (CPI). Other housing costs (maintenance), we expect, will have risen by 0.1% m-o-m (CPI). For RPI specifically, we see depreciation up 0.5% m-o-m (and see further upside risks to our estimate). On mortgage interest payments, we expect momentum to be up, with the index rising 1.6% m-o-m. On transport, we expect airfares to have risen by 2.6% m-o-m. We can nonetheless draw important conclusions from a near-term inflation point of view. The initial impact of the conflict on euro area inflation will be dominated by the price of Brent and its pass-through to fuel prices. Meanwhile, on the basis of current market energy prices, we expect the impact of domes- tic gas and electricity price changes on HICP will likely be moderate. Since the pass-through of Brent prices to consumer fuel pric- es is similar across countries, cross-country differences will be dominated by national governments’ responses to curb fuel price increases. records.text: European Rates Weekly 16 April 2026 Citi Research 10 The EU has completed its H1 26 funding target at a record pace with more than two-thirds already done. However, based on the revised recovery plans and current progress, RRF will not be fully utilised. Whilst the recent election results are likely to allow EU disbursements to Hungary to proceed, its impact on EU’s supply needs is likely to be limited. The same applies to the €90bn loan to Ukraine, which is more likely to affect EU’s 2027 funding needs given its elevated liquidity position. As such, we maintain our €165bn supply forecast for the EU this year. EU’s weak performance versus swaps and other EGBs since the loan was announced is unlikely to reverse soon, given the EU’s historical supply pattern combined with our expectation that the Ukraine loan is likely to be rolled into EU’s term funding. The outstanding EU debt has almost reached €800bn. According EU Debt Securities data, since the start of SURE loan programme in 2020 the EU has raised €1.028trn in bonds (€756bn) and Bills (€272bn). As of 16 April 2026, €792bn of these remain outstanding, of which €755bn in bonds and €36.9bn in Bills. The bulk of the outstanding bonds (€640bn) comprise of bonds that were issued to finance the NGEU programme, but it also includes €82bn of SURE bonds. The decoupling of Schatz spreads relative to a simple gauge of 2y EGB dispersion (cross-sectional standard deviation of 2y French, Spanish and Italian paper relative to €STR OIS) since mid-2024 is also noteworthy: we interpret this break in correlation as consistent with the ECB’s progressive transition to a demand-driven liquidity provision framework and the seemingly high bar for balance sheet extension in the face of sovereign fragmentation risk going forward (as well as, more recently, the structural change in Germany’s Federal fiscal stance). In other words, the backdrop for German paper financing has structurally shifted from 2022’s collateral scarcity to the current collateral abundance. records.text: reasury controlled accounts. New Hydrocarbons law is a step forward The new Hydrocarbon Law approved earlier this year is central to renewed investor interest. It allows private and foreign firms to operate upstream. It also introduces flexible royalty rates that can be reduced for marginal or high investment projects, and it permits international arbitration. Strategic control over pricing and exports remains with the state preserving government influence over the sector. The downside of the law is that a high degree of discretion remains in the hands of the authorities regarding taxation for each project. Investors are also concerned about legitimacy of the law. Several oil and gas companies show interest, but some have objections Major international oil companies have responded positively (more details in Management Comments section). Chevron, Shell, Repsol, Eni, Maurel & Prom, and BP are negotiating expanded projects. Chevron aims to scale up operations in the Orinoco Belt while Shell plans to develop eastern Venezuela oil and gas fields. Exxon Mobil and ConocoPhillips have sent evaluation teams but emphasize the need for fiscal stability and long-term contract durability. Conoco has said that before returning it needs to be repaid the arbitrations claims (estimated above $12bn).

Australia and New Zealand RBA working to get ahead of the curve. While trend inflation expectations in n Australia have remained anchored, near-term household expectations ticked up notably, and given the shifting tone by RBA, our economists this week shifted to a baseline for two further hikes in May and June to a 4.60% terminal rate (vs 4.35% before). This week’s labor market data — and the market reaction to it — remained stable, although it is likely too early to see the impact of the conflict yet. Further ahead, however, we expect the financial conditions tightening to be a drag on activity—our economists estimate the hit to global growth at 0.5pp—while factors behind the larger jump in petrol and diesel prices versus other DMs should more clearly skew intermediate and longer-term forwards lower, especially with the RBA increasingly willing to front-load rate hikes. While the apparent progress towards reopening the Strait on Friday has brought relief across rates curves, we think the RBA ’s reaction function leaves room for further AUD curve flattening in multiple scenarios. records.text: While visibility into the timing (and launch) of new markets remains low, we believe that expanding into international markets will play a key role in driving trip growth. In terms of the regulatory landscape for autonomous commercial vehicles - international frameworks (incl. the Vienna Convention, UNECE) and EU instruments (AI Act, General Safety Regulation) have a type-approval framework and mandate rigorous active safety features, which could limit widespread deployment of L4/L5 autonomy. In our view, this will likely limit the near-term scaling of Waymo in international markets over the next 5 years (e.g. we expect international markets to account for 10% of total Waymo trips in 2029). That said, by 2035, we expect for international trips to account for ~30% of Waymo’s total paid trip volume. Longer-term, we view international markets to be a stimulant to trip growth, and in the near-term, we see the announced markets as having the potential to increase awareness in robotaxis. Specifically in tourist destinations such as London and Tokyo, tourism/novelty effects could remain (previously highlighted in Exhibit 24) and also drive awareness of the service and eventual adoption as Waymo expands into new markets. records.text: Spotlight on Waymo: Framing Operating Assumptions and the Path to $8 bn+ Gross Bookings by 2030E Waymo initially launched in Phoenix during 2018 and began serving fully autonomous commercial rides in 2019. Since their launch, the company now operates in 11 cities across the US, and expects to lay the groundwork in 20 markets this year (link). Within these markets, Waymo serves over 500k paid rides weekly (as of March 2026), a rate which has more than doubled since April 2025. This ramp resulted in over 15 mn rides being completed during 2025, serviced by a fleet of >1,800 vehicles (GSe). While Waymo expects to lay the groundwork for ride-hailing operations in 20+ cities during 2026, our assumptions around launch timing remains relatively conservative given the level of predictability/visibility surrounding the regulatory environment. For example, while self-driving cars can be tested in Washington D.C., the vehicles cannot complete rides in a fully autonomous manner (link). In terms of our assumptions surrounding specific launch markets, the company has announced a number of test cities across US and international markets - all of which vary in terms of traffic patterns, weather/climate and rideshare demand trends. Our current launch assumptions revolve around markets which have: a) a top 50 MSA (Metropolitan Statistical Area) by population; & b) testing currently underway. That said, we have pushed back our ECB hike forecast in response to the central bank’s tone and lack of urgency, which should mechanically somewhat reduce near-term policy-path uncertainty and support some further drift lower in implieds; the counterweight is that the overall uncertainty regime remains elevated, which argues for an ongoing risk premium embedded in volatility. The recent decline in delivered volatility matters here: with positioning cleaner, the proba- bility of “forced” convexity demand and gap-style moves should fall somewhat (even if it remains above that of a typical low-vol regime). That sets up a window where volatility can normalize somewhat further without requiring a strong directional view on rates—especial- ly if macro outcomes land inside a narrower band and headline risk continues to de-intensify. records.text: We also view Regionals as less compelling on a relative basis. Spreads have now compressed back toward the pre-2023 range, when they traded inside Money Centers. But we are skeptical that fundamentals (or technicals) warrant a return to that regime. While the overhang from the early 2023 US Regional banking crisis has clearly faded, we view credit quality as less well positioned (vs. Money Centers) in terms of scale, breadth, and diversification of business models. Regionals also face a maturity wall in bail-in debt that begins to ramp next year (Exhibit 5). To us, this suggests some room for modest spread widening as refinancing needs rise and new supply is digested. Put differently, both Yankees and Regionals look priced for a benign outcome, with limited compensation for the risks that remain. The better place to move down the stack is in Money Centers Our broad preference is to remain higher in the capital structure given rich valuations across bank types. That said, for investors willing to move lower in the stack, Money Center subordinated debt provides a more compelling opportunity. In our previous Japan Macro Watch, we noted that "we believe the BoJ would proceed if the probability exceeded 60% by the end of the week prior to the policy meeting (i.e., 24 April)." The OIS market currently shows less than 20%, which fell from around 50% after Governor Ueda's speech (reading on behalf by deputy governor Himino) on Monday (see " Deep Speak: An AI-driven read on tone shifts at the Fed, ECB and BoJ"), and we think this is unlikely to rise back above 60% by the end of next week. Our new BoJ call forecasts the next rate hike on 16 June, followed by October (to 1.25%), April 2027 (to 1.5%), October 2027 (to 1.75%), and April 2028 (to 2.0%); this means our rate hike expectations after October this year are unchanged. We see the risk of faster rate hikes, but it depends on currency market development (i.e., JPY depreciation pressure likely prompts the BoJ to raise rates faster as the government also wants to prevent further JPY depreciation, which would raise living costs of households). Key Takeaways We see Japanese investors demand for JGBs continuing to be more selective and less structural this fiscal year. Japanese lifers: even higher super-long JGB yields are unlikely to bring life insurers back as consistent buyers. Lifers have largely closed their ESR-related duration gap, liability duration is shortening, and new business is shifting toward shorter- duration product. Japanese banks: We see bank demand as mainly tactical, with buying likely only if yields cheapen relative to expectations for the BoJ terminal rate. Pension funds: we continue to see rebalancing being the key driver. Geopolitical scenario outcomes and the subsequent relative asset class performance should be a factor. With the BoJ now focusing on the risk of a growth slowdown as disruption persists in the Strait of Hormuz, we see belly-sector JGBs outperforming as inflation risk premia fade if growth fears dominate. records.text: US swap spreads Risk sentiment has improved on further progress towards an extension of the ceasefire agreement. Stocks have recovered their losses, with the S&P500 reaching record highs this week. Swap spreads have also found support in recent weeks, widening from their peak stress lows in March. However, they are still below pre-war levels and still tighter year-to-date ( Figure 5 and Figure 6). Overall, front-end spreads have outperformed, given benign funding conditions and softness in repo rates. Long-end (30y) spreads had a larger drawdown on the risk-off move, but have shown signs of stabilization. Our VA proxy that measures variable annuities' sensitivity to equity/rate changes has moved back into paying territory ( Figure 7). Meanwhile, large US banks have kicked off Q1 earnings season in earnest and have begun issuing debt after exiting blackout. There has been little pressure on spreads from swapped issuance flows. As volatility continues to subside and conditions normalize, we believe fundamentals should reassert themselves. Long-end (30y) spreads are sensitive to the fiscal outlook, and we believe market participants are beginning to believe this reflects a deterioration in the fiscal outlook from loss of revenues and increased war-related expenditures. On tariffs, the effective rate has fallen to 9%, instead of increasing to the 15% in the CBO baseline. records.text: Deutsche Bank. Research 4 Our AI tool’s response when asked to assess if the accounts are hawkish or dovish: An analysis of the latest ECB Governing Council meeting accounts reveals a decidedly hawkish tone (6/10). Despite opting to hold interest rates steady, the council's discussions and guidance were dominated by concerns about upside inflation risks. The decision is best described as a "hawkish hold"—a tactical pause driven by extreme uncertainty rather than a belief that the current policy stance is sufficient. The justification for this hawkish view is extensive. A central theme was that the war in the Middle East has fundamentally altered the inflation outlook, with the new baseline anticipating inflation will be "materially above 2% in the near term." Consequently, the Council explicitly stated that risks to the inflation outlook are tilted to the upside, particularly in the short term. Significant concern was expressed regarding second-round effects, with the memory of the 2022 inflation surge potentially leading to higher wage demands and firms raising prices more readily. The Council also acknowledged that standard models might not capture the full non-linear impact of the shock and highlighted price pressures extending beyond oil to gas, electricity, and fertilisers. The decision to hold rates was framed as a prudent measure amid "exceptional uncertainty," providing an "option value of waiting" before a potential hawkish move. records.text: Agency MBS Lower cap conventional CMO floaters have more room to tighten This morning’s optimistic news flow about the Strait of Hormuz reopening and continued talks between the US and Iran have led to risk assets appreciating sharply. MBS market spreads have also tightened, with current coupon nominal spreads returning to levels last seen on February 27th. While 10-year yields are still about 30bp higher, interest rate volatility (1yr x 10yr vol) has completely re-traced. In this context, we review current valuations in the MBS market and contrast them with pre-war levels (Exhibit 1). Although higher coupon OASs are 7bp tighter than pre-war levels (for FN 5.5s and 6.0s), we continue to find value in these coupons. The tighter OAS largely reflect the higher mortgage rates, as 10-year Treasury yields have not fully re-traced lower. As we noted last week, prepay response has been relatively weak recently and is unlikely to pick up even if mortgage rates rally a further 10-15bp from current levels. Lower cap conventional CMO floaters remain 5-10bp wider than pre-war levels, as market pricing of rate cuts has not fully reversed. We believe DMs for the lower cap conventional CMO floaters have the potential to compress further as markets normalize. On the one hand, we think there is more room for markets to price out hikes following the dovish presser from the BoC. On the other hand, we think the near-term bias towards energy- exporting currencies and risk-sensitive currencies may continue to put downward pressure on USD/CAD. Next week's CPI release and the Business Outlook Survey will two important inputs for expected messaging at the April BoC. If CPI and inflation expectations are both contained, then we think there is room for markets to price out hikes and put upward pressure on USD/CAD. Japan Macro Watch17 April 2026 ab 3 Fiscal policy discussion This past Monday, the 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) yield, which serves as Japan's benchmark for long-term interest rates, reached 2.49%, marking its highest level in about 29 years since June 1997 (it currently stands at 2.40%). The main reasons for this rise are the surge in crude oil prices driven by heightened tensions in the Middle East, the depreciation of the JPY, and increased inflation expectations (as well as expectations of BoJ's policy rate hikes). However, the underlying factor is a lingering concern over the proactive fiscal policies of the Takaichi administration. The government now provides a subsidy to address soaring gasoline prices. As this subsidy is adjusted to maintain a maximum retail price, it is difficult to estimate the exact amount of necessary funds for the subsidies, but the reserves in the budget for the fund are anticipated to be depleted by June or July, according to estimates by Nomura Research Institute (see link). As a result, there is a possibility that the government may compile a supplementary budget for this fiscal year by the end of the current regular Diet session ending in summer. While no official decision has been made yet, both the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and opposition parties have raised the issue, heightening caution among bond investors. While potentially surprising, this actually reflects the market's becoming increasingly efficient at repricing on seasonal carry. However, we find some evidence that the cumulative expected carry of the next three months is positively correlated with index returns this month. Under this specification, contemporaneous carry-adjusted real yield changes remain the dominant and significant driver of returns across all maturities. Forward carry aggregated over a three-month horizon is modestly positive at the front end and loses significance moving out the curve, but it does not meaningfully increase explanatory power. These results make sense if investors pile into TIPS ahead of positive carry season and reduce allocations ahead of negative carry season. In 2025, the GCC pledged USD 3.8tn in FDI to the US. Assuming a 10-year horizon, it implies GCC will increase its FDI by five times current levels. We estimate that GCC sovereign wealth funds allocate roughly 55% of international investments to US assets. GCC financial and security ties to the US revealed its trade-offs when GCC countries became a military target for Iran. We think this good prompt a re-evaluation of allocations to the US. However, GCC makes up only around 4% of total foreign holdings of US assets, so we do not anticipate that the impact of such a move would be meaningful. Over a 10-year horizon, GCC has pledged USD 382 bn of additional FDI per year Oil exporters typically recycle their current account surpluses in USDs. There are three channels through which this could shift which include 1) not realizing FDI commitments 2) non-USD denominated oil transactions and 3) reduced buying of US assets. Oil exporters naturally tend to have large current account surpluses, which are recycled into assets in the rest of the world. Historically, a significant proportion of this goes towards the US, partly because oil transactions occur in USDs.
