records.text: Deutsche Bank. Research ▪ ECB speakers: Scenarios: Consensus is shifting towards the adverse scenario due to the war, though some members still see the economy near the baseline. Reflecting the significant uncertainty, key figures like Lagarde place the economy "in between" the two scenarios. Second-Round Effects: A hawkish vigilance prevails, with intense focus on preventing a wage-price spiral and the de-anchoring of inflation expectations. Several members have pledged "forceful action" if these risks materialize. Conditions for a Hike: While not "self-evident" for all (Rehn), clear triggers for a hike include the conflict continuing (Wunsch) or inflation spreading from energy (Kazaks). Notably, some members, like Muller, do not require "full visibility" on second-round effects before acting.. Timing of hike: An April hike is considered "an option, but just one option" (Nagel), though many, like Villeroy, feel it is "very premature" to debate specific dates, preferring to wait for more data. ▪ DB’s outlook: Following the March meeting we changed our ECB call and now expect rates to be hiked to 2.50% this year (25bp increases in June and September). This new baseline assumes the ECB will act to manage inflation persistence risks without imposing a significant cost on growth (2.50% is at the upper range of neutral). records.text: 2 Europe Economic Weekly | 17 April 2026 Weekly view Getting cold feet about April IMF meetings are ongoing, and they always come with plenty of Central Bank speak. While the week is not over and we still have quite a few speakers in the schedule, what we heard this week reinforces our view on what the ECB will do from here. As a reminder, we pencil in rate hikes in June and July 2026, 25bp each. We still don’t rule out an April hike, especially if energy prices moved closer to the ECB’s adverse scenario again. But equally, we think the economy cannot stomach these levels of policy rates for long. Cuts are likely to follow, particularly because ECB forecasts are on the optimistic side when it comes to growth and have a lot of energy pass-through into core inflation. Hence, we have pencilled in quarterly cuts from Jun-27. We would expect a terminal rate at or below 1.5% in 2028, with risks of getting there earlier, especially if gas prices do not rise as much or as durably as our commodity team expects. Indeed, recent ECB speakers, including the hawks, have consistently sent a message that they have time to take decisions. Even Executive Board member Schnabel said this week that there is no need to impose unnecessary cost on the economy and that the ECB can afford to take time to analyse the shock. LLC Global Markets Daily: Trading Terms of Trade in FX with Risk-Neutral Expressions 16 April 2026 | 4:08PM EDT Terms of trade (TOT) has been a key driver of FX returns since the start of the war n with Iran, consistent with the typical pattern in periods of elevated commodity price volatility. But broader risk sentiment has played a nearly comparable role, leading to the underperformance of some key energy exporting currencies relative to their shifts in terms of trade (e.g., NOK, CAD) and less intuitive day-to-day correlations that have made tactical trading more challenging relative to the energy shock of 2022. Commodity price volatility relative to rates and equity market volatility appears n to be a key driver of the difference. In the current shock, shifts in volatility have been more coincident across assets than they were in 2022. Intuitively, in that scenario, FX investors can get caught wrong-footed if purely positioned around the TOT implications. If rates and equity vol pick up again alongside an increase in commodities vol, n investors can more consistently benefit from trading TOT when positioning only in high-beta energy exporters and importers. For autos, the potential combination of consumers choosing to own AVs personally longer-term, plus an increase in miles traveled enabled by the improved experience, leads us to our base case view that the long-term average for SAAR will remain relatively similar to the historical ~16 mn level. However, in a bear case scenario in the long-term where all miles traveled use AV rideshare, we estimate that US SAAR could be 3-6 mn units lower. Over the 10-year horizon, we impose a rise in the neutral rate (r*) only on the back of higher productivity growth, as informed by our replication of the Rachel and Summers model (see Results section). The net result is that changes to the policy rate in our exercise are rather limited, as by the time disinflationary forces from AI start to accumulate, higher r* compensates for that. More than a pinch of salt: We treat these results with caution when translating them into forecasts. ▪ In practice, policymakers are unlikely to cleanly distinguish between cyclical and structural forces. We expect them to update structural estimates of nominal neutral rates only with a lag. records.text: autonomous trucking could represent a c. €3 billion revenue opportunity for them by 2030, driven by a Software as a Service (SaaS) model that offers high-margin, recurring income whilst enabling customers to reduce their total cost of ownership by 15-20%. The strategy utilizes Daimler’s Fifth Generation Freightliner Cascadia, an autonomous-ready platform featuring fully redundant safety systems integrated directly into the assembly line. To further enhance its proprietary “Virtual Driver” software, Daimler acquired Algolux in 2023 for AI-based self-driving perception while maintaining a partnership with Waymo. Operational testing is currently active in New Mexico, Texas, Arizona, and Michigan, with a primary focus on the high-volume freight lane between Laredo and Dallas. Investment thesis: We are Neutral rated on Daimler. records.text: Boost to both supply and demand: There is no clear consensus on how much AI will impact economic growth. Published estimates of the GDP impact of AI have an unusually wide distribution. Several estimates are close to yearly gains of 0.1–0.8pp to GDP growth, but timeframes of these impact vary. Risk scenarios range from infinitely positive to negative growth impacts (see page 8). Leaving aside the ‘first hand’ estimates from technology leaders, many of these exercises reach markedly different conclusions despite being based on similar, apparently sound methodologies. Our results suggest that AI will lift GDP meaningfully between now and 2034. The average of our central scenario for three economies – the US, eurozone and UK – is for GDP to be 4% higher by 2034 than in a baseline in which we assume no AI shock. The projected growth arises not only from higher productivity but also from stronger demand in expectation of such productivity gains. In the US, this ‘sentiment’ channel is worth around a third of the estimated near-7% GDP lift by 2034. Stronger, hotter US economy: Of the economies we study, the US is likely to see the biggest benefits from AI. records.text: UK Economics 16 April 2026 Citi Research 2 A strong print, but an overstated one. Taken together, we believe February’s data points to an economy that is performing better than feared but not as strongly as the headline suggests. The 0.5% m/m GDP gain reflects a combination of mean reversion in volatile services components and energy-driven strength in production, neither of which provides a firm foundation for sustained momentum. Underlying growth appears positive but modest, and the balance of risks remains tilted toward renewed softness as higher energy prices and lingering weakness in manufacturing feed through. As such, while February represents a welcome improvement relative to January, the strength of the print should be treated with caution – particularly ahead of the March data, which will be more informative about whether services momentum is genuinely durable or once again distorted by volatility. records.text: 8 Modelling the AI shock is complicated by exponential improvements in AI technology and the possibility that Artificial General Intelligence will be able to further develop itself. Our analysis uses an historical approach to model AI technology, using past examples to draw parallels, producing results that are easier to interpret. The increase we expect in US productivity until 2034 is larger than in the first stages of the ICT and electricity revolutions but smaller than in the late stages of those precedents (Figure 9), thus being conservative to a certain degree, particularly compared with other estimates. As history captures diffusion of technology, we see it as the best guide to model the effects of technology on productivity and economic growth. We input past productivity shocks in a model that assumes economic agents react rationally by increasing consumption and investment. This takes into account agents’ behaviour changes in response to shocks, partly defending our framework against the so-called Lucas critique of overreliance on historical data (Lucas, 1976). That said, the unprecedented nature of AI raises the risk that our estimates vastly underestimate the GDP impact. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has pointed to AIs helping to advance AI research. records.text: Canada Economics Weekly 13 April 2026 Citi Research 2 In many ways, the spring of 2026 is feeling very similar to the spring of 2025. The BoC is keeping rates on hold for now, with near-term upside risks to inflation from a new supply shock (tariffs then, oil now). CFIB price plans have risen back above the target range (see below), suggesting that even core inflation could be somewhat stronger in the next few months. The unemployment rate is averaging around 6.7%. But demand indications remain weak and last year, weak demand eventually proved to lead the trend of slowing underlying inflation. As activity evolved softer than the BoC expected at the beginning of 2025, officials ultimately cut rates by 50bp over the September and October meetings. Our fundamental view remains that a negative output gap, consistent with the unemployment rate still in a 6.5- 7% range, will not close without accommodative rates; 3-5 year yields that matter most for mortgage rates are even a bit higher than a year ago. The next few months of data could show modestly rising employment, stronger Q1 domestic demand, and some stickiness even in core inflation. But we expect these dynamics to reverse by the summer and still expect policy rates to fall to 1.75% - 50bp worth of rate cuts, also like last year. Figure 1. While the terms of the HEI contracts vary across issuers, they generally provide an initial investment amount of about 15-20% of the borrower’s home value and use automated valuation models (AVM)/home price indices for estimating future home prices. HEI contracts offered by Point Digital Finance, Inc (PNT) typically discount the initial home value enabling investors to capture potential gains from the outset. UNSN structures the repayment amount as the sum of the initial investment and a fraction of the change in home value, while other issuers generally structure the repayment amount as a multiple of the initial investment share of home value. The repayment amount also incorporates a maximum IRR cap (commonly referred to as ‘cost limit’), which helps protect borrowers who may otherwise experience very high interest rates if they exited the HEI contracts early. records.text: The last big shock: The US ICT revolution ran from about 1980 to 2004. The borders are harder to define than for the electrification revolution: we start from the advent of the personal computer, but arguably one could start only from the early internet adoption and extend further into the 2010s to capture further developments of the digital economy. This time we focus on US data, as it was the epicentre of this technological wave, much like what we see now with AI. After filtering the data, we estimate that ICT improvements boosted US productivity growth by 20bp a year in the early stage and 80bp in the late stage. Great moderation: This so-called Great Moderation period was less eventful in terms of global shocks than the rest of the 20th century, characterised by low macroeconomic volatility and inflation convergence towards (newly created) central bank targets. Nevertheless, it encompasses both the fallout of the 1970s oil shocks, which led to the high-interest-rate environment of the early 1980s, and the early- 2000s tech bubble. During 1980–2004, US real GDP growth averaged 3.1% y/y, with a peak contraction of 1.8% y/y in 1982 – significantly shallower than the UK’s 1920s slump. This moderation certainly contributed to the strength of capital formation, which doubled in the later stage of this period. records.text: 15 Fig. 23: Models suggest that US unemployment declines following a TFP shock Sources: Bloomberg, US Department of Labor, Macrobond, BNP Paribas Concerns about the impact of AI on the labour market have been raised by headlines of layoffs in the technology sector, statements from experts in the field and microeconomic data on employment trends for certain professions (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025); but there seems to be little correlation with initial jobless claims in the US. Anecdotal bias: If AI causes a significant rise in unemployment, this would have to be visible in standard economic metrics. Relying on anecdotal evidence to draw conclusions can be problematic, as it lacks context regarding broader trends. As the ability of AI to replicate the human cognitive process is unprecedented, we do not dismiss these concerns. However, we expect limited impacts on unemployment rate for two reasons. ▪ The AI supply shock has been preceded by a demand shock. Agents have already anticipated the potential economic impact and have boosted investment in AI infrastructure, helped by a rise in equity prices. This has boosted demand for labour, and our estimations show that this effect can last for a long time (see page 18). This is the driving force behind the resilient unemployment rate in our modelling (see Figure 23). While that is our base case we would not assign certainty to that. There are paths in which the ECB looks through the shock or potentially waits for a little longer to move. Non-linear effects on the activity could be one. Gas prices behaving better, as they have so far, could be another one if they questioned the forecast for inflation in 2028. And less of a fiscal response than assumed could do the trick, too. In a way we feel the conversation has shifted at the ECB. It went from “start in April or June”, to “let’s move in June, absent surprises”, with some doves now daring to even question that move. Second, we insist on what we said above. Cuts would need to follow those hikes. And with gas prices where they are now, these cuts could come much faster than 2H27, our current base case. The market still is not pricing enough of those. Germany: energy pain vs defence gain The energy price effect will affect the real economy, too. Germany will clearly be at the forefront of that. The manufacturing sector had just found a bottom in early 2026, and fiscal stimulus could have helped to generate some upside. records.text: we prefer it to taking results from a literature review for two reasons. ▪ Historical examples illustrate the multi-year path of the TFP shock. We use this to model the timing, shape and speed of acceleration of the shock in NiGEM. ▪ As we look at TFP as a whole, historical examples capture how technology shock diffuses to other technologies, which will likely be especially important for AI. As the productivity increase from electrification revolution spilled over to other technologies, we are confident that taking the path implied by this historical example avoids underestimating the effect of diffusion. That is not to say that speed and magnitude will be the same, as current progress banks on past improvements, namely on communication technologies in the case of AI. An alternative would be to look at the literature. While there is more literature on ICT’s effect on TFP growth, there are limited numerical estimates of how electrification contributed to faster economic growth (see Figure 40). Literature suggests that late-stage ICT could have contributed to productivity growth of 0.5– 0.9pp a year. The future ain’t what it used to be: the cost of deliverable deterio- ration We sometimes oversimplify the choice between buying spec pools and rolling TBAs. In the very short term, the decision often boils down to a comparison between the carry differential and the relative cost of convexity. When the roll trades special and nominal payups approach their full even-OAS theoretical value, investors tend to lean towards TBAs—but of course, life’s not usually that cut and dry. But in the medium to longer term, there’s another cost imposed on the TBA buyer—deliverable deterioration—that is well understood but impre- cisely quantified. Clearly, its cost should be a drag on the performance of any TBA strategy that is held for a material amount of time. Empirically, that deterioration would have cost a FN 5 or 5.5 investor around 6 ticks/year since the beginning of 2023; models peg the fair value even higher. The biggest movement has occurred in UK rates, which looks at odds with the UK also seeing the biggest downgrade to growth expectations by the IMF yesterday. This could change once we get more data on the hit to growth, but for now central bank hawks are in the ascendency. Canadian CPI and PriceStats The Bank of Canada is one of the few central banks where tone has not become notably more hawkish, but that may need to change. records.text: M Idea 6 The effective tariff rate and tariff receipts The tariff rate on US imports fell to 8.5% in the February 2026 data On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court struck down the President's authority to impose tariffs under IEEPA. Section 122 tariffs will replace IEEPA tariffs in the short term, though uncertainty rises after the 150-day period when Congress would need to extend those tariffs. Replacing IEEPA with Section 122 tariffs of 15% and considering composition effects of US imports, we estimate baseline tariffs near 11%. Our estimate of "core" tariffs (ex fuels, gold and AI-related imports) remains closer to 13-14%. In our view, near-term tariffs are likely capped below 'Liberation Day' levels—at least until Section 232 and 301 investigations are complete. In the February 2026 data, the effective tariff rate is estimated at ~8.5%. Sweden The domestic picture has shifted materially since our last publication. 1Q GDP is tracking a contraction, March CPI surprised sharply to the downside on both core and headline mea- sures, and the announcement of a temporary ceasefire around 7-8 April has prompted a broad repricing lower in Riksbank hike expectations. Our economists have trimmed their 2026 GDP growth forecast to 2% (vs Riksbank's 2.2%), with the drag from higher energy prices concentrated in 2Q and 3Q. March CPI surprised sharply to the downside (see here): CPIF ex-energy fell to 1.1% oya, 0.4% below the Riks- bank and consensus expectations, marking the fifth consecutive downside surprise. Head- line CPIF printed at 1.6% oya versus our and consensus expectation of 2.2% oya and the Riksbank's 2.3% oya, dragged lower by weak food prices and a much softer-than-expected energy price increase. Core (CPIF ex-energy) is set to slide further to around 0.3% oya by July as the halving of food V AT to 6% works through, though PMI price readings flag some upside risk to near-term inflation (see here). Overall, the various measures may dampen Eurozone inflation by about 0.1pp, but quantifying the total impact and notably the timing is challenging. While we acknowledge uncertainty about the future and the possibility that AI causes unprecedented job destruction, the frameworks that come to this conclusion are often based on fixed- size supply side view of the economy, where stronger output does not spur additional demand for labour. Limited impact on monetary policy: Our results show limited impact on policy rates in the long run. By the time higher productivity starts to bring down inflation, higher r* prevents central banks from lowering policy rates meaningfully. History rhymes: Our results are consistent with the historical evidence we gathered. Neither the electrification nor the ICT revolutions caused massive job shedding; price dynamics were highly affected by cyclical conditions and central banks reacted to them. records.text: widespread displacement of labor. Stronger demand results in tighter labor markets. The unemployment rate gradully falls to 3.9% by the end of 2026 and remains there through 2027. The unemployment rate picks up to 5.5% in 2026. After rapid Fed cuts, labor markets begin to recover. The unemployment rate ends 2027 around 5%. Inflation Oil pushes headline inflation higher in 2026, but second-round effects on core are limited. Tariff pass-through ends and disinflation in rents keep services gradually decelerating. Core PCE ends 2026 at 2.7% and 2027 at 2.3%. The positive productivity shock raises supply and is disinflationary to a small degree. Core PCE falls to 2.5% in 2026 and 2.0% in 2027. The disinflation process pauses, and in 2H26 there is a step-up in inflation despite lower oil prices. Core PCE ends 2026 at 3.1% and 2027 at 2.3%. Oil pushes inflation to a higher peak than baseline, but it also falls faster in 2027. Headline and Core PCE end 2026 at 3.5% and 3.0%. Federal reserve policy The Fed responds to employment softness and disinflation with cuts. We expect 25bp cuts in September and December, to a terminal range of 3.0–3.25%. Strong growth makes the Fed stop the cutting cycle in 1H26. As the impact from tariffs fades and disinflation resumes, the supply story becomes more evident. The Fed resumes gradual cuts by year-end and continues in 2027 to a terminal range of 2.75-3.0%. The Fed remains on hold through most of 2026, then raises rates in 4Q26 as inflation rises

Financial conditions eased again this week on optimism around Middle East developments. The terminal Fed policy rate drifted down but remains more than 25bp above pre-Iran levels; this likely overstates the shift in expectations for the Fed’s (real) policy stance given that the higher terminal rate mostly reflects increases in near-dated term premia and inflation expectations. Our economists updated their economic forecast and now expect no further Fed rate cuts . Incorporating that into our yield projections doesn’t move the 10y UST forecast more than a few basis points, as we have been assuming a relatively quick reversal of any additional Fed cut from here. records.text: US Economic Perspectives17 April 2026 ab 18 Exchange rates and import prices Import prices for consumer goods have been trending up over the past nine months and on net are a little above where they were a year ago. These import prices do not include tariffs, so the effective cost of imported goods will have risen notably more than this import price index suggestsI m p o r t p r i c e s h a v e c h a n g e d l i t t l e o v e r t h e p a s t 1 2 m o n t h s , b u t o n c e w e a d d t a r i f f s t h e y a r e u p 9 % t h r o u g h N o v e m b e r . That said, the import prices themselves (i.e. ex tariffs) are not notably pushing inflation up or down. After depreciating from mid-November to mid-February the broad trade-weighted dollar has recovered much of that downward movement and is back at a level consistent with late-2023. Overall the movement in the dollar is likely to add little upward or downward pressure on import prices and inflation. Container freight costs according to Drewry are not far from their pre-pandemic level. In contrast, the Harper Petersen index continues to be very elevated. These freight costs are also generally not included in US import price statistics but the recent moves, on net, are probably not affecting broader inflation significantly. records.text: Supply-induced demand: From our analysis, the US emerges as the clear winner of the AI productivity shock, with activity rising materially compared with other economies. This broadly matches the data and narrative available for 2025. The average 0.6pp boost to productivity growth over 2025–34 and concomitant strength in business investment compound over time, leaving the GDP level almost 7% above a non-AI counterfactual in 10 years. Over our forecast horizon (2026–27), this implies a boost of about 0.4pp to GDP growth. The rapid increase in demand in the form of investment and consumption, driven by sentiment and equity price effects, results in short-term inflationary pressures, with a peak impact of 0.2pp on inflation in 2026. As productivity gains accumulate over time, we expect these pressures to subside, and inflation is likely to return to the level it would be without any shock by 2029. Thereafter, the productivity gains may exert some downward pressure on prices. For monetary policy, our models indicate a slightly tighter stance may be warranted in the near term. This is due to the cyclical position of the economy, with the demand boost contributing to higher inflation. In the longer term, faster productivity growth should dampen price pressures but also boost the neutral rate of interest (r*). records.text: Canada Economics Weekly 13 April 2026 Citi Research 3 Housing remains weak in Q1 Existing home sales fell a modest 0.1%MoM in March but declined 33% QoQ annualized in Q1 as a whole. This will weigh on Q1 GDP growth through details of residential investment. In the last few years, there have been clear patterns of weaker winter home sales even in seasonally adjusted data. This difficulty in seasonally adjusting low-activity winter months could mean a rebound of monthly sales into Q2. Stronger or stable housing data would add to other data over the next few months that we expect to indicate little need for a near-term shift in BoC policy (see above). However, if anything, somewhat higher rates could be a new headwind to activity. And ultimately, monthly fluctuations in sales may not be the best indication of actual demand trends. We think prices are a more reliable signal of demand for housing. Home prices fell again in March, down 0.4%MoM and 4.6%YoY. The ratio of home sales to new listings of homes for sale remains very low, suggesting the soft price trend will continue, at least over the next ~6 months. We think it is very unlikely that the BoC would hike rates with home prices consistently falling over the last few years. Figure 3. A new labour market: In 1982, the US unemployment rate reached 9.7%, after which it entered a downward trend as the ICT revolution unfolded. If in the case of electricity strong external factors drove up unemployment, the greater stability of the 1980s and 1990s allows for a cleaner analysis of the labour market. During the period, the unemployment rate broadly decreased, helped by accommodative monetary policy and positive risk sentiment – especially in the second half of the 1990s – spurred by the ICT revolution itself. This latter consideration is an important historical comparison. Even assuming that some technologies may replace jobs, if policy pushes to maintain a positive output gap while risk sentiment remains positive thanks to the perceived economic benefits of the new technology, the net result can still be of lower unemployment in a period of strong technology adoption. Despite this benign setting, the dot.com bubble burst in 2000, depressing equity market valuations in the tech sector for several years. Nevertheless, a timely response from the Fed helped the economy recover quite swiftly, and productivity growth was not significantly affected. records.text: eform: Gold and Strategic Minerals Mining reform is also moving forward. The National Assembly approved the mining law allowing private, foreign firms to exploit gold and strategic minerals. It also extends concession terms to thirty years (with ten-year potential extension). The law also introduces caps on royalties (up to 13% of the gross production value of the mineral and up to a 6% on companies carrying out primary mining activities). Mineral deposits remain the property of the state. US authorities have authorized limited transactions with Minerven, Venezuela state owned mining company, under US legal jurisdiction. The US has also facilitated the commercial processing of Venezuelan gold. For example, Trafigura agreed to purchase ~650-1000 kg of gold from Venezuela’s state-owned mining company Minerven under a US authorized framework (representing around $100mn). Proceeds are routed through supervised channels. Trafigura will support a gold sourcing program to improve traceability and compliance after years of illegal mining .

In scenario #2, we assume that the 3Mx3M/1Yx1Y OIS curve remains near current levels (at -15bp). Finally, in scenario #3, we assume flattening of this curve back towards -40bp, a scenario that represents growth concerns causing markets to price in more easing in the near term. records.text: most visible. As expected, we see wholesale prices (3-year high in Mar at 3.9% yoy) to be the first to get impact by elevated global commodity prices. Going ahead, we expect WPI to rise further, likely climbing north of 5%. Meanwhile, headline CPI inflation remains insulated from the cost pressures so far. We expect the pass- through in retail prices to come with a lag and expect the impact to intensify in 2H2026, following the elections in five major states in India. While the bilateral trade with the Middle East was impacted in Mar, overall trade deficit was lower – likely affected by lower shipments owing to closure of Strait of Hormuz. Moving forward, we expect trade deficit to likely inch up following the inventory adjustment and supply normalization. Week ahead In the coming week, we turn our focus to the monetary policy meetings in Indonesia and Philippines. We expect BI to keep the policy rate unchanged at 4.75%, and expect BSP to hike the rate by 25 bps to 4.50%. On the data front, we expect both Japan-style core CPI (ex-fresh food) and BoJ-style core CPI (ex-fresh food and energy) to moderate to 1.5% yoy in Mar (vs 1.6% in Feb) and 2.3% yoy (vs 2.5% yoy in Feb), respectively. Meanwhile, we expect exports to rise sharply to 10.0% yoy in Mar (vs 4.0% in Feb). The pickup mainly reflects the fading effect of LNY holidays, rising semiconductor prices and one extra working day vs last year. In Singapore, we expect core CPI inflation to rise to 1.7% yoy (vs 1.4% in Feb).

records.text: US Economic Perspectives17 April 2026 ab 8 US Economic Perspectives UBS Research Recent data and near-term forecast March PCE inflation Based on the March CPI, PPI, and import prices, we project headline PCE prices increased 0.67% in March and core PCE prices increased 0.29%. A 0.29% core PCE price increase in March is less than in the past few months, but still well above the 0.17% increase consistent with the FOMC's 2.0% target or the 0.10% increase in March last year. These monthly projections, along with small projected upward revisions to January and February, would put 12-month headline PCE price inflation at 3.49% through March — a notable uptick from 2.80% in the most recent release and 2.36% in March last year. 12-month core PCE inflation would be at 3.19% — up from 2.97% in the most recent release and 2.67% a year ago. This 3.2% core PCE price projection is notably stronger than the 2.6% core CPI inflation, as a result of slowing rents (which receive less weight in PCE prices), strong PCE financial services prices (which are adding roughly 30bp more than usual to the CPI-PCE wedge) and other weighting and source differences. One aspect to watch in the March PCE price data is the use of PPI legal services as the source data for PCE legal services prices. records.text: 30 Fig. 51: Late-stage ICT was accompanied by deregulation in US Digital investment comprises investment in computers, communication equipment, software and electrical transmission. Early stage is 1980–86 and late stage is 1994–2004. Sources: OECD, BEA, Macrobond, BNP Paribas With time, further developments like the personal computer made the technology more accessible, accelerating deployment and eventually culminating in the internet adoption. As network economies became clearer, there was development and investment to scale up these technologies. This is in line with the productivity J-curve argument – GPTs require complementary investment before fully materialising its potential to boost productivity, which at first remains constant and then suddenly accelerates (see Brynjolfsson et al., 2018). Deregulation: In the US, the 1980s and 1990s also saw a break with the command- and-control regulatory framework of the analogue era to a framework of minimal government intervention and market-driven industry. Arguably, this allowed further competition and fostered innovation (contrary to UK’s the 1882 Electric Lighting Act), boosting investment during the late stage of the ICT revolution. This highlights the key role of regulation in allowing the disruptive capacity of new technologies to spill over to the rest of the economy to unleash its full impact on productivity. Like in 2020, fiscal authorities could be forced to intervene to avoid nonlinear effects on activity that further dampen the labour market. However, this could be troublesome, as countries, such as the US, already experience some fiscal disequilibria. In this scenario, the way to extract excess profits and redistribute them as needed would probably be via taxation, which is then redistributed via subsidies or reskilling programmes. Examples from history in Japan and Sweden show similar initiatives on the back manufacturing sector automation (see Figure 31). However, tax competition among countries could make this process difficult. Diluting market power: Another option is that policymakers guide the AI revolution so that it ends up resembling electrification. In this scenario, the surplus of the technology would mostly accrue to consumers immediately, and the policy action would take place ex ante, through regulation, industrial policy or public investment. We think the AI Continent Action Plan is trying to nudge the EU in that direction. Taxes can also help align these incentives, with deductions for AI companies that enter joint ventures with EU firms for AI diffusion, promoting knowledge transfer (see Garicano, 2026). records.text: ast majority of reserves are in USDs, changes in trade patterns could warrant a reassessment of reserve allocations. The vast majority of GCC exports reflect energy priced in USDs. As a result these countries accumulate USDs in their reserves. Large USD reserves allow GCC countries (ex-Kuwait) whose currencies which are pegged to USD to defend or threaten to defend their peg. The pegs themselves remove FX risk from their main source of income and reduce friction when it comes to foreign investment. GCC do not disclose their reserve currency breakdown, but most “guestimates” place it at almost all USD. As a guideline, Hong Kong is also pegged to USD and in its latest disclosure, reported a USD reserve allocation of 79.1%. China and BRIC countries’ share of GCC ex-Kuwait trade has grown considerably whilst the U.S. has declined to 5% (Fig.XX). If GCC exports diversify from USD to FX, both the peg and reserve allocations would be misaligned with trade invoicing. We model a diversified reserve allocation to reflect these trade shares with 71% in USD. Assuming the starting point is 100% of reserves allocated to USD, a reduction to 71% could lead to selling of USD 250bn.

The St. Louis and San Francisco districts reported little change, while the Boston and New York districts reported modestly declining activity. records.text: Robotaxi deployments and market size accelerating, aided by safety and consumer adoption Global AV deployments are accelerating. We show current and planned deployments for Waymo, Uber, Lyft, Zoox, Pony AI, Baidu, WeRide, Mobileye, May Mobility, and Grab in Exhibit 11 and Exhibit 12 (we consider this a representative but not exhaustive list of deployments). We also note partnerships with Grab and Bolt exist, similar to plans from Uber and Lyft, to deploy in unspecified cities across several AV providers (e.g. WeRide, May Mobility, etc). In other words, while the productivity shock alone could cause a rise in joblessness, the associated positive sentiment (demand) shock more than offsets the negative impact on the labour market. ▪ While AI expands supply, in equilibrium, higher productivity creates more demand and leads to more job gains. While this causes sectoral shifts (some recent US data supports these trends), eventually a larger and more productive economy should feature more jobs. Empirical evidence supports our claim: Historically, positive productivity shocks have not increased joblessness. This seems to be true both in the long and short run: empirical evidence shows that even quarters after a productivity shock, the unemployment rate declines (see Trehan, 2003). Nevertheless, other external shocks might prompt corporate restructuring and an adjustment in the labour market that could lead to a jobless recovery (see Global economic impact of AI: The future is coming faster, 30 October 2023). A good historical example of this dynamic is the ICT revolution. The US unemployment rate rose at the beginning of the 1990s in response to monetary policy tightening, which lead to a shallow recession, but then it fell sharply from 7.5% to just below 4% by 2000s, all while TFP growth accelerated significantly. records.text: 17 April 2026 Fed Notes Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 2 Timeline on balance sheet changes Will Warsh endorse the ample reserves regime and adopt the consensus view that balance-sheet reduction will only occur gradually over time following regulatory changes? One prominent difference between Warsh and other candidates for Fed chair was how outspoken he was about a desire for the Fed to operate with a smaller balance sheet. Warsh argued that shrinking the Fed’s balance sheet over time could reduce inflation by decreasing the money supply and tightening broad financial conditions, thus opening the door to policy rate cuts. While there was some excitement around this topic when Warsh was first nominated, our sense is that the consensus has coalesced around a drawn -out process that first requires changes in bank regulation to reduce demand for reserves. This case has been pres ented by a number of Fed officials, including Vice Chair of Supervision Bowman, Governor Miran, and Dallas Fed President Logan, among others. Focus will be on whether Warsh confirms this more gradual pathway to balance -sheet reduction. One key related poi nt of interest will be whether Warsh endorses the Fed’s current ample reserves regime or advocates serious consideration of a return to scarce reserves. More broadly, we think Warsh could suggest a comprehensive review of the Fed’s balance sheet and implementation policies and emphasize that the process of implementing any changes could take years.
